summaries.summary: It is the first day of fall, and Pete the Cat feels blue because he likes summer better. Mom tells him to remember things he loves about autumn. Pete visits Grandma and helps bake pumpkin pies, then puts a pumpkin in his backpack. In the corn maze, Pete gets lost with friends and takes a corn cob. Grandpa helps him knit a warm scarf, and Pete saves some yarn. Pete rides on a hay wagon with his family and packs hay. With Callie, he picks apples, eats apple donuts, and puts an apple in his backpack. Pete plays football, scores a touchdown, and takes Bob’s football. At home, he rakes and jumps in leaf piles, then collects leaves. His backpack bursts with souvenirs. Pete and Mom use them to decorate the Thanksgiving table. Family and friends come, eat, laugh, and tell stories. Pete discovers that he loves many autumn things, but most of all he loves his family and friends.

On the first day of fall, Pete the Cat feels blue because he likes summer better. Mom suggests he remember what he loves about autumn. Pete visits Grandma, helps bake pumpkin pies, and puts a pumpkin in his backpack. In the corn maze, he gets lost with friends, then takes a corn cob. Grandpa teaches him to knit a cozy scarf, and Pete saves leftover yarn. Pete enjoys a bumpy hay ride with Bob, Mom, Dad, and Grandpa and packs hay. With Callie, he picks apples, eats treats, and saves an apple. After Pete scores a touchdown playing football with Bob, he borrows Bob’s football. At home, Pete rakes and jumps in leaf piles, then collects colorful leaves. His backpack bursts with souvenirs. Pete says, “I love autumn.” Mom says the souvenirs would make great Thanksgiving decorations, and Pete helps fill a basket. Family and friends gather, eat, laugh, and tell stories. Pete knows he loves his family and friends most all year long.

We are family. I promise to work hard, do what is right, go to school, read, follow the rules, and respect the game plan. I promise to run full court, show up, get back up, and let my magic shine. I promise to try new things, enjoy the happy that change can bring, smile, speak with kindness, and stay strong and humble in wins and defeats. I promise to ask for help, reach for my star, ask questions, find answers, and believe in next time and second chances. I promise to use my voice, stand up for what is right, and keep fighting when things get tough. I promise to stand tall, throw the alley-oop, and uplift others. I promise to respect elders and peers, and leave new places better than I can. I promise to stay true, keep my head up, and never give up. I promise to dream big, love bigger, be a team player, and be a winner. I promise to cross bridges, break down walls, rise with the sun, and learn from falls. I promise to be courageous, free, strive for greatness, and be me.

The speaker will go to school, read, follow rules, respect the game plan, and run full court. After falling, they will get back up and let their magic shine. They will stay open to new things, smile, speak with kindness, and remain strong and humble in wins and defeats. They will ask for help, ask questions, find answers, reach for their star, and believe in next time and second chances. They will use their voice, stand up for what is right, and keep fighting when things get tough. They will throw the alley-oop, uplift others, respect elders and peers, and leave new places better than I can. They will stay true, keep their head up, and never give up. Finally, they promise to dream big, love bigger, cross bridges, break down walls, learn from falls, and be courageous, free, and themselves.

Ordinary Mary picked blue berries from a vacant lot. She put them in a big brown bowl on Mrs. Bishop’s porch. Mrs. Bishop was happy and baked blueberry muffins. She gave plates to five people, including paper boy Billy Parker. Billy ate every crumb and then brought papers to people instead of throwing them in bushes. Each person passed kindness to five more people. Mr. Mori helped people with heavy bags. Mario helped Joseph, and Joseph gave Sahar a new bag. Sahar cheered Sophia, and Sophia called people to make them happy. Dr. Tom gave balloons to hospital patients. Peter helped Eric, and Eric invited his shy sister Dai to the park. Dai helped Louise, who gave food to Amara. Amara gave Kate a show ticket. Kate sent Mary a heart necklace. Mary’s one good deed traveled from person to person. In 16 days, love touched billions of people. The world changed because Ordinary Mary did one good deed. The story says one good deed can help make the world better.

Moana wakes under warm sand when Hey Hey lands on her. She finds the heart of Te Fiti safe in her grandmother’s shell necklace. Her boat and supplies are on a strange rocky island, and a giant fish hook carved in a rock makes her think Maui lives there. A huge Maui appears and lifts her boat. Moana tells him she is Moana of Motunui and asks him to sail with her. Maui jokes, thinks she is his fan, and writes an autograph on her oar with Hey Hey. Moana says he stole the heart of Te Fiti and must put it back. Maui shows tattoos that move and tells how he raised the sky, brought fire, slowed the sun, caught winds, and fought monsters. Then he picks up Moana and puts her in a cave. He says he will take her boat, then rolls a boulder over the entrance, leaving her in the dark.

Moana pushes out of warm sand and finds Hey Hey with a coconut on his head. She checks that the heart of Te Fiti is safe in her grandmother’s shell necklace. Her canoe and supplies are on a shore, where a rock has hundreds of fish hooks carved into it. Moana thinks Maui may live there. A huge shadow appears, and Maui lifts her canoe. Moana hides, then meets the giant tattooed demigod. Maui calls himself a hero and jokes while moving tattoos show his great deeds. Moana tells him he stole Te Fiti's heart and orders him to sail with her and return it. Maui acts as if she should thank him, but Moana refuses. He boasts about raising the sky, bringing fire, slowing the sun, capturing winds, and defeating monsters. Then Maui grabs Moana and puts her inside a cave, saying he will take her boat. He rolls a boulder across the entrance, trapping her in darkness.

I am Sam," says Sam-I-am, but the other person says, “I do not like green eggs and ham.” Sam asks if they will eat them in many places, including a house, with a mouse, in a box, with a fox, in a car, in a tree, on a train, in the dark, in the rain, with a goat, or on a boat. The person says no each time and asks Sam to let them be. Sam keeps asking and says, “Try them, try them, and you may.” At last, the person agrees: “I will try them.” They taste the green eggs and ham and say, “I do. I like them, Sam-I-am.” Now they will eat them in a boat, with a goat, in the rain, in the dark, on a train, in a car, in a tree, in a box, with a fox, in a house, with a mouse, here and there, and anywhere. They thank Sam-I-am.

Sam-I-am repeatedly asks a person to try green eggs and ham. The person says, “I do not like them,” and refuses to eat them in many places, including a house with a mouse, a box with a fox, a car, a tree, a train, the dark, the rain, with a goat, or on a boat. Sam-I-am keeps asking, but the person keeps saying no and asking Sam to let them be. At last, Sam-I-am says, “Try them, try them, and you may.” The person agrees to try them if Sam will let them be. After trying the green eggs and ham, the person says, “I like them, Sam-I-am.” The person then says they will eat them in all those places and anywhere. The person says they are so good and thanks Sam-I-am.

Winnie the Pooh wakes suddenly at night and hears a strange noise saying “War, war, war, war.” He opens his door and meets a new animal named Tigger. Tigger says he likes everything, so Pooh gives him honey, but Tigger says Tiggers do not like honey. Pooh takes him to Piglet for haycorns, but Tigger does not like those either. They visit Eeyore for thistles, but Tigger bites a bee and learns he does not like thistles. Piglet says they should ask Christopher Robin for help. At Kanga’s house, Tigger searches the cupboard and finds nothing he likes. Then he tastes Roo’s extract of malt and discovers that Tiggers like it best. Kanga kindly gives him more, and Tigger stays at her house. Afterward, he has extract of malt for breakfast, dinner, and tea, sometimes with Roo’s breakfast as medicine. Piglet tells Pooh that Tigger has been strengthened quite enough.

One night, Winnie the Pooh hears a strange “War, war, war, war” outside his door. He meets Tigger, a bouncy new animal who says Tiggers like everything, so Pooh expects him to enjoy honey. In the morning, Tigger attacks Pooh’s tablecloth, then refuses honey. Pooh takes him to Piglet for haycorns, but Tigger refuses those too. Piglet joins them to visit Eeyore, whose thistles Tigger says Tiggers like best. Tigger bites a bee in the thistles and discovers that Tiggers do not like them. The friends go to Christopher Robin and Kanga for help. Tigger searches Kanga’s cupboard but finds nothing he will eat. Then he gulps Roo’s extract of malt. He smiles and says, “So that’s what Tiggers like.” Afterward, Tigger lives at Kanga’s house and eats extract of malt for every meal, sometimes having Roo’s breakfast as medicine. Piglet thinks Tigger has been strengthened quite enough.

Most squirrels gather nuts and climb trees, but Mr. Peanuts is unusual. He cooks hot dogs on a tiny grill, plays “Moonlight Sonata” on the piano, and reads books aloud. Sometimes he feels lonely, so he writes to Cousin Squirrel and asks him to visit. After waiting and checking his mailbox every day, Mr. Peanuts gets a happy reply. He cleans his home, makes the bed, bakes a hazelnut chocolate cake, and gets ready for the visit. Cousin Squirrel arrives for breakfast, and they eat pancakes. Then they ride in a wagon, play chess, and pack a picnic. Cousin Squirrel adds crunchy peanuts to his peanut butter sandwiches, and Mr. Peanuts thinks they taste scrumptious. That night, they build a campfire and tell ghost stories about the haunted tree and the one-eyed owl. The next day, they eat ice cream. Mr. Peanuts and Cousin Squirrel have a wonderful time together. Having a friend makes everything twice as fun.

Most squirrels gather nuts and climb trees, but Mr. Peanuts is unusual. He cooks hot dogs on a tiny grill, plays “Moonlight Sonata” on the piano, and reads “A Tale of Two Cities” and “Good Night Nut” aloud. Sometimes he feels lonely, so he writes to Cousin Squirrel and invites him to visit. After waiting, Mr. Peanuts receives a reply saying Cousin Squirrel will come soon. Mr. Peanuts cleans his home, prepares a bed, bakes hazelnut chocolate cake, and gets very clean for the visit. Cousin Squirrel arrives for breakfast, and they eat pancakes. They ride in a wagon, play chess, and have a picnic with peanut butter sandwiches and crunchy peanuts. That night, they build a campfire and tell ghost stories about the haunted tree and one-eyed owl. The next day, they eat ice cream. The two unusual squirrels have a wonderful time together, and having a friend makes everything twice as fun.

Once there was a plain gray fish named Tidler. He had a big imagination and told a different tall tale every day. He said he rode a seahorse, flew with a ray, and dived with a dolphin. At school, Tidler was often late, and the other fish called his stories silly. Little Johnny Dory liked them and told them to his granny. Soon, the stories traveled from fish to fish. On Wednesday, Tidler was dreaming up his tallest story when a fishing boat caught him in a net. He escaped, but he was lost and scared in the ocean. Then he heard his own stories. Tidler followed them from anchovies to a shrimp, a whale, a herring, an eel, a lobster, a seal, a starfish, and a place. The place led him to Granny Dory. Tidler swam back to school at 3. “The story led me home again,” he said. Little Johnny Dory told it to a writer, who wrote it down.

Tidler was a plain gray fish with a big imagination who told tall tales about why he was late to school. On Monday, he said he had escaped a mermaid after finding a treasure chest in a shipwreck. On Tuesday, he said a squid captured him, but a turtle rescued him. Other fish called these stories silly, while Little Johnny Dory loved them and passed them along through many sea creatures. On Wednesday, Tidler dreamed up his tallest story and failed to see a fishing boat or its net. The fishermen threw him back into the sea. Lost among strange lights and fish, he heard his own adventures being retold. He followed the story through anchovies, a shrimp, and other sea creatures until a place led him to Granny Dory. At three o’clock, Tidler returned to school. He said the story had led him home, but some fish still called it silly. Little Johnny Dory said it was not just a story and told it to a writer friend, who wrote it down.

John says James used to be his friend, but now James is his enemy because James always wants to be the boss. James carries the flag, takes all the crayons, grabs the best digging spoon, and throws sand. When they were friends, John invited James to his birthday party, shared pretzels and an umbrella, and showed him where the horny toad lived. They even had chickenpox together. Now John thinks about poking James, hiding his crayons in the suit, and telling people James should not go to school. John goes to James’s house to say that James is his enemy and will have no one to play with. John says, “I’m not your friend anymore.” James says they are enemies. But then John asks James to roller skate. James says okay and offers John a pretzel. John says thank you.

John says James used to be his friend, but now James is his enemy because James always wants to be boss. James carries the flag, takes all the crayons, grabs the best digging spoon, and throws sand. John goes to James’s house and says he is not James’s friend anymore. James answers that they are enemies. Then John asks James to roller skate. James agrees and offers John a pretzel. John thanks him. Their angry words quickly turn into playing and sharing again.

The world is full of colors. Yellow is like a submarine, and everyone lives in a Yellow Submarine. Purple is like rain, and Purple Rain falls. Red is for 99 L balloons over Strawberry Fields on Ruby Tuesday, and a lady in red is there. Blue is for Judy Blue Eyes and blue jeans in Blue Suede Shoes. Lucy is in the Sky with Diamonds. A black dog and a black bird jam together. A White Rabbit rides a white limo to the White Room. Everybody looks Pretty in Pink in a pink Cadillac among Pink Houses. The man on the Silver Mountain rides a horse by the Light of the Silver Moon. A Green River crosses Big Green Country, where a funny frog plays a Green Tambourine. Maybe It's Not Easy Being Green. Here Comes the Sun. The rain ends, Purple Haze lifts, and the Yellow Submarine returns. The colors meet in rainbows on an orange-colored sky. Colors rock all around.

In a world full of colors, a Yellow Submarine travels around. Yellow appears in “Yellow Submarine,” while purple comes with rain and “Purple Rain.” Red fills the sky with 99 L balloons above Strawberry Fields on a Ruby Tuesday, and a lady in red can be seen. Blue is all about Judy Blue Eyes and a blue jean taking a stroll in Blue Suede Shoes. Lucy appears in the sky with diamonds. A black dog and a black bird jam together. A White Rabbit rides a white limo to the White Room. Everyone looks Pretty in Pink in a pink Cadillac moving past Pink Houses. A man on the Silver Mountain rides a horse by the Light of the Silver Moon. A Green River crosses Big Green Country, where a funny frog plays a Green Tambourine. Then Here Comes the Sun, the rain ends, and Purple Haze lifts. The Yellow Submarine is back. The colors meet in rainbows on an orange-colored sky, and all the colors rock around.

The story asks what it would be like to wake up with a wild animal’s nose. A tapir’s bendy proboscis grabs leaves and roots. A rabbit’s twitching nose smells danger. Its whiskers help it squeeze through spaces. An elephant’s trunk carries logs. It sprays water and picks up peanuts. A grizzly bear tracks food from far away before hibernation. A warthog sniffs and digs for roots. A saiga’s nose filters dust and warms icy air. A star-nosed mole finds food in the dark and underwater. A rhino uses its horn to guard babies. Its nose finds food and enemies. A giant anteater pokes for insects with its long nose. It breathes underwater through that nose. A horseshoe bat uses nose sounds and echoes to catch bugs. A hammerhead shark follows scents to find fish. These wild noses are useful. However, people do not need them to spray water, dig, catch flies, or swim underwater. Luckily, you do not have to choose. Your people nose helps you breathe, smell, and hold glasses. Best of all, it helps you look like you.

The story asks what it would be like to wake up with a wild animal’s nose instead of a human nose. A tapir’s muscular proboscis grabs leaves, while a rabbit’s twitching nose and whiskers find food and danger. An elephant’s trunk carries logs, sprays water, and picks up peanuts. A grizzly bear tracks food from far away before hibernation, and a warthog smells and digs for roots. A saiga’s nose filters dust and warms icy air. A star-nosed mole uses moving rays to feel for food underground or underwater. A rhinoceros uses its horn and sharp smell to fight, guard babies, and find food. A giant anteater sniffs out insects and breathes underwater through its nose. A beret’s horseshoe bat uses its nose to aim sounds and catch insects, while a hammerhead shark follows scents through separated nostrils. These noses would be useful, but people do not need them to spray water, dig, catch flies, or snorkel. In the end, a human nose is perfect for breathing, smelling, holding glasses, and looking like you.

One day, you wonder what it would be like to wake up with a wild animal’s nose. A tapir’s nose can bend to grab leaves. A rabbit’s nose twitches and helps it smell danger. An elephant’s trunk can carry logs, drink water, and spray a shower. A grizzly bear can smell food far away before winter. A warthog uses its nose to find roots underground. A saiga’s nose keeps out dust and warms cold air. A star-nosed mole uses its nose to feel for food in dark water and soil. A rhinoceros uses its horn and nose to guard and find food. A giant anteater smells ants and termites and breathes underwater with its nose. A beret’s horseshoe bat finds insects by listening to sounds from its nose. A hammerhead shark follows fish smells to find dinner. These noses are useful, but you do not need one to dig, spray water, or catch flies. Luckily, your people nose helps you breathe, smell, and look like you.

Finn the Frog welcomes a child to his book and says he will make lunch. He cooks famous pasta with fire-roasted tomato sauce and Italian lily pad, but the child does not like the green stuff. Finn makes his granny’s meatloaf, but the child calls it mushy. Next, Finn serves meat soaked in pond water with whipped potatoes, but the child says it is stinky. Finn learns the child wants grilled cheese, so he makes one. He forgets to flip it, and the sandwich burns. The book catches fire, but the child helps Finn put it out. Finn makes another sandwich, but the child chooses the slightly burnt one because it is a favorite. Finn names it “Totally Toasted Cheesy Pleasy” and realizes he should ask what the child likes instead of guessing. The child burps, and Finn calls it a compliment. Finn sees that mistakes are not always bad and offers hot dessert.

Finn the Frog welcomes a child to his book and says he will make lunch. An earthquake shakes the book, but Finn learns the child is simply hungry. Finn cooks Famous Freddy’s pasta, made from fire-roasted tomatoes and lily pad, but the child does not like the green stuff. Next, Finn makes his granny’s meatloaf, but the child calls it mushy. Finn then serves marinated meat with whipped potatoes, but the child says it is stinky. Finally, the child asks for grilled cheese, so Finn makes it, but he forgets to flip it and burns it. The book catches fire, and the child helps put it out. The child takes the slightly burnt sandwich because it is a favorite. Finn realizes he should have asked what the child likes and names it Totally Toasted Cheesy Pleasy. A burp compliments Finn, and he offers hot dessert.

Dory was a young blue tang fish with short-term memory loss. Her parents, Jenny and Charlie, taught her to play hide-and-seek, but she forgot the game. When she was little, Dory became separated from them and wandered the ocean looking for her family. She met Marlin, who was searching for his son Nemo. Dory helped him, and they brought Nemo home. Later, a memory led Dory to the Jewel of Morrow Bay, California. Marlin and Nemo went with her. Dory was taken to the Marine Life Institute, where she met Hank, a seven-tentacled octopus, and her old friend Destiny. Hank helped her find her parents, but they were being sent to Cleveland. Dory found her parents, who had waited years for her. Then she helped rescue Marlin and Nemo from the truck with help from Hank and her sea friends. They drove the truck into the ocean. Back on the Great Barrier Reef, Dory lived with her family and friends. She enjoyed the view with Marlin and remembered the happy moment.

Dory is a blue tang with short-term memory loss who is separated from her parents, Jenny and Charlie, as a child. Years later, she meets Marlin, helps him find Nemo, and lives with them on the Great Barrier Reef. After a memory of her family returns, Dory travels with Marlin and Nemo to the Marine Life Institute in California. She meets Hank, a seven-tentacled octopus, and friends Bailey and Destiny, but humans place her in quarantine. Dory finds her childhood home, learns her parents searched for her, and becomes lost in the Institute. With help from her friends, she reaches Marlin and Nemo, but they are sent toward Cleveland. Dory’s parents find her in the ocean, and she remembers that Marlin and Nemo need help. Dory, Hank, and their friends rescue them by driving a transport truck into the ocean. Everyone returns to the Great Barrier Reef, where Dory’s parents and friends live with her. Dory enjoys the view with Marlin and feels she will remember the moment forever.

In Santa Cecilia, Miguel Rivera lived with his big family and Mama Coco. On Dia de los Muertos, they remembered family members who had died. The Riveras had one rule: no music, because Mama Imelda’s musician husband broke her heart. But Miguel loved music and secretly learned guitar. When Abuelita destroyed his guitar, Miguel took Ernesto De La Cruz’s guitar from his tomb and strummed it. Then Miguel could see skeletons, so he crossed a marigold bridge with Dante into the Land of the Dead. Mama Imelda would not bless his dream. Miguel teamed up with Hector to find Ernesto. Ernesto welcomed Miguel, but Miguel learned that Ernesto had poisoned Hector and stolen his songs. Hector was Miguel’s real great-great-grandpa. Hector began to disappear because Coco was forgetting him. Miguel returned home with a blessing and sang “Remember Me” to Mama Coco. She remembered Hector and told the family about him. The Riveras changed their rule, and Miguel could become a musician with their support.

In Santa Cecilia, Miguel Rivera lived with his family, including Mama Coco. On Dia de los Muertos, they remembered relatives who had died. Miguel loved music, but the Riveras banned it because Mama Imelda had her heart broken by her musician husband. Miguel secretly learned guitar. When he tried to perform, Abuelita broke his guitar. Miguel found a familiar guitar in Ernesto De La Cruz’s tomb and crossed a marigold bridge with Dante to the Land of the Dead. He needed a family blessing to return home. Mama Imelda refused to bless a musician, so Miguel joined Hector, who knew Ernesto. They searched and performed together, but Miguel left Hector to find Ernesto. At Ernesto’s fiesta, Miguel sang and was discovered as a living boy. Ernesto welcomed him, but Miguel learned that Ernesto had poisoned Hector and stolen his songs. Ernesto threw them into a pit. Hector revealed he was Miguel’s great-great-grandfather and wrote “Remember Me” for Coco. Hector and Imelda gave Miguel their blessing to go home. Miguel sang “Remember Me” to Mama Coco, who remembered Hector and shared his stories. The family accepted music, so Miguel could follow his dream.

Callie and her twin brother, Charlie, have curly hair, brown eyes, a love of hot chocolate, their dog Harriet, and names that start with C. But they are not exactly alike: Callie is two minutes younger, loves the moon and talking, while Charlie is goofy, hates math, and likes jets and helicopters. As babies, Callie talked and showed love, but Charlie was quiet and did not play or say, “I love you.” Mommy learned that Charlie has autism, so making friends, showing feelings, and staying safe can be hard for him. Callie learns that Charlie shows love through actions. He smiles at her, plays holding-hands games, cares for Harriet, and helps when she gets hurt. Charlie also loves sharing his collections and piano playing. Sometimes words unlock inside him. After Callie bangs her toe, Charlie pats her back and says, “Don’t cry, Callie. I love you.” Callie is blessed to be Charlie’s sister and counts their love among her Charlie blessings every day.

Callie and her twin brother, Charlie, have always been together. They share curly hair, brown eyes, hot chocolate, their dog Harriet, and many activities, but they are not exactly the same. Callie loves the Big Dipper, the moon, and talking, while Charlie is goofy, hates math, and notices jets and helicopters. As babies, Callie showed love easily, but Charlie stayed quiet and did not play or say “I love you.” Mommy learned that Charlie has autism, which makes friendship, feelings, and safety harder for him. Callie and Mommy watch over him, even when his actions are dangerous or he seems far away. Callie learns that Charlie shows love through actions. He smiles at her, plays holding hands, cares for Harriet, shares his collections, and helps when she gets hurt. Sometimes Charlie says “I love you.” After Callie bangs her toe, he pats her back and repeats, “Don’t cry, Callie. I love you.” Callie says autism does not have Charlie and feels blessed to be his sister.

It's Christmas Eve, and Santa is coming to bring toys to girls and boys. Children try to catch him, but they chase a smaller prize: the elf. The elf says, “I'm the Elf Snatcher 3000!” and says he has style, grace, and never quits. Santa takes him to deliver gifts, while children set traps. At Emma's house, the elf dodges a tinsel net. At Jaden's house, he sees a double-sided trap and puts Jaden on his naughty list. He stops for candy canes, but Santa lowers him into a dangerous room where a bon-bon boom may happen. With one second left, he finishes the gifts, but the children zap his tushy. Next, a family grocery store has a huge food avalanche. Dinner shoots ham and gravy, then dessert. The elf and Santa tumble down a waterfall above the eggnog river, but they work together and deliver yummy. Their night is nearly done. The elf says, “Merry Christmas, everyone!”

On Christmas Eve, Santa travels through town delivering toys while children try to catch his elf, the Elf Snatcher 3000. The elf says he is stylish, graceful, and never quits. Santa takes him to Emma’s house, where he dodges a tinsel net, then to Jaden’s house, where he avoids a double-sided trap. At another house, candy canes tempt him, but he keeps working. Santa lowers him into a dangerous room with a bon-bon boom, and the elf escapes with one second left. After the elf safely brings the gifts, the children zap his tushy. His radar then leads him and Santa to a family grocery store. Inside, an avalanche of food catches them. A dinner cannon shoots ham, gravy, and dessert as they run. Santa and the elf tumble down a waterfall above the eggnog river. Working as an awesome team, they deliver yummy food and leave as their night ends. They wish everyone Merry Christmas.

On Monday morning, Detective Wilcox and Captain Griswold, MFIs, get a call from Miss Rabbit: her carrot cake is missing. They find crumbs, carrots, and frosting everywhere, but no broken door or window. Miss Rabbit says the cake disappeared while she took a catnap. The detectives question Fowler the Owl, Porcini, and Hot Dog. Each seems suspicious, but Hot Dog’s wide pawprints do not match the thief’s small, narrow footprints. Hot Dog admits he baked a cake after finding Miss Rabbit’s mess, but says he did not take her cake. The detectives use his cake and two cameras to watch for the thief. During the night, Miss Rabbit’s cake disappears again. The videos show that Miss Rabbit, wearing pajamas, whiskers, and frosting, sleepwalked and ate it. Hot Dog has baked another cake, so the party can happen. Everyone eats it, but it is crunchy because Hot Dog used dog biscuits. Porcini and Hot Dog finish every crumb.

On Monday morning, Detective Wilcox and Captain Griswold, MFIs, investigate Miss Rabbit’s missing carrot cake. They find crumbs, carrots, and frosting everywhere, but no broken entry, so they question Fowler, Porcini, and Hot Dog. Fowler says Miss Rabbit walked toward Porcini’s in pajamas and suspects Porcini. Porcini says Miss Rabbit visited him, then he walked her home; he blames Hot Dog. At Hot Dog’s house, Wilcox finds carrots and cake ingredients, but Hot Dog says he baked a replacement cake and did not steal the first one. Small footprints prove he is not the thief. The investigators use Hot Dog’s cake and cameras to watch the rabbit hole. After waiting all night, they discover Miss Rabbit sleepwalked and sleep-ate her own cake. Hot Dog still has another cake, so Miss Rabbit can keep her party. The cake is crunchy because Hot Dog used dog biscuits. Porcini and Hot Dog eat every crumb, and Hot Dog says, “Now that’s how you make a cake disappear!”

It was Monday morning when Detective Wilcox and Captain Griswold got a call: Miss Rabbit’s carrot cake was gone. They went to her hole and found crumbs, carrots, and frosting everywhere. Miss Rabbit said she had left the cake to cool, then taken a catnap. Fowler the Owl said Miss Rabbit had walked toward Porcini’s. Porcini said Miss Rabbit came to him, and Hot Dog said he had seen the mess and baked another cake. Wilcox found carrots leading to Hot Dog’s house, but small footprints showed Hot Dog was not the thief. The detectives put cameras near Miss Rabbit’s kitchen and waited. The cake disappeared again. The video showed Miss Rabbit walking, eating, and taking the cake while asleep. Miss Rabbit was sleepwalking and sleep eating. Hot Dog had baked an extra cake, so the party could happen. Everyone ate cake, but it was crunchy because it had dog biscuits. Porcini and Hot Dog ate every crumb.

After school, Little Red Chicken tells Papa that her teacher said every story has an “elephant of surprise.” Papa explains that this is really an “element of surprise,” a part that makes readers say, “Whoa!” Chicken wants to find an elephant in each story. In The Ugly Duckling, the duckling joins the swans and discovers he is an elephant. In Rapunzel, the prince climbs her hair, and Rapunzel surprises him by being an elephant. Papa says this is silly, but Chicken asks to try The Little Mermaid. The mermaid gets legs, but they are elephant legs. Then Papa tells a story about a father whose daughter loves elephants. There are no elephants in the dresser or refrigerator, but he sends her to elephant school. Chicken knows an elephant will appear at the end. Papa agrees, and Chicken says it is a great surprise. Then Papa helps her with her math homework.

After school, the little red chicken told Papa that her teacher said every story had an “elephant of surprise,” meaning an unexpected part. Papa explained that the phrase was “element of surprise,” but Chicken wanted to find an elephant in each story. In The Ugly Duckling, the ugly duckling joined the swans and discovered he was an elephant. In Rapunzel, the prince climbed her hair, but Rapunzel surprised him by being an elephant. In The Little Mermaid, the mermaid’s wish gave her elephant legs. Papa said Chicken had put an elephant in every story and decided to tell one without elephants. Chicken drew the pictures as Papa described a father whose daughter loved elephants. He found no elephants in the dresser or refrigerator, and he sent her to elephant school. At the end, Chicken realized there was an elephant in Papa’s story after all. She called it a great surprise, then asked Papa to help with her math homework.

Ricoberto moves to a new classroom from Venezuela. The children laugh because they do not understand his words. His teacher says his name and homeland softly and beautifully. When the teacher asks about summer, children talk about France, Maine, India, Spain, and South Carolina. They show shells and souvenirs. Ricoberto has empty hands. He remembers staying home, caring for his little sister, reading books, and laughing with her. His lunch is different, and his friend Nadja asks what is inside. At playtime, the climbing bars, running, and team game feel too hard, so he stands outside. Then Ricoberto shares his story. Angelina tells the class that she spent summer with her little sister, reading and telling stories. She says staying on their block felt like going everywhere. Ricoberto hears that Angelina has a name like his sister’s. The room opens wider for them. Sharing stories helps make space for them.

It's Halloween, and Pete the Cat is excited to go trick-or-treating in his superhero costume. Pete hopes nothing too spooky happens, but his dad brings flashlights, and they go outside. The wind rustles the leaves, and Pete sees something moving in a tree. It is just an owl. At a neighbor's house, Pete hears a strange sound, but it is Callie, who joins them. At the next house, Pete finds a scarecrow and meets Mrs. Gold, the crossing guard, in an awesome, spooky-but-not-too-spooky costume. Then Pete and Callie see glowing jack-o-lanterns and get one piece of candy from Pete's teacher. Something behind them is their friend Emma, "not spooky, but groovy." Pete's dad says they will visit one last house. A spooky ghost scares Pete, but it is Grandma. Pete and Callie get treats and hugs. Trick-or-treating was not too spooky after all. It was full of sweet surprises. Happy Halloween!

Long ago, a village stood beside Lake Ontario. In a great wigwam lived an invisible being whom only his sister could see. She said a woman could marry him only if she had seen him.

A poor man had three daughters. His cruel older daughters made the youngest sit by the fire, burning and scarring her. They called her “rough-face girl” and laughed at her.

The older sisters wore fine clothes and claimed they could see the invisible being, but they could not answer questions about his bow and sled runner. They went home ashamed.

Rough-face girl had only broken shells, birch bark, and old moccasins. She made clothes and walked bravely to the wigwam. She saw the invisible being in the rainbow, the Milky Way, and the beauty of earth and sky.

His sister saw her kind heart. Rough-face girl answered her questions correctly, so the sister welcomed her. The invisible being appeared and called her beautiful. After she bathed in the lake, her scars vanished and her hair grew long and glossy. They married and lived together in great gladness.

Mr. Incredible and Elastigirl are supers with three children: Violet, Dash, and Jack Jack. After supers are sued, the government makes them hide as a normal family, so they become Bob and Helen Parr. Bob secretly accepts Mirage’s mission to fight Omnijoin, a robot that learns from every attack. Patient Pig wakes up excited because today is the big basketball game. She eats breakfast and triple-knots shoes, but takes so long that she misses the bus. She walks to the playground and arrives after the game starts. Eager Eagle welcomes her, and she joins the team. During the game, Eagle calls for a pass and scores. Later, Pig passes to thoughtful threehorned Harpic, who scores, but Pig never gets a shot before the game ends. Eagle tells Pig she was amazing because she passed whenever someone was open and helped the team win. They wish they could play like each other, so they agree to help each other. Together they build a practice place with cones, boxes, baskets, and defenders. Pig practices dribbling and shooting while Eagle rebounds and passes to her. After hours, they are tired and happy. They say Pig’s plans and Eagle’s excitement helped them work harder, and they agree they could not do it without each other.

Eager Eagle hurries to a big basketball game without eating breakfast or tying his shoes. He catches the bus, runs to the court, and quickly scores many times. In the fourth quarter, he slows down because he has no energy. He tries to stop Adventurous astronaut, but he trips on his untied shoelaces, hurts his beak, and cannot finish the game.

Afterward, Eager Eagle tells Patient Pig she was amazing. He admits that scoring is fun, but he wants to be more patient and pass the ball. Patient Pig teaches him to look for an open player instead of forcing a shot. Tired but happy, they agree that even though Eager Eagle is eager and Patient Pig is patient, they are a great team when they meet in the middle.

On Day One, Akiak and her team began the 1,151-mile Iditarod race from Anchorage to Nome. Ten-year-old Akiak had led seven races but never won, and she wanted to win her last race. With Mick guiding the sled, Akiak led the dogs safely through mountains, snow, and icy trails. The team moved into first place, but deep snow hurt Akiak’s paw. Mick sent her to be flown home, yet she escaped before the plane left. Akiak followed the trail alone through a blizzard, hiding in a snowdrift until morning. She passed through Unalakleet and Shaktoolik, escaped people who tried to catch her, and found food at Koyuk and Elim. Hungry and tired, she kept chasing the team. Near Safety, Mick’s team lost the trail. Akiak showed them the right way and helped them discover that Ketchum’s team had gone the wrong way. She jumped into the sled and led Mick to Nome. After ten days, Akiak won the race, and the crowd cheered.

Akiak won the race, and the crowd cheered the courageous dog who had run alone. Mick said, “Akiak knew it. The other dogs knew it too.”

Each day, a fish swam around his bowl. On Day Four, Mr. Bubbles arrived and only bubbled. Plants, Mervin the snail, Fred the crab, a pirate ship, Roda and Clark, and Cha Cha soon crowded the bowl. Fred snapped at the fish, Mervin fainted, and everyone needed something. Roda and Clark expected babies, Mr. Bubbles got tangled, and the bowl filled with slime. The fish saw himself in a mirror and felt he did not look like himself. On Day Twelve, he shouted, “This is my bowl! I want my bowl back!” The next day, he moved to a tiny bowl of clear water. But he missed everyone and worried about them, so he cried. On Day Fourteen, he returned to the enormous tank. Mr. Bubbles, Mervin, Fred, Cha Cha, Roda, Clark, and twelve baby guppies were there. The fish learned that the mirror showed all of them together: “Twice.”

A fish records life in his bowl. At first, he swims alone, but soon Mr. Bubbles arrives, followed by plants, Mervin the snail, Fred the crab, a pirate ship, Roda and Clark, and Cha Cha. The bowl becomes crowded and messy. Fred tells the fish to stay on his side, Mr. Bubbles gets tangled, and Cha Cha asks for sunscreen. When Roda and Clark announce babies, the fish shouts, “This is my bowl! I want my bowl back!” He is moved to a tiny bowl of clear water. Although it is tiny and clear, he worries about his friends and wonders whether they miss him. After a sad night, he returns to the enormous tank. Mr. Bubbles, Mervin, Cha Cha, Fred, Roda, and Clark are happy to see him, along with twelve baby guppies. The fish realizes they are a big family. A mirror had made him think he looked different, but it actually showed everyone together.

Dragon loves to dance, but his terrible smell causes a disaster called “Smell Again.” The town’s alarms ring, people leave, and a city crew in hazmat suits cleans the streets because they think the smell is toxic waste. Mom is away, so the child must help Dragon smell nice. The child knows Dragon hates baths, so first paints his dirt stains and collects red, blue, and green art supplies. Then the child sprays Mom’s perfume, puts many cookies in Dragon’s socks, and tries skunk spray, but Dragon still stinks and looks unhappy. Dragon’s smelly toes have even bothered a neighbor. At last, Dragon shows that he wants a bath. The child learns that bath time can be fun with warm water, bubbles, splashing, and playing. Dragon takes a bath and tries scented socks. His smell is fixed, and the child promises not to use a skunk next time.

The narrator’s dragon is fun, but he smells terrible. Everyone remembers “Smell Again,” when his pungent flames filled the streets, the town’s alarms cried, “Everyone, you must get out,” and city workers in hazmat suits cleaned what they thought was toxic waste. With Mom away, the narrator must fix Dragon’s smell before another stinky disaster. A bath seems obvious, but Dragon hates bath time, so the narrator paints over his dirt, sprays him with Mom’s perfume, and puts cookies in his socks to cover his smelly toes. Nothing works, so the narrator tries skunk spray, hoping it will hide Dragon’s smell. Dragon looks dismayed and seems to prefer bath-time bubbles. The narrator finally gives him a bath and discovers that water, bubbles, splashing, and playing are fun. Dragon is also willing to try scented socks. In the end, things work out, Dragon’s funk is addressed, and the narrator promises Mom that a skunk will not be involved next time.

The story starts with “Inside, outside.” It then gives a “Slow guide” and a “quick stride.” Next come “Slip, slide,” and “tossed aside.” A “Hug” comes with “cried,” and then “Tears dried.” The next words are “Decide. Push. Goodbye.” After goodbye come “Pump, fly,” and “Wet pride.” Then there is “Run beside,” followed by “Coast, glide.” At the end, “Inside, outside” are “side by side,” and there is a “Ride.” The words come in this order: inside, outside, slow guide, quick stride, slip, slide, tossed aside, hug, cried, tears dried, decide, push, goodbye, pump, fly, wet pride, run beside, coast, glide, inside, outside, side by side, and ride. The story uses short phrases for each step. It begins inside and outside and finishes inside and outside, side by side, with a ride.

Inside, outside. A slow guide moves with a quick stride. There is a slip and a slide, and something is tossed aside. A hug is followed by a cry, and then the tears are dried. A decision is made. There is a push, and someone says goodbye. A pump sends something flying, leaving wet pride. Someone runs beside it. Then there is a coast and a glide. Inside and outside come again, side by side. Finally, there is a ride.

The events move in short steps. They begin with inside and outside, then pass through slow guide and quick stride. The slip, slide, and tossed aside lead to hug, cried, and tears dried. Decide, push, and goodbye come next. After pump and fly, wet pride appears. Run beside follows. Coast and glide come after that. The ending returns to inside, outside, side by side, and finishes with ride.

When I feel scared, I may see strange shadows in my room. I may hear creaking, ticking, and whooing noises, and these sounds can make me feel scared. I sometimes wonder if something is hiding in my bed or even under my bed. My heart goes boom, boom, boom. I shiver, and I cannot bear to look. Then I take a few deep breaths. I look for my happy things. I use my light to check my room. I look at my bed, and I look under it. I see that there is nothing hiding there. I check my bed and under my bed with my light again. I see nothing to be scared of at all. After I breathe, find my happy things, and check with my light, I can see that there is nothing to be scared of at all.

Kamala searches for superheroes in her family and community. Her mom’s hugs make Kamala feel special. Her cooking and words help Kamala believe she can do anything. Her sister Maya is someone she can count on, and her dad helps her feel brave by calling, “Run, Kamala, run!” Her grandparents stand up for what is right. Her best friends keep one another safe, and Mrs. Wilson teaches about plants, songs, and tadpoles. Mrs. Shelton is kind, while aunts and uncles help Kamala explore. Her family works hard. Aunt Chris studied at Howard University, and Kamala’s mom became a scientist. Uncle Baloo became an economist, Aunt Sarahla became a doctor, and Aunt Jimmy worked with computers. After college, Kamala becomes a lawyer and later a senator. She works with others to help children and learns that heroes are everywhere, including inside you. Heroes are kind, brave, fair, helpful, and ready to make a difference. The Hero Code asks people to promise to be their very best selves and help and protect others.

Kamala believed superheroes were everywhere, so she searched her family and community. Her mother made her feel special with hugs, cooking, and encouragement. Her sister Maya was someone she could count on, while her dad helped her feel brave. Her grandparents stood up for what was right: her grandmother spoke for hurt women and taught health, and her grandfather helped make India free. Kamala’s best friends kept one another safe, and Mrs. Wilson taught her about the world and dreams. Mrs. Shelton showed kindness, while aunts and uncles helped her explore. Kamala’s family worked hard: her mother became a scientist, and other relatives became an economist, doctor, or computer worker. After college, Kamala became a lawyer and senator, working with others to help children. She learned that heroes are ordinary people who are kind, brave, fair, helpful, and curious. The Hero Code asks people to make others feel special, protect those in need, work hard, and be their very best selves.

It was Christmas Eve, and the house was quiet. The children slept in their beds, dreaming of sugar plums, while Mama and the narrator rested. Then a loud clatter woke the narrator. He ran to the window and saw Saint Nicholas in a tiny sleigh with eight reindeer: Dasher, Dancer, Prancer, Vixen, Comet, Cupid, Donder, and Blitzen. They flew up to the roof with a sleigh full of toys. Saint Nicholas came down the chimney. He wore fur and carried a bag of toys. He had a round belly, rosy cheeks, a pipe, and a happy laugh. He winked, so the narrator knew there was nothing to fear. Saint Nicholas filled all the stockings. Then he went back up the chimney, jumped into his sleigh, and flew away with his reindeer. As he left, he called, “Merry Christmas to all and to all a good night.”

They fell out while he played soccer, so everyone teased him and sang about Arthur and his girlfriend. On Valentine’s Day, Sue Ellen found a card signed Arthur, and everyone laughed because they thought Arthur loved her. Arthur felt embarrassed and went to his tree house. Arthur saw erased letters: f, r, and a. He guessed Francine. At the movie, Francine smiled. Arthur asked her to close her eyes and count to 10. She asked if she could open them.

Hi, how are you? I'm okay. I like to try a lot of different things. I'm not great at all of them, but I enjoy them just the same. I'm an okay skipper. I'm an okay climber. I'm an okay marshmallow roaster. I'm an okay tightrope walker. I'm an okay left fielder. I'm an okay right fielder. I'm an okay diver. I'm an okay hider. I'm an okay pumper. I'm an okay sledder. I'm an okay kite flyer. I'm an okay tug-of-war player. I'm an okay sharer. I'm an okay headstander. I'm an okay pancake flipper. I'm an okay fisher. I'm an okay swimmer. I'm an okay lightning bug catcher. One day, I'll grow up to be really excellent at something. I don't know what it is yet, but I sure am having fun figuring it out.

The speaker says, “Hi, how are you?” and answers, “I’m okay.” They like to try a lot of different things. They are not great at all of them, but they enjoy them just the same. They are an okay skipper, an okay climber, an okay marshmallow roaster, an okay tightrope walker, an okay left fielder, an okay right fielder, an okay diver, an okay hider, an okay pumper, an okay sledder, an okay kite flyer, an okay tug-of-war player, an okay sharer, an okay headstander, an okay pancake flipper, an okay fisher, an okay swimmer, and an okay lightning bug catcher. One day, they will grow up to be really excellent at something. They do not know what it is yet, but they are having fun figuring it out.

Once there was a busy triangle. It held up roofs, supported bridges, made music, caught wind for sailboats, and became pie and sandwich slices. Its favorite job was slipping into place when people put hands on hips, so it heard the latest news and told friends.

One day, it wanted more sides and angles. The Shape Shifter changed it into a quadrilateral. It did new jobs, especially being book pages that taught it stories for friends. Soon it wanted more again. It became a pentagon, then a hexagon, and then many more shapes. The pentagon heard secrets but could not tell friends. The hexagon loved a beehive, but friends felt ignored.

At last, the many-sided shape rolled down a hill, crashed into fences and trees, and felt dizzy, lonely, and sad. It asked to be a triangle again. The Shape Shifter changed it back. The triangle was happy, did its old jobs, heard the latest news, and told friends. Its friends were glad it was back.

Orion is afraid of many things, but the dark frightens him most. Mom says he has a big imagination, yet bedtime still feels terrible. One night, Orion tells the dark to go away. The dark comes inside his room! Orion introduces himself, and the dark says, “Let’s go on an adventure.” They explore dark places in the house, such as the closet, under the bed, the basement, and down the drain. Orion discovers that some dark places are fun. Then they hear strange sounds outside. Together, they find the sounds, and nothing is frightening. Orion still feels scared of the darkest place, so they travel up into the night sky. There, he learns that the dark can be fun, interesting, and magical. The dark becomes his friend. At sunrise, the dark begins to fade. Orion says goodbye and asks if it will return. The dark promises, “I’ll never be far away.” From that night on, it never is.

My name is Orion, and I am afraid of many things, especially the dark. One night, after trying to make the dark go away, I shouted at it. The dark came into my room and introduced itself. It told Orion to stop being afraid and invited him on an adventure. Together, they explored dark places in the house, such as the closet, under the bed, the drain, and the basement. The places were more fun than frightening. Then they searched for scary sounds outside and discovered that the sounds were not scary. Orion still felt afraid, so the dark took him into the night sky, where the dark was darkest. Orion learned that the dark could be fun, interesting, magical, and his friend. At sunrise, the dark began to fade. Orion said goodbye and asked it to return. The dark promised, “I'll never be far away,” and was never far away from then on.

Donald feels sad because summer and fall are over and winter is cold. He remembers fun times with Mickey: riding in the glove balloon, camping, hiking, fishing, planting vegetables, riding bikes, and jumping in leaves with Pluto. Mickey says winter has special fun too. He takes Donald in the toon plane to see snowy mountains and trees. They fly high, but they get cold and almost run out of gas. They get home safely. Daisy gives them hot chocolate, but Donald still thinks winter is not for him. The next day, the friends go skating at Star Lake. Donald slips and spins, but Goofy puts a pillow under him, so he falls on it instead of on his bottom. Donald keeps skating and soon has fun. He wants to build a snowman, go snowshoeing, and go skiing. Winter passes quickly. When spring comes, Donald feels sad because winter is over and he had so much fun.

Donald feels sad because summer and fall are over, and he thinks winter has no fun things to do. Mickey takes him in the toon plane to see snow-covered mountains and trees. Donald likes the beautiful view, but the cold makes both friends shiver, and they nearly run out of gas. They get home and drink hot chocolate, but Donald still doubts winter can be fun. The next day, Donald and his friends go skating at Star Lake. Donald slips and spins, but Goofy puts a pillow under him, so he does not fall hard. Donald keeps skating and soon becomes good at it. He is having fun. Then Daisy names more winter activities: building a snowman, snowshoeing, and skiing. Donald wants to do them all, and winter passes quickly. When spring comes, Donald feels sad because winter is over. He had fun doing many winter activities.

Lily tells Dad she needs a new bike, but Dad explains that a need is something people have to have, while a want is something they would like. They decide to spend money only on needs. Lily’s old raincoat is too small, so Dad helps her find an affordable coat that will keep her dry. She learns that dentist visits are needs, but bowling, mini golf, and ice cream are wants; they choose a free park and a healthy snack instead. At the grocery store, Lily helps identify milk, vegetables, and toilet paper as needs, but Dad explains that root beer is a want. At the hospital, Lily names doctors and medicine as needs, while Mom says televisions are wants because patients can get better without them. Dad then explains that wants can be bought after needs are paid for. They plan to ride bikes to the park tomorrow and buy ice cream, although Lily jokes that her stomach thinks it is a need.

Lily wants a new bike because Dad asks her to watch less TV and play outside. Dad explains that a need is something people have to have. Exercise is a need, but Lily can ride her old bike. Her old raincoat is too small, so Dad helps her find one on sale. Lily goes to the dentist, even though she says her teeth have fallen out. Dad says bowling, mini golf, and ice cream are wants, not needs. They play at the free park and get a healthy snack. At the grocery store, Lily helps choose milk, vegetables, and toilet paper. Dad says root beer is a want, so they skip it. At the hospital, Lily learns that doctors and medicine are needs, but TV is not. Dad says they can buy ice cream after buying what they need. Tomorrow, Lily and Dad will ride bikes to the park. Lily says her stomach thinks ice cream is a need.

In November, the leaves change color, and family and friends gather because Thanksgiving is near. The child flies to visit cousins, helps clean and cook, and finds an apron at the general store. With family, the child visits a pumpkin patch, makes pies with Grandma, and creates a turkey placemat. The child looks at old pictures, builds a puzzle with Big Brother, and hikes through a park. During the celebration, the family watches a parade and football, gives canned food to people, and talks with Dad by phone. Everyone prepares the kitchen, sets the table, and cooks together. Guests arrive, eat full plates of food, and receive hugs. The child repeats, “I am thankful. My heart grows. Love fills me from head to toes.” At the end, family and friends are together, and Thanksgiving is here.

Edward Bear bumps downstairs behind Christopher Robin. Christopher Robin asks for a story about Winnie-the-Pooh, a bear who lives in the forest under the name of Sanders. One day, Pooh hears bees buzzing in an oak tree and climbs up for honey. He falls through the branches into a gorse bush, then goes to Christopher Robin for help. Christopher Robin gives him a blue balloon. Pooh gets muddy and floats beside the tree, pretending to be a small black cloud. The bees remain suspicious while Christopher Robin walks with an umbrella and Pooh sings a cloud song. Pooh decides they are the wrong bees and asks Christopher Robin to shoot the balloon. The first shot misses, but the second pops it, and Pooh floats down. His arms stay raised for more than a week because they are stiff from holding the string. Christopher Robin remembers other adventures, but Pooh does not remember them well, so he likes hearing the stories again. Christopher Robin carries Pooh away, and Pooh bumps up the stairs behind him.

Bumpity bump! Little Blue Truck and Toad drove home through thunder, lightning, and heavy rain. Their warm garage was a welcome sight, so they went inside and shut the door. Soon, Goat, Hen, Goose, Cow, Duck, and Pig asked to come in because they were wet, cold, or frightened. Little Blue said, “There’s room for you and you and you,” and everyone gathered around. Inside, they were warm and dry while the rain helped thirsty plants grow. The friends listened to the storm. Duck called thunder a noisy racket, and Goat and Pig said it was not scary. After a while, the clouds moved away and the night became still. Cow said it was time to go home, so Blue gave everyone a bedtime ride. He said good night to each friend under the moon and stars. Blue and Toad drove home together. Toad went to bed, and Little Blue Truck fell asleep.

On December 5, 1959, twenty-year-old Steve comes home from a swim meet and finds his father struggling to breathe. He runs for an ambulance, but Dad dies before help arrives. During shiva, Steve is angry and avoids his family’s grief until Mom gives him a box from Dad’s closet. It contains a letter and Steve’s childhood treasures. Dad apologizes, explains he wanted to prepare Steve for adulthood, and says he loved him deeply. A Brooklyn Dodgers ticket brings Steve a happy memory and recalls Dad’s advice to stay close to family, faith, and friendship.

In 1948, eight-year-old Steve lives for baseball and hopes to attend the Dodgers’ opening day. Dad explains Jackie Robinson’s importance, the team’s progress, and discrimination against Black people. Steve also hears that Pete Reiser is injured and Jackie must lose weight. At school, Steve and Senna discuss baseball, but Steve’s pranks, fights, missing homework, and hallway stickball lead them to push Miss Malakin over a hedge. Steve receives a ten-day suspension and loses opening day.

Steve is twenty and wants to be a doctor, but he often argues with his father. One day, Dad cannot breathe, and Steve runs for an ambulance. Dad dies, and the family sits shiva. Mom gives Steve a box from Dad’s closet. Inside is a letter and an old Brooklyn Dodgers ticket. Dad’s letter says he loved Steve and saved his boyhood treasures. The story goes back to 1948, when eight-year-old Steve loves the Dodgers. Dad tells him about Jackie Robinson, who plays with white teammates, and about unfair laws that separate Black and white people. Steve also hears that Pete Reiser is hurt and Jackie must lose weight. At school, Steve plays tricks, misses homework, fights, and plays stickball indoors. His teacher, Miss Malakin, plans a home visit. Steve and Senna push her over a hedge. Steve is suspended for ten days and cannot go to the Dodgers’ opening day.

On Monday, Mrs. Fibonacci says almost everything can be a math problem. On Tuesday, the child starts seeing math everywhere: time, shirts, food, classmates, pizza, school subjects, money, and even family words. The child feels worried and becomes a “math zombie.” At school, Rebecca brings 24 cupcakes for 24 children, but wants Mrs. Fibonacci to have one too. The child says, “I’m allergic to cupcakes,” so everyone gets a cupcake and no fractions are needed. At home, more confusing problems appear. The child goes to bed and dreams of being trapped in a room covered with problems. With one piece of chalk, the child breaks it in half, puts the halves together, and makes a hole. The child escapes and breaks the math curse. On Wednesday morning, the child adds the time and knows the answer is 7:41. Life seems great until Mr. Newton says almost everything can be a science experiment.

Long ago, Te Fiti's heart was stolen, and darkness spread. Monsters stalked the waters, so people stayed on their island and forgot how their ancestors sailed. Years later, Moana was born with the sea in her spirit. The ocean chose her to restore Te Fiti's heart. She crossed the reef and found the demigod Maui. Together, they entered Lalitai, battled a giant crab, and got Maui's magical fishhook. On their journey to Te Fiti, Maui taught Moana wayfinding, and she helped him control his powers. At the mother island, they met the fire monster Takea. Maui fought, but Moana saw deeper and sang to Take Ah. With her heart returned, Take Ha became Te Fiti again. Darkness became light, and the islands grew green and bright. Te Fiti welcomed Moana and her people to sail again. Moana returned home, taught her people wayfinding, and led them to explore the seas as proud, free voyagers.

Rossy shouted “Land ahoy!” while looking out to sea with her telescope. A chunk of ice broke away, carrying them out to sea. Gasper feared the deep water and did not know how to return, but Rossy reminded him they were brave explorers. They tried using their flippers to row and asked a snow petrel for directions. When the current pushed them away, Antarctic silverfish pushed the iceberg, and a blue whale smashed through blocking ice. They headed toward land, but the iceberg began melting. The animals helped them move faster, yet the ice disappeared too quickly. Rossy told Gasper they would have to swim and encouraged him as the others cheered, “Gasper! Gasper! Gasper!” Gasper jumped into the cold water and followed Rossy, using his flippers. They reached home safely. Rossy praised him for getting them through their most dangerous adventure. Gasper felt proud but said he could not have done it without his trusty first mate.

“Land ahoy!” Rossy and Gasper are penguins exploring at sea when a piece of ice breaks, leaving them on an iceberg. Gasper is afraid to swim, but Rossy reminds him that they are brave explorers. They try to find land by climbing, jumping, and rowing with their flippers. A snow petrel shows them the way, but the current pushes them the wrong way. An Antarctic silverfish pushes the iceberg, but it becomes stuck, and a blue whale breaks the ice blocking them. On the way home, the iceberg starts melting, so they must swim. Rossy encourages Gasper, while the animals cheer for him. Gasper jumps into the cold water and follows Rossy, using his flippers. They reach home safely and return to their families. Rossy says Gasper got them through their most dangerous adventure. Gasper feels proud, but says he could not have done it without his trusty first mate.

Dusty Crop Hopper was a famous racing plane who wanted only to race. During practice, his engine was damaged, and Dottie warned him that flying too fast could make him crash. While friends searched for parts, Dusty went to Piston Peak National Park to train as a firefighter. Maru gave him pontoons, and Blade taught him to scoop water and drop fire retardant. Dusty made mistakes, including wasting retardant and nearly being pulled over a waterfall. He told Blade his engine was damaged and that he might never race or fight fires. Blade told him not to give up because he could save lives. When fire threatened Fusel Lodge, Dusty helped rescue guests and saved two RVs on a burning bridge. His warning light flashed, but he kept flying; then his engine failed, and he crashed. Maru built him a new engine from spare parts. Dusty woke up, earned his firefighter certification, and became a hero both as a racer and a lifesaving firefighter.

Harris goes out. He asks George, “Will you be good?” George says yes. He hopes he will be good. In the kitchen, George sees a cake, Cat, and some lovely soil. He loves cake, playing with Cat, and digging soil, so he eats the whole cake and ruins the place. When Harris comes back, George thinks, “I said I’d be good.” He also thinks, “I hoped I’d be good, but I wasn’t.” George says, “I’m sorry.” He offers Harris his favorite toy. Harris thanks him. He asks George to go for a nice walk. Outside, George sees a cake, but he goes straight past it. He sees lovely soil, but he does not dig. He does not even try to chase Cat. Cat is surprised. Something smells very interesting. It is a rubbish bin. George likes rubbish more than anything. What will George do?

Yunhai moves from Korea to America and feels nervous when classmates tease her Korean name, so she tells them she has not chosen an American name. At home, her mother says Yunhai is beautiful and means she is different in a good way. At school, classmates make a jar of possible names, while Yunhai shares her Korean name stamp with Joey. Her grandmother’s letter reminds her that, despite the distance between Korea and America, she will always be her Yunhai. After Mr. Kim and Joey say her name correctly, Yunhai decides she likes her own name best. She writes Yunhai in English and Korean on the chalkboard and explains that it means grace. The class practices saying it. Joey returns the name jar, which he had taken so Yunhai would keep her name, and Yunhai keeps the suggested names as souvenirs. Joey then shows her his Korean stamp. It says Chinu, meaning friend, and he smiles at her.

Yunhai moved from Korea to America and started at a new school. She missed her grandmother and kept a red pouch with a wooden name stamp. On the bus and at school, children had trouble saying Yunhai, so she thought about choosing an American name. Her mother said Yunhai was beautiful. At school, her classmates put many names in a jar for her. Yunhai thanked them, but she still felt unsure. She showed Joey her stamp, and he said it was beautiful. After reading a letter from Grandma, Yunhai decided she liked her own name best. She told the class that Yunhai means grace, and everyone practiced saying it. Joey had taken the name jar because he wanted Yunhai to keep her own name. He brought it back and asked for a Korean nickname. Joey showed her his Korean nickname: Chinu, which means friend. Yunhai and Chinu smiled.

Farmer Bailey loved fall. One day, his truck hit a man in the road. The man was alive but scared, and Farmer Bailey took him home. Mrs. Bailey made him comfortable, and Katie watched him. A doctor found a bump on his head and said he had lost his memory. The stranger wore rough leather clothes and did not understand words. He learned to use a pitchfork, never got tired, and liked the Bailey family. He also liked rabbits and watched geese fly south. The stranger stayed for weeks. He saw red and orange trees in the north, but the Bailey farm’s trees were still green. He thought the green was wrong. He pulled off a leaf and blew on it. Then he left in tears. The air became cold, and the green leaves changed color. Every fall, the Bailey trees turn bright colors one night. Frost on the windows says, “See you next fall.”

Nate the Great is on vacation with his dog, Sludge, when Claude asks for help. Claude lost his grocery list. Nate learns some foods on it: salt, milk, butter, flour, sugar, tuna fish, eggs, and baking powder. Nate and Sludge follow streets and use a map, but they do not find the list. The wind blows the map toward Rosamond’s house. Rosamond has found a paper and thinks it is a recipe for cat pancakes. Annie’s dog, Fang, also holds a paper, but it is Nate’s map. Nate makes Sludge bark, and Fang drops the paper. Nate gets it, but learns it is only his map. Then Nate makes pancakes and has an idea. Rosamond’s cat pancake recipe has all the foods from Claude’s list. Nate tells her, and she gives him the paper. Nate returns the list to Claude. Claude comes late. The case is solved, and Nate finishes his vacation.

In France, a selfish prince turned away an old beggar woman who offered a red rose during a storm. She revealed she was an enchantress, changed him into the Beast, turned his subjects into household objects, and made villagers forget the castle. A music box maker named Maurice found the castle, took a white rose for Belle, and became the Beast’s prisoner. Belle came to rescue her father and took his place. At the castle, Lumiere, Cogsworth, Mrs. Pots, Chip, and other servants hoped Belle and the Beast would fall in love before the rose’s last petal fell. Belle helped the injured Beast, and they shared books, meals, play, and a dance. The Beast gave her a magic mirror so she could save Maurice. When villagers attacked, the Beast was badly hurt. Belle told him she loved him just as the last petal fell. The curse lifted, and everyone became human. The prince and Belle celebrated, opened a schoolroom, and began a happy life together.

The Color Monster wakes up feeling confused because his emotions are all jumbled up. A friend tells him to separate his feelings and put each one in its own jar, then helps him understand them. Happiness is yellow, and it makes him laugh, jump, dance, play, and share. Sadness is lonely and blue; it makes him hide, be alone, and cry. Anger burns red like fire and can make life seem unfair, but being nice can make it disappear. Fear hides like a mouse, making him feel tiny and unable to face gray shadows, but help can guide him. Calm is quiet and green. It helps him breathe slowly and deeply and feel at peace. After each feeling is placed in the right jar, the Color Monster can rest, and he feels much better. Then his friend notices something new: he looks different and asks how he feels now.

Thelma felt sad because she wished to be a unicorn, even though her best friend, Otis, told her, “You’re perfect as you are.” When she found a carrot, she tied it to her nose and pretended to be a unicorn. A truck nearly hit her, spilling pink paint and glitter over her. People thought she was a real unicorn, so Thelma became famous and enjoyed being a superstar. Soon, however, fans chased her everywhere, screamed, cried, laughed, and demanded autographs. Some people were mean, too. One dark night, Thelma admitted, “I thought that I’d feel great, but all I feel is lonely.” She cleaned off the sparkles, threw away her horn, and walked past the crowd. Nobody noticed her. Under their favorite tree, Otis asked about her trip. Thelma said she would rather be herself. She told Otis that everyone is special and should keep being who they are.

Minli learns that the king’s page, torn from the Book of Fortune, is the borrowed line she seeks. Its words change with each situation, and that night they say, “you only lose what you cling to.” The king realizes his family treasured the page because of an ancestor’s greed, but clinging to it is the true loss. He gives it to Minli, believing it should return to the book. Outside the City of Bright Moonlight, Dragon visits the stone lions and tells them his story. The lions explain that the Old Man of the Moon once gave them a red string of destiny to protect the city from a growing crack. They never used it because the king restored harmony, so the male lion gives the string to Dragon. The next morning, Minli and Dragon meet in the forest and discover they each have a possible borrowed line: the page and the red string. They decide to ask the Old Man of the Moon which one is real.

Minli showed the king the line she needed. The king revealed a glowing page torn from the Book of Fortune. In moonlight, its words said, “You only lose what you cling to.” The king understood that his family had held the page too tightly, so he gave it to Minli. Outside the city, Dragon went to the guardian lion statues because he missed Minli. The lions told him that a dragon had once destroyed the magistrate’s palace and that the city had nearly cracked during bad times. The Old Man of the Moon had given them a red string of destiny to hold the city together. When peace returned, they kept it unused. The male lion gave the red string to Dragon, who called it the borrowed line. The next morning, Minli escaped the city with the page and found Dragon. They discovered they each had a possible borrowed line and decided to ask the Old Man of the Moon.

Gerald was a tall giraffe with a long, slim neck, crooked knees, and thin legs. He was good at standing still and eating tree shoots, but he could not run without buckling. At the yearly jungle dance in Africa, the animals danced beautifully. Gerald tried to join them, but they laughed and said, “Giraffes can't dance.” Gerald felt useless and sadly walked away. In a little clearing, he looked at the moon. A cricket told him that different creatures may need different songs. The cricket played his violin, and Gerald listened to the grass, trees, and branches in the breeze. Soon Gerald’s hoofs shuffled, his neck swayed, and his tail swished. He threw his legs sideways, did a backward somersault, and leapt into the air. “I am dancing!” he cried. The other animals came and watched in amazement. They called him the best dancer and asked how he learned. Gerald bowed and said, “We all can dance when we find music that we love.”

Luca and Alberto are sea monsters. They are friends. In the beautiful seaside town of Portorosso, they build and ride a scooter and have an amazing, thrilling time together. Julia is a human girl, not a sea monster. She stands up for her friends and protects them from a bully named Aircolay. Luca learns to ride a bicycle. It is not easy at first, but his friends cheer him on. Julia points to a train headed to her school and tells Luca that he can go to school too. When Alberto is trapped, Luca is ready to rescue him. When Julia gets hurt, Luca and Alberto go back for her. Together, the three friends make a great team and become the Portorosso Cup champions. Friends may part ways and not see each other often, but they will be friends forever. Luca can always count on his friends.

Three little bears face a spooky old tree. One bear carries a light, one carries a stick, and one carries a rope. They dare to go into the tree. Next, they find a twisty old stair and dare to climb it. Inside, one bear has a light, one has a stick, and one has the shivers. The bears find a giant key. They also find a moving wall. They go through the wall and enter a spooky old hall. There they meet Great Sleeping Bear. Now one bear has a light, and two have the shivers. The bears dare to go over Great Sleeping Bear because they have already entered the tree, climbed the stair, gone through the wall, and reached the hall. Afterward, they have no light, stick, or rope, and all three have the shivers. To escape, they go up a ladder, through the floor, down a slide, and out a door. The three little bears run fast and get home safe at last.

One day, Danny visits a museum and wishes he could play with a dinosaur. A dinosaur appears and lets Danny ride on his back. They travel through town, where the dinosaur is mistaken for a car, helps a lady with her bundles, climbs carefully, watches a ball game, and says he can swim. He avoids eating grass marked “Please keep off.” They eat ice cream and visit the zoo, but everyone watches the dinosaur instead of the animals. Danny’s friends ask for rides, and the dinosaur gives them a fast trip around the block. The children teach him to shake hands and roll over, then play hide-and-seek. He cannot find them, but they find him each time he hides until they pretend not to find him. The dinosaur wins. When it gets late, he says goodbye and returns to the museum because he is needed there. Danny goes home alone after their wonderful day, though he cannot keep a pet so large.

It is Christmas Eve at the dollhouse. Pandy is excited and leaves a Christmas pickle for Santa Kitty, because he loves pickles. Figgy the elf calls from the North Pole and asks Gabby for help. Gabby takes Pandy, and Baby Box uses a magical cardboard kitty sleigh to fly them there. At Santa Kitty’s workshop, the friends work together. Pandy makes a scuba kitty, Figgy makes a robot, and Gabby makes a doll. They box and bow the toys, then load the last gifts into Santa Kitty’s sleigh. Santa Kitty thanks them and recognizes Pandy. He invites Gabby and Pandy to ride with him and the reindeer kitties, led by Candy Cane, to deliver presents to the dollhouse. They toss gifts from the sleigh, and the presents float down. Santa Kitty gives Pandy and Gabby a Christmas pickle. Then snow begins to fall, and Pandy remembers that Christmas is full of magic and surprises. Santa Kitty wishes everyone a perfect night.

One Easter morning, Pete the Cat cannot find his Easter basket. He follows a trail of colorful jelly beans to Callie’s house, where they find candy eggs. Pete and Callie follow the trail to Alligator’s house, then follow marshmallow chicks to Gus’s house. Gus joins the search, and the friends follow lollipops to Turtle’s house. Turtle joins them, and they follow chocolate bunnies to a colorful little house in the garden. The Easter Bunny opens the door and admits he has Pete’s basket because he never gets one of his own and borrowed it. Pete smiles, hugs him, and says, “That’s okay. I understand.” Pete puts some candy in an empty basket and asks Callie, Alligator, Gus, and Turtle to add candy from their baskets. They fill it with treats and give it to the Easter Bunny. He is happy and eats a jelly bean. The friends promise to make him a basket every year. Sharing is the sweetest gift of all.

From his first day of school, Lance Cottonwood was a student. He learned to be a leaf, move in the wind, and turn yellow. But his final test was falling from his tree to the grass. Lance was afraid to fall. His neighbor Doug was an evergreen, so Doug could stay on his branch all winter. Lance was a cottonwood, and cottonwoods lose their leaves in Autumn. One by one, the other leaves let go. Lance made excuses and stayed in the tree. The leaves called him a scaredy leaf. Lance tried to stay all winter like Doug, but he was the only leaf left. His teacher said, “It’s okay to be scared. I’m here to help you.” Lance told her about gutters, windshields, and the dog’s spot. Then he saw children playing in leaf piles and collecting leaves. He felt better. Lance took a deep breath, let go, and floated gently to the pile. He passed his test. “You did it, Lance! The gang’s all here!”

Days with Mommy are always full of fun, laughter, and play. In the morning, she counts down from ten while the child gets ready and searches for a teddy. While shopping, Mommy carries many bags and lifts the child when the walk home is too long. In the park, she helps a ladybird stuck on its back. When the roundabout makes the child fall and cry, Mommy kisses and rubs the hurt until it feels better. They bake together, make a mess, and create a delicious cake. Mommy also fixes broken toys. They hang colorful washing, play football, and fly with bedsheets as capes. When the child is hungry and grumpy, Mommy makes dinner for the child and teddy. At bath time, they splash and laugh, then Mommy wraps the child in a towel. At bedtime, she makes the child comfortable, gives a kiss, and sings a tune as the child falls asleep. Mommy makes each day special, and the child looks forward to tomorrow because Mommy is always the light of my day.
