In Monterey Bay, Kermit, a selfish, greedy old crab, lived alone in a rock castle and filled his cave with useless objects. After chasing a glittering tin can, he was grabbed by a dog and nearly buried, but a boy rescued him and returned him to the sea. Kermit wanted to reward the boy with a bicycle, yet he had no money. He tried to help the boy catch a fish, but the fish dragged him into the deep ocean. Kermit escaped a monstrous blue shark by hiding in an old chest, where he discovered gold coins. For three months, he carried two coins at a time to his cave, replacing his rubbish with treasure. When he could not find the boy, a pelican learned that the boy lived with his family in a small, three-room red shack beside the train track. The pelican carried Kermit there, and Kermit dropped the gold down the chimney. The family used it to buy a TV, toys, and bicycles, and saved the rest in a savings account.

In Monterey Bay, Kermit was an old crab who lived alone in a rock castle. He was mean and greedy because food was scarce, so he collected everything and filled his cave. One day, a shiny tin can tricked him onto the shore. A dog grabbed him and dug a hole, but a boy saved Kermit and put him back in the sea. Kermit wanted to thank the boy, so he tried to catch him a big fish. The fish pulled Kermit far into the ocean. Kermit hid in an old chest from a shark and found gold inside. For three months, he carried two gold coins at a time to his cave. A friendly pelican helped him find the boy’s home, a small red house beside the train track. Kermit and the pelican dropped the coins down the chimney. The boy’s family used the gold for a TV, toys, bikes, and savings. Kermit gave away his treasure to thank the boy.

Cars help people travel on busy roads, and they come in many sizes and shapes. A driver starts the car and follows traffic lights, road markings, and signs. The steering wheel turns the car left or right, mirrors show other traffic, and pedals stop or speed up the car. Cars need care, so people check oil, pump tires, fill the tank with fuel, wash the car, and use wipers to clear the windscreen. A convertible can have its top down. A four-wheel drive has thick tires for rough ground, while racing cars go fast. Police cars use sirens and flashing beacon lights to chase criminals or help at crashes. Limousines carry movie stars, presidents, and queens, and people can ride in taxis. Too many cars can cause a traffic jam, but clear roads make a country journey pleasant. A picnic is packed, safety belts are buckled, and the journey begins. The engine powers the car, wheels move it, hand brakes keep it still, and the boot stores baggage.

Flounder called to Ariel, “Wait for me!” Flounder asked whether there might be sharks in there, but Ariel told him, “Don’t be such a guppy.” Ariel saw something wonderful and asked what it was. Neither friend knew, so they decided to ask. Suddenly, Flounder shouted, “Shark!” A shark caught Flounder, and Ariel said, “Shark, you caught him!” Flounder was relieved and danced. Ariel told him not to worry because the shark was just a big bully. Flounder wished he were more like Ariel because she was not afraid of anything. He said she loved excitement and adventures and always wanted to know everything. Ariel agreed that adventures were exciting. Then she whispered, “Shh. Look, Flounder.” They looked at a shape. Flounder said Ariel was the best singer under the sea. Ariel thanked him and said he was the best at being her friend. Flounder said he loved the mermaid being part of his world. Ariel said she loved being part of his, too.

Chairs at school are not happy. Children sit on them, sit hard, smell their feet, rock back, drag them, swing them, and ride them like bikes. Food gets smeared on them, and sometimes people let out a yucky fart. The chairs say, “No, it’s not much fun being a chair.” One night, the chairs gather in the classroom and go on strike. They write letters asking for respect and kindness. In the morning, the children cannot find their chairs. They stand all day, and some fall when they forget. Soon, standing is not fun, even though they can do their schoolwork. The children write letters back. They say they are sorry and promise not to rock on the chairs or fart. They say chairs help them rest, feel comfortable, and focus while learning math, studying the planets, and doing art. The chairs miss the children, so they return. The children are kind and keep their promise.

Things change when a unicorn moves into town. The goat feels less cool because the unicorn rides faster, makes it rain cupcakes, wins the talent show with prancing, and turns things into gold. The goat shows a quarter magic trick, but the unicorn’s magic is greater, so the goat thinks the unicorn is a showoff and wonders how anyone can be friends with him. The goat smells goat cheese pizza and explains that goats have cheese. The unicorn tastes it and loves it, but can eat only glitter and rainbows because of his sensitive stomach. The goat envies the unicorn’s horn, while the unicorn admires the goat’s cloven hooves, which help him stand on steep hills and climb mountains. They discover their differences can help them: the unicorn’s horn is bad for soccer, but the goat’s horns may be perfect. The unicorn suggests they become an unstoppable team. They choose to play at the park, and the goat realizes they could be friends.

Jack the cat builds a dry, cozy, perfect nest to attract a chicken whose egg can become an omelette. A chicken lays a small egg, but a duck pushes her out and lays a medium-sized egg. Then a goose pushes out the duck and lays a large egg. The birds fight over the nest and refuse to leave, even when Jack calls “Fire!”, “Flood!”, and “Wolf!” Jack tells them about an empty, better nest nearby, so they flap away. He arranges the three eggs for breakfast, lunch, and dinner. The eggs hatch, so Jack cannot make omelettes. A baby chick, duck, and goose call Jack “Mama,” “Ma,” or “Memo.” The chick cries “Try me!”, the duck cries “Feed me!”, and the goose cries “Play!” Jack hides, but the babies find him and return him to the nest. They are cold and tired, so Jack cares for them. He puts them in the nest and climbs in too. As the babies sleep, Jack realizes it truly is the perfect nest.

Lilo and Stitch were excited because it was Pet Day at school, and Nani reminded Stitch to be on his best behavior. At school, children presented many pets, but none looked like Stitch. While Stitch examined the class frog, Mr. Fibs, the frog escaped, and Stitch chased him into a science room. Instead of returning to class, Stitch made a stink bomb, sending everyone outside. He followed the crowd to the cafeteria, where Mr. Fibs caused a food fight by jumping onto a tray. Stitch kept chasing him through the school, stopping to explore rooms. Then he remembered Nani’s words and hurried to find the frog. In the gym, Stitch dodged rubber balls and caught Mr. Fibs. He returned just in time for Lilo’s presentation. Lilo introduced Stitch as her best friend and part of her Ohana, which means family. After school, Nani heard Stitch had behaved well, so she offered ice cream. Stitch agreed that it was the best Pet Day ever.

Lilo and Stitch were excited. It was Pet Day at school. All the kids brought pets to class. Nani told Lilo to hurry because she would be late. Stitch nodded and went with Lilo. At school, pets were big, small, fluffy, or scaly, but none looked like Stitch. The class pet was a frog named Mr. Fibs. Stitch chased Mr. Fibs when he hopped away. The chase took Stitch through classrooms and halls. In a science room, Stitch made a stink bomb, and everyone ran out. In the cafeteria, Stitch missed Mr. Fibs, and the frog spilled food everywhere. Stitch followed him from room to room. He stopped to look at interesting things, but remembered Nani’s words about best behavior. At last, Stitch caught Mr. Fibs in the gymnasium and hurried back to Lilo’s class. Lilo introduced Stitch as her pet, best friend, and part of her Ohana, which means family. After school, Lilo said Stitch was on his best behavior. Nani said this called for ice cream. It was the best Pet Day ever.

On November 4 in Harlem, New York, the Baths welcomed Patricia. She copied her brother and believed, “Anything boys can do, girls can do too.” A chemistry set sparked her interest in science. Her parents taught her that everyone was equal and that education was the key to success. Although nearby high schools excluded Black children, Patricia traveled by train and finished high school in three years. She attended college and medical school, where unfair rules did not stop her. While studying eyes, she discovered that Black patients were blind twice as often as white patients. She planned to make eye care a public priority, taught students, and started the first eye-doctor training program led by a woman. In Europe, she studied lasers and invented a laser probe that helped patients see. She also created a place whose motto said healthy vision was everyone’s right, rich or poor, Black or white. Patricia, known as Dr. Bath, cared more about helping people than fame. Readers should stay focused, push forward, and not listen when others say they cannot help the world.

People call many princes Prince Charming because lazy bards and minstrels leave out heroes’ names in songs about rescues and adventures. In fact, Charming is an adjective, not a name. Prince Gustav hates this title, and he is fearless but has no idea how to use a sword. One day in Stormhogen, Rosilda Stiffenkrauss and her 11 children saw a hungry troll eating their beets. Rosilda ordered it to leave and threatened it with a shovel, so the troll agreed. Gustav then charged in, mistook beet juice for blood from an eaten child, and attacked the troll. The troll knocked Gustav around, but Rosilda hit it with her shovel and sent it back to the forest. Gustav blamed the troll and worried about the children, although they were safe. Rosilda explained the truth and demanded payment for the ruined garden. When she called him Prince Charming and asked why he had not used a ladder to rescue Rapunzel, Gustav angrily said his name was Gustav and complained about the song-spitter.

Danny Day has lived every day twice since he was born, so his 11 and a half calendar years feel like 23 years to him. On the first, “discard day,” he can fake being sick, play video games, and do dangerous stunts because everything resets when he wakes up, except his memory. He once ate 17 candy bars, drove his parents’ car, did donuts in a church parking lot, and broke his leg testing a bed-sheet parachute. On the second, “sticky day,” normal life and consequences remain, so Danny goes to school on time, does chores, and avoids trouble. The double days can also be a curse, because a difficult event, such as moving behind a truck from Houston to Idaho, lasts twice as long. As a child, Danny’s parents thought he was insane because he remembered events they did not, but Dr. Donaldson helped him and convinced them he was not insane. Danny does not know why this happens. He suspects his February 22nd birth at 2:22 a.m. may matter, but he has no proof. He is Danny Day, and he lives every day twice.

"Prince Charming" is not one person’s name. Bards used it for many princes and left out their real names. Prince Liam fought a monster, Prince Duncan woke a princess because dwarves told him to, Prince Gustav tried to rescue Rapunzel, and Prince Frederick danced with Cinderella. They all disliked being called Prince Charming. In Stormhogen, a hungry troll came into Rosilda Stiffenkrauss’s beet garden. Rosilda took her shovel and told it to leave. The troll dropped the beets and started away. Then Prince Gustav charged in and fought it because he thought the red beet juice was blood from children. The troll knocked Gustav down and broke parts of the farm. Rosilda hit the troll with her shovel, so it left. Rosilda told Gustav the children were safe and asked him to pay for the damage. Gustav said his name was Gustav, not Charming, and promised the royal treasurer would send money. Rosilda then asked why he had not used a ladder to rescue Rapunzel, making him angry.

My name is Danny Day. Danny lives every day twice. The first time is a discard day. At night, the day resets, but Danny remembers it. He can fake being sick, play video games, do pranks, eat candy, and try wild stunts. He broke his leg jumping from a garage roof, but the injury disappeared when the day reset. The second time is the sticky day. Then everything stays, so Danny goes to school, does chores, and behaves carefully. Sometimes living a day twice is hard. Danny must spend four days traveling behind a moving truck from Houston to Idaho. When Danny was little, his parents thought he was insane because he remembered things they did not. Dr. Donaldson helped Danny and his parents. Danny does not know why this happens. He thinks his birthday, February 22nd at 2:22 a.m., may be a clue. Danny knows only that he lives every day twice.

Hannah loved gorillas. She read books, watched them on television, and drew pictures, but she had never seen a real gorilla. Her father was always busy with work, so they never went to the zoo together. Before her birthday, Hannah asked for a gorilla. In the night, a small toy gorilla appeared. Hannah threw it aside, but it came alive and asked her to go to the zoo. Wearing her father’s hat and coat, the gorilla carried Hannah through the trees. The zoo was closed, but they climbed over the wall and visited the gorillas, orangutang, and chimpanzee. Hannah thought the orangutang and chimpanzee were beautiful but sad. Then they went to the cinema, ate, and danced on the lawn. The gorilla took Hannah home and promised to see her tomorrow. In the morning, Hannah saw the toy gorilla and smiled. She told her father about the night. He wished her a happy birthday and asked if she wanted to go to the zoo. Hannah was very happy.

Aladdin, Jasmine, Rajah, and Abu saw the biggest parade of the year. They saw a snake charmer, a fire-eater, peacocks, silk-covered elephants, and tigers led by a young girl. Jasmine showed Aladdin that Rajah could balance fruit and slice it with his claws. Aladdin told Abu and Rajah to walk with the parade while he and Jasmine returned to the palace. Abu came back upset and showed that parade folks had taken Rajah. Jasmine and Aladdin chased the parade on the magic carpet, but it crashed into clotheslines. Abu stayed to help Carpet while Jasmine and Aladdin crossed rooftops and jumped down near the parade. Jasmine hugged Rajah before he was put in a cage, but the parade master said Rajah was his tiger because he wore no royal collar. Jasmine proved Rajah was hers by tossing him a melon, which he sliced. The parade master apologized and made Jasmine and Rajah stars of a special show. Jasmine was glad to have her friend back.

Nikolai wanted to be a good person, but he did not know the answers to three questions: When is the best time to act? Who is most important? What is the right thing to do? His friends gave different answers, so he went to Leo the turtle, who lived in the mountains. Leo was digging a garden, and Nikolai helped him. During a storm, Nikolai heard a panda crying for help. A fallen tree had injured her leg, so he carried her to Leo’s cottage and made a bamboo splint. He then found her cold, frightened baby in the forest, brought it inside, and reunited it with its mother. The next morning, the panda thanked Nikolai, and his friends arrived. Nikolai still felt he lacked the answers. Leo explained that the most important time was now, the most important person was the one with him, and the most important thing was doing good for that person. These were the answers to Nikolai’s questions.

Buzz had a pet fly named Fly Guy. One day, they were bored, so Fly Guy said, “Funzie!” and they went for a walk. They played chase and cooled off in a fountain. They met a girl named Liz, whose pet fly, Fly Girl, was chasing her. Buzz explained that flies could be pets, and Liz showed that Fly Girl could do tricks too. Buzz said Fly Guy ate gross stuff, while Liz said Fly Girl ate grosser stuff. Buzz said Fly Guy could say his name, and Liz said Fly Girl could say her name. Then they took the flies to the swings. Fly Guy and Fly Girl sat together and talked in Fly-talk. They told each other, “You are nice,” and then said, “Wuzzle, what’s up?” which meant, “Let’s be friends.” Buzz and Liz said goodbye. Buzz then said, “Funzie!” because playing with Liz, Fly Guy, and Fly Girl had been fun.

Buzz had a pet fly named Fly Guy. Fly Guy could say, “Buzz.” One day, Buzz and Fly Guy were bored, so Fly Guy said, “Funzie!” They went for a walk, played chase, and cooled off in a fountain. They saw Liz, a girl running with her pet fly, Fly Girl. Buzz said flies could be pets, and Liz said Fly Girl was her pet. Buzz and Liz told each other about their flies. Fly Guy ate gross stuff, Fly Girl ate grosser stuff, and both flies could say their people’s names. Buzz asked Liz to play on the swings. Fly Guy and Fly Girl sat side by side and talked in Fly-talk. Fly Guy said, “Was little wuzzle,” meaning, “You are nice.” Fly Girl said, “Was a wuzzy,” meaning, “You are nice too.” Then they said, “Wuzzle, what’s up?” meaning, “Let’s be friends.” Buzz and Liz said, “See you soon.” Buzz said, “Funzie! That was fun.”

Jack could not sleep after a strange trip with his sister, Annie. They had found a tree house in Frog Creek Woods, used its books and wishes to visit the time of dinosaurs, and come home. Before dawn, Annie wanted to find the tree house’s magic person, so Jack went with her. In the tree house, Annie wished to visit a castle. The tree house spun, and they arrived in a misty land. They crossed a drawbridge and entered a feast, but guards caught them and put them in a dungeon. Annie used her flashlight like a magic wand, and the guards ran away. Jack found a secret passage, but he fell into the moat. The children escaped the water, and a knight on a black horse carried them back to the tree house. Annie wished them home. Jack found a blue bookmark with the same M as the gold medallion. He learned that the book owner and the medallion’s owner were the same person.

Dave lived nearly 200 years ago and was a slave. He used dirt and water from the river to make heavy clay. He carried and mixed the clay, then threw it onto his spinning potter's wheel. Dave kicked the wheel fast. He pressed the clay with his hands and made a jar. He pinched the clay to make ridges. The jar grew very large, but its heavy walls could fall. Dave made long clay coils and put them around the jar to make it strong. He smoothed the sides with wet fingers. The jar held grain, salted meat, and memories. While it dried, Dave made a brown glaze from wood ash and sand. Before the jar hardened, he wrote on it with a stick: "I wonder where is all my relation friendship to all and every nation." Dave wrote to let us know that he was here.

Two friends see an animal and argue about whether it is a duck or a rabbit. One friend says it has a bill, will eat bread, makes “Quack!” sounds, flies, and drinks water. The other says it has ears, will eat a carrot, makes “Step, step, step, step, step” sounds, hops, and cools its ears in the grass. They watch it move through the swamp, and one friend uses binoculars, but still cannot agree. They call to the animal as “ducky-ducky” and “cute little rabbit,” which scares it away. Afterward, each friend blames the other. Then one admits the animal may have been a rabbit, while the other starts thinking it was a duck. They stop arguing and ask what to do next. When they look again, they see another animal. One calls it an anteater, but the other says it is a brachios seros.

Mr. Watson and Mrs. Watson live with their pig, Mercy, at 54 Dearoo Drive. They hear about a movie called When Pigs Fly at the Beu drive-in. The movie has bottomless buckets of popcorn with real butter. Mercy loves butter, so the Watsons take Mercy, Baby Lincoln, Eugina, Stella, and Frank to the movies. At the Beu, Mercy smells butter and jumps out of the car. She eats a child’s buttery popcorn and then runs from people. She eats popcorn from many cars. People scream, laugh, and chase her. Animal control officer Francine Pallet follows with a net. Officer Tomalo comes to help. Leroy Ninker tries to use his lasso. A fire truck comes too. Firemen Ned and Lorenzo stop Mercy by offering toast with a great deal of butter. The Watsons find Mercy, and everyone eats toast together. They do not see the movie, but Mrs. Watson says it is a happy, inspirational love story.

It was summer, and a boy had a tree house, baseball, and his best friend, Stanley. Then Jeremy Ross moved next door to Stanley. The boy did not like Jeremy because Jeremy struck him out, laughed, and had a trampoline party without him. He made an enemy list and put it in his tree house. His dad made secret Enemy Pie and said the boy must spend a day with Jeremy and be nice to him. The boy went to Jeremy’s house. They rode bikes, played on the trampoline, threw water balloons, ate lunch, and played at the boy’s house. Jeremy taught him to throw a boomerang, and the boy let Jeremy into the tree house. They played games and ate macaroni and cheese. At dinner, Dad served Enemy Pie. The boy warned Jeremy not to eat it, but Dad ate it too. The pie was delicious. Jeremy invited the boy to play again. The boy lost his enemy and gained a friend, but he still did not know how to make Enemy Pie.

Derek, a longtime newspaper worker, sorts old photographs for disposal and finds a 1962 picture of Lucia Rennicks’s murder in Candlewood Park. In the background, a black-clad figure seems to stare at him. He later finds a 1973 murder photograph from the same place, showing the identical figure, so he believes the Candlewood Park strangler has appeared at both crimes. Derek decides to report the evidence, but sees that young photographer Nick is working in the park. Thinking Nick is in danger, Derek races there. His car crashes into a lorry and is destroyed by a passing train before he can help. Meanwhile, Nick searches the wooded slope for landscape photographs. He finds the frightening figure, but discovers it is a rusted Boer War statue that vandals left there years ago. Nick turns and looks back over the empty playground after discovering it was the statue. Then a hand grips the back of his neck with the strength of iron.

Derek works at a newspaper and sorts old photographs in a filing room. He finds a 1962 photograph of Lucia Rennicks, a schoolgirl murdered in Candlewood Park. In the background, he sees a tall figure dressed in black, watching the police and the camera. Derek does not remember seeing it before. When he finds a 1973 photograph of another unsolved murder in the same place, the same figure is there again. Derek thinks the two murders may be linked and worries the figure is the killer. He decides to tell the police, but sees in the diary that young photographer Nick is alone in Candlewood Park. Derek rushes to save him, but his car crashes and bursts into flames. In the park, Nick finds the black figure: it is an old, rusted Boer War statue. Then, as Nick turns away, a hand grabs his neck with an iron grip.

Pete was a perfectly predictable, practical, uncomplicated Pig until a stormy night brought Pickles, a wet escaped elephant, into his house. When a clown asked whether Pete had seen her, Pete hid her under the couch, but Pickles left behind a dandelion. The next day, Pete found her chained inside a circus tent and freed her. He disguised Pickles and took her home, though her snoring and large changes to his yard did not please him. Pickles planned adventures, including diving near Niagara Falls, sledding on the Matterhorn, visiting Tahiti, and traveling through Venice. Pete became upset by his new, complicated life and told Pickles to leave. Then a broken pipe flooded the house. Pete reached the last open window, but Pickles could not climb out. He stayed with her through the night, sharing every breath until firemen found them. The exhausted friends slept together, then awoke to pick blueberries on Pluto’s dandelion moons while Pete sang Italian love songs.

A year after the devious Fox took their gingerbread boy, the lonely old woman and lonely old man baked a Gingerbread Girl with candies and licorice hair. While she baked, she heard them remember that her brother should not have run away or trusted the Fox, so she decided things would be different. She escaped from the oven and ran along his path, singing, “I’ll run and I’ll run with a leap and a twirl. You can’t catch me, I’m the Gingerbread Girl.” Farmers, a pig, an artist, a cow and calf, a dog walker with three dogs, and schoolchildren and teachers chased her, but she outran them all. At the same river, the Fox promised to carry her safely, then tried to eat her. She moved from his tail to his back and head, tied his snout with licorice hair, and rode him toward the crowd. She brought the Fox home, secured him, and helped bake more gingerbread. The happy house was never lonely again. Later, she taught the Fox manners with gingerbread crumbs, and they rode together while she sang that she had outfoxed the Fox.

At the bookstore down the street, friends gathered for fun and listened as a storyteller began reading about the Gingerbread Man. The Gingerbread Man popped off the page and ran away, saying, “Run, run, as fast as you can!” He said the children could never catch him because he was too fast, especially with help from the boy who never grew. The children tried a clever trap, but he said they needed a magic spell and a wizard. They made more traps, yet the world's greatest detective saw through one, and Robin Hood helped the Gingerbread Man escape another. A large spring trap caught nothing because his friends helped him get away, and it broke. Perhaps the boy with magic beans and his cow helped him, while Alice and the Mad Hatter guided him through the shelves. He found no trap and celebrated another victory, but he noticed the children looked sad. Although he was free, he wanted their smiles and laughter, so he returned to give the tale a happily ever after. He called, “Run, run, as fast as you can. Can you catch me? I'm the Gingerbread Man.”

A little old man and a little old woman make a Gingerbread Man, shaping his body, adding raisin features, and baking him. He jumps from the oven and runs away, calling, “Run, run, fast as you can. You can't catch me. I'm the Gingerbread Man.” The old couple chase him, but he refuses to return because he would rather run than be their snack. He escapes a butcher, a black-and-white cow, and a muddy old sow, repeating his boast and adding each one to his list. Then he meets a fox. The tricky fox pretends not to hear, so the Gingerbread Man comes closer and speaks loudly. When the fox grabs him, the Gingerbread Man is gone in a snap, snick, lap, and lick. The old couple, butcher, cow, and sow stand and stare sadly at the fox, who has not left a single crumb for anyone.

It was cold outside, so Maddie and his mother made gingerbread inside. They followed a cookbook recipe, but Maddie peeked in the oven before eight minutes had passed. A Gingerbread Baby jumped out and shouted, “I am the Gingerbread Baby, fresh from the pan. If you want me, catch me if you can!” He escaped from Maddie’s parents, the cat, dog, goats, Martha, Madeline, and a mama pig. While he ran, Maddie made a second gingerbread boy and waited the full eight minutes without peeking. The Gingerbread Baby escaped villagers and a fox, then hid in the milk-and-cheese man’s can, but his singing gave him away. Everyone chased him, so he followed a familiar smell into the woods and found a candy-covered gingerbread house. He ran inside, and the crowd found only crumbs. When they returned, Maddie’s parents told him they had not caught the Gingerbread Baby. Maddie held the house he had made. Only he heard the Gingerbread Baby say, “I’m the little Gingerbread Baby, lucky as can be, to be living in the house that Maddie made for me.”

The students in Mrs. Brisbane’s class love caring for Humphrey, and A.J. takes him home for the weekend. At A.J.’s house, the Thomases keep the television and radio loudly playing all the time, so Humphrey cannot sleep. He escapes his cage, crawls behind the TV, and pulls out its plug. The family thinks the TV is broken and begins arguing, but then Mr. Thomas remembers fun weekends without television. The family plays cards, tells stories, and spends time together quietly. The next day, Garth visits to help A.J. care for Humphrey because he cannot have Humphrey at his house. A.J. and Garth clean the cage, build a maze, and play games with the other children. When Mr. Thomas discovers the unplugged TV, he turns it on, then agrees with Mrs. Thomas to leave it unplugged. Humphrey finally enjoys peace and quiet and falls asleep.

The kids in Mrs. Brisbane's class love caring for Humphrey, and A.J. takes him home for the weekend. At A.J.'s house, the TV and radio are always loud, so Humphrey cannot sleep. He has a big idea: he escapes his cage and unplugs the TV. The family thinks the TV is broken. Without it, they tell stories, play cards and games, and go outside. Then Garth Tugwell visits to help A.J. care for Humphrey. The boys clean the cage, build a maze, and play Crazy Eights with the other children. Later, Mr. Thomas finds the TV unplugged and turns it on. Mrs. Thomas sees the children happily playing outside, so she asks to keep it unplugged. Mr. Thomas agrees and unplugs it again. The house becomes quiet, and Humphrey says, “No, no, no,” when Mr. Thomas asks if he minds peace and quiet. Then Humphrey falls asleep.

After racing practice, Lightning McQueen wanted to rest, but Mater asked him to go tractor tipping. Mater honked at sleeping tractors, and Frank the Combine chased them. Lightning and Mater escaped, but Mater broke Frank’s fence and left tire tracks in wet asphalt. Doc was unhappy, so Mater repaired the road while Lightning practiced. Doc then told Mater to fix the fence. Mater fell asleep, and the tractors escaped and wandered into town. They made a mess of the new road, so Mater and Lightning worked all night to repair it and round up the tractors. By race day, the road was smooth, and cars came from all over. Mater brought the tractors to watch Lightning race. Lightning quickly took the lead and won. He thanked Mater for helping him practice by pulling Bessie. Then Lightning and Mater led the tractors back to Frank with a shiny trophy.

Pie is a humble pie who likes to help best friend Jake, a cake. Jake is good at school, sports, and parties, while Pie works quietly in the background. For a science project, Mr. Barryman lets them choose partners. Jake is busy and does not come to work, so Pie feels worried and overwhelmed. When Jake arrives, Pie says, “I need help. I cannot do the project alone.” Jake says he is sorry and agrees Pie is right. They work together all night, and their project becomes a success. Mr. Barryman praises their teamwork, and both friends get to shine. Pie learns that being humble does not mean staying unseen or letting others walk all over Pie. Pie can ask for help, speak up, and take credit for Pie’s work. Jake learns that being excellent also means helping friends when they need him. Pie is still humble, but now Pie is proud and ready to fly.

Chicken saw that Scarecrow wanted a walking stick instead of his hat, so she found Badger, who wanted ribbon instead of his stick. Crow wanted wool instead of ribbon, Sheep wanted glasses instead of wool, and Owl wanted a blanket instead of glasses. Donkey wanted long feathers instead of his blanket because flies bothered him. Chicken quickly pulled three feathers from herself and tied them to Donkey’s tail. He gave her his blanket, and Chicken swapped it with Owl for his old glasses. She took the glasses to Sheep for wool, the wool to Crow for ribbon, the ribbon to Badger for his walking stick, and the stick to Scarecrow for his battered old hat. Scarecrow could rest his tired arms on the stick. Chicken filled the hat with fresh, sweet-smelling straw. Duck admired the new nest, but Chicken said she would not swap it for anything.

Tommy is five and loves water, his mom, and especially his older brother, Now. Now is brave, wise, and skilled at many things, but he tells Tommy that lying is not cool. When Tommy lies about his teddy bear, Now does not believe him when Tommy truly loses his treasure-box key. Now explains that lies hurt feelings, damage relationships, and cause people to lose trust. Tommy feels sorry, and he learns from Now’s honesty when Now admits making a messy cereal catapult and cleans it up. Now teaches Tommy a secret T sign to remind him to tell the truth. Later, Tommy uses it when Mom asks whether he brushed his teeth. He tells the truth, brushes them, and feels proud. At a playground, Tommy finds a boy’s shining-eyed dino and returns it instead of keeping it. The boy and his mom praise him, and Tommy thanks Now for teaching him to stay true. Now hugs him and says honesty is Tommy’s superpower before they plan to build a Lego tower.

Tommy is five and loves water, his mom, and his older brother, Now. Tommy thinks Now is brave, wise, and cool. One day, Tommy lies about losing his teddy bear. Then he really loses the key to his treasure box, but Now does not believe him. Now says that lies make people lose trust. Tommy feels sorry because his joke hurt Now’s feelings. Later, Now makes a spoon catapult and honestly tells Mum about the kitchen mess. He cleans it up, and Mum says honesty is impressive. Now teaches Tommy that truth helps people trust you and that lies can hurt relationships. He shows Tommy a secret T sign. Tommy uses it to tell Mum he did not brush his teeth, then brushes them. At the playground, Tommy finds a shiny-eyed dino. He returns it to a boy instead of keeping it. The boy and his mom praise Tommy. Now hugs him and says honesty is his superpower.

Sarah does not want to go to school because it is her first day. Her mother says the bus will arrive in five minutes and tells her to meet her at the front door. Sarah wishes Benny could come because she is scared, and Benny the Brave appears as a member of Team Super Crew. Sarah explains that she fears the faraway school, a teacher with gigantic teeth and a long, slimy tail, a squirmy, squishy lunch, and having nobody to play with. Benny says it is okay to feel scared and asks, “What if” she loves adventures, has a pet turtle like Benny, finds her favorite cheese sandwich and a big chocolate chip cookie, or is not the only new student? At school, Sarah introduces herself to Penny, who is also new. Sarah asks what if she is brave and can do anything. Benny tells her she is brave and has that power inside her whenever she needs it. Sarah goes to her mother, wondering if the power has always been there.

“Cozy up, Little Critters,” the song says, asking them to settle down, curl up, and listen close. The coyotes sing along while the tumbleweeds roll in the night. A solid glow shines as the wind starts to blow. The Little Critters are told to lay still. The cowboy lullaby and the cowgirl’s sweet kiss will put them to sleep on a long night like this. The full moon is still bright, but the Little Critters will settle down, close their eyes, and dream. The lullaby repeats, “Sweet dreams, Little Critters. Sweet dreams.” It is getting late, and it is time to tuck them in. The song says, “You close your eyes,” while the lullaby continues. The cowboy lullaby and the cowgirl’s sweet kiss are sung again. Even though the full moon still shines, sleep time comes, and sweet dreams come to the cowboys.

Many years ago, Gagira the Panther found a lost man cub in the jungle of India. He took Mowgli to a wolf family. Rama and the mother wolf raised him with the wolf cubs. Mowgli loved the jungle. Gagira watched because danger was near. A snake nearly caught Mowgli. Gagira saved him. Shere Khan, a fierce tiger, wanted to kill Mowgli. Because of this, Rama agreed Mowgli must go to the man village. Mowgli ran away, but Gagira followed. Baloo the bear found Mowgli. He sang about the bare necessities. Then monkeys took Mowgli to King Louie. King Louie wanted the secret of man's fire. Baloo's disguise caused a chase. The temple fell down. Shere Khan attacked Mowgli. Baloo held his tail. Lightning set a tree on fire. Mowgli used a burning branch to scare Shere Khan away. Later, Mowgli saw a girl from the man village. He helped her carry water home. He found where he belonged, and Gagira and Baloo went home.

In London, Pongo the Dalmatian lives with songwriter Roger. Roger spends hours at his piano, and Pongo wants them both to have companions. One day, Pongo pulls Roger into a pond beside Anita and her Dalmatian, Pita. Roger and Anita marry, and they move with Pongo and Pita to a new home. Their cook, Nanny, cares for them. Pita has fifteen puppies, but Cruella De Vil wants to buy them for fur coats. Roger refuses. Later, two crooks kidnap the puppies. Pongo and Pita use the Twilight Bark to send news. Colonel and Sergeant Tibs discover the puppies at Devil Mansion with ninety-nine puppies. Pongo and Pita rescue all of them, but Cruella and the crooks chase them. The dogs hide their spots with fireplace soot and ride in a moving van. Cruella crashes into it, but her car hits the crooks. Back home, Roger and Anita count one hundred and one puppies. They buy a country home called Dalmatian Plantation.

Alex asks Mom to let him take Mikey Gigan's baby iguana when Mikey moves, because otherwise Stinky's dog Lurch might eat it. Mom doubts this, but Alex says iguanas are quiet, cute, and cuter than hamsters. He promises to keep the cage in his room beside his soccer trophies, yet Mom explains that iguanas can grow over six feet long. Alex says that will take fifteen years, when he will be married and living in his own house. He then says the iguana could be the brother he wants, although Mom reminds him about baby Ethan and the class fish that jumped into spaghetti sauce. Alex promises to feed the iguana lettuce, give it water, and clean its cage. Mom offers a trial basis of one or two weeks and warns that his room must also be clean. Alex agrees to try hard and pay for lettuce with his allowance. After Mom asks if he is sure, Alex says he wants an iguana. Mom tells him to look on his dresser, and Alex excitedly thanks her.

On a moonlit beach, three thieves examine jewels stolen from Carlotta Grimstone, including the Crack in the Sky and Makepeace Diamond. When the third thief's necklace breaks, its seven moonstones form a glowing circle. The stones show each thief a frightening prophecy: one will be caught, another will die by water, and two born together will die together within thirteen years. Police arrive, the thieves flee, but the second thief slips into a waterfall and dies.

Years later, March McQuinn steals a bicycle in Amsterdam to help his father, world-famous cat burglar Alfred McQuinn, escape the Grand Hotel. Alfie throws March a glowing stone, then falls from the roof and dies. March escapes with the stone, remembering Alfie's final message: “Follow the falls to the day.” Grieving and pursued by police, March clutches the stone, promises not to let his father down, and realizes he is being followed.

Under a full moon, three thieves admire jewels stolen from Carlotta Grimstone, including famous cursed stones. A thief takes a necklace of seven moonstones, but it breaks, and the stones form a glowing circle. The moonstones show terrible futures: one thief will be caught, one will die by water, and two born together will die together. Police arrive, and two thieves escape with the moonstones. They hide in an icy cave, but one slips near a waterfall and is swept away. In Amsterdam, March McQuinn steals a bicycle to meet his father, Alfred “Alfie” McQuinn, after a jewel theft. Alfie signals March to leave and tosses him a small blue-white stone, but then falls from the hotel roof. Alfie dies after asking March to “find Jewels” and “Follow the falls to the day.” March runs from the police with the stone and the breakfast bag. He remembers his father, promises, “Don’t let him down,” and keeps moving when he realizes someone is following him.

A child shows Piggy a new toy and says, “I love my new toy!” Piggy asks what it does, but the child has no idea. Piggy thinks it may be a throwing toy because he loves throwing toys. He throws it, and the child says, “Yes, zip!” Piggy throws it back, saying, “Here it comes! Zoom!” The toy breaks, and the child says, “I broke your toy!” Piggy is mad because his new toy is broken. The child says, “I am sorry.” Soon, Piggy says he does not care. They use a break-and-snap toy, saying, “Break! Snap!” Piggy asks the child to play with the new toy, but the child says no. The child wants to play with Piggy because friends are more fun than toys. The child says, “You’re it!” Piggy says, “No. You are the end.”

In the Enchanted Forest, the dark fairy disguised herself as a blue butterfly and led a white kitten to a deep well. The kitten fell in, bumped her head, and cried until the Sugar Plum Fairies rescued her with a wand. She could not remember where she lived, so she flew with them to the North Pole. Mrs. Claus agreed to care for her, and Santa named her Iris because her eyes were the color of the iris flower. Iris became best friends with Santa’s dog, Fudge, and helped Mrs. Claus watch for Jack Frost. One day, Iris slept while Jack hid the brownie ingredients, but Mrs. Claus solved his riddle and found them in the cabinets. Jack received no brownies and stopped playing that trick. Iris also helped Santa load gifts and guarded them from Christmas goblins with her snowball Cannon. On Christmas Eve, the reindeer flew with magic from the orange fairy, while the North Wind and Man in the Moon helped light Santa’s way. After helping, Iris went to sleep.

On the first day of kindergarten, Adam Krupp wakes up. Brenda Heath brushes her teeth, Christopher Beaker finds his sneaker, and Danny Hess rushes to dress. Emily Moco cools her coco, Fran Lister kisses her sister, and Gwen Mcgunney packs her bunny. Henry Fetter fights his sweater, while Ian Lowe says, “I won't go.” Jessie Syke peddles her bike, Kiki Wong hops, and Lenny Loom says, “Roover room.” Maddie Lindo looks out the window, Noah Bond climbs, and Ophelia Nye hugs goodbye. Patricia Packer sneaks a cracker. Quentin Wend and Raffa Mack high five. Sarah Von Huff is first off. Tommy Tuttle jumps a puddle, Ursula Crew ties her shoe, and Vicky Denzel bites her pencil. Miss Bindergarden gets ready for kindergarten. Wanda Chin marches in, Xavier Rowe yells hello, Yolanda Pound looks around, and Zach Blair finds his chair. “Good morning kindergarten,” says Miss Bindergarden. The fun begins, with animal names from Adam alligator to Zak zebra.

Mabel, Dipper, and Wendy work at the Mystery Shack. When Wendy invites the twins to meet her friends, Dipper says they are thirteen so they can join the teenagers. The group visits a condemned convenience store rumored to be haunted. They eat treats and discover chalk outlines, but Dipper steps on one, causing the ghosts to trap the teenagers in a television, video game, cereal box, and floating store. The ghosts possess Mabel and announce that the trespassers will stay forever. Dipper notices the victims were doing ordinary teenage things and realizes the ghosts hate teenagers. He admits he is twelve, not a teen, and the chaos stops. Two ghosts explain that teenagers once annoyed them and caused their deaths with loud rap music. To free Dipper’s friends, Dipper must perform the Lamby Dance in a lamb costume. His dance frees everyone. Wendy hides the embarrassing truth and tells the friends Dipper defeated the ghosts with a bat. Impressed, they invite the twins to hang out again at the Mystery Shack.

Mabel, Dipper, and Wendy work at the Mystery Shack. Wendy invites the twins to meet her friends, the cool kids. They go to an abandoned convenience store that people say is haunted. Inside, they have a food fight, but Dipper steps on a chalk outline. The lights go out, and the ghosts trap the teenagers in a TV, a video game, and a cereal box. Mabel becomes possessed, and the store turns upside down. Dipper notices that the ghosts are hurting people for normal teenage actions. He tells the ghost he is twelve, not a teenager, so the chaos stops. Two ghosts explain that they hated teenagers because teens once bothered them and loud rap music caused their deaths. They will free everyone if Dipper does a funny dance. Dipper puts on a lamb costume and performs the Lamby Dance. The ghosts release his friends. Wendy says Dipper defeated the ghosts with a bat, and everyone invites him back to the Mystery Shack.

Hamlet is a pig who likes books, poems, and clean shirts. He asks Mom and Dad to read his new book about a dragon that does not want to be a dragon. Dad rolls into the mud, and Hamlet’s sister and brother laugh at his poems and clean shirt. When supper comes, the pigs rush across the Mud Hole. Hamlet is not hungry, so he walks to the farmer’s pond. Under the rising moon, he writes a poem. In the pond, he sees his twin and calls him Eggs. Hamlet reads poems about a pig, the wind, and a cantaloupe moon. Eggs waves and bobs in the water, but a cloud covers the moon, and Eggs fades away. Hamlet says goodbye. Then he hears small voices. They say they liked his poems and ask him to read to them.

Highlighters are bright and colorful. They help children see important words and make black-and-white pages shine. But students often treat them badly. They press them hard, crack them in chairs, bend them, chew their ends, and lose their caps. Without caps, the ink dries, so the highlighters cannot brighten pages. Students of all ages toss them in bins with pencils. The highlighters have had enough. During recess, they choose the brightest highlighter to write a big yellow note: “The highlighters are going on strike.” They say they are tired of being treated like junk, and students will see only black and white pages until things change. After recess, the students find the note and read it. They huddle and write a reply. They say sorry and promise to use the highlighters gently, replace their caps, and stop hurting them. The highlighters think the students are sincere and give them a chance. They warn that if mistreated again, they will walk out and strike again.

Mike, the one-eyed monster, tells jokes in Boo’s bedroom to collect laughs for Monstropolis, but Boo is quieter than usual. She points to pictures about school and says, “School starts. No photos.” Mike understands that Boo needs a fun vacation story and pictures for her class, so he takes her through her closet door to Monsters, Inc. He borrows an old camera, and Boo’s laugh makes the lights flicker. Mike surprises Sully on the laugh floor, and Sully hugs Boo while monsters show her their tricks. They race around Monsters, Inc. and Monstropolis, taking many photos before school begins. When Sully learns Boo wants to show a photo at school, he says humans must not know about the monster world. Boo looks sad, so Sully allows one photo and chooses it. At school, no one believes Boo’s story until she shows the picture. Her teacher thinks Sully looks like Bigfoot, but Boo says, “That’s Kitty!”

After shopping, Fred, Velma, Shaggy, Daphne, and Scooby-Doo drive home. They drive through a heavy snowstorm. They take a wrong turn, and the Mystery Machine stops because its battery is bad. Since they could freeze, the gang leaves the van to find help. Scooby-Doo leads them to a dark, boarded-up house, where they enter through a loose window. They hear two crooks counting money from a bank robbery in the basement. The gang hides upstairs, but cold and danger keep them inside. They move furniture against the basement door to block the crooks, while Scooby runs outside with a flashlight to get help. The crooks try to break through, but the police arrive after seeing Scooby. The officers take charge of the crooks and call a tow truck for the Mystery Machine. They learn the crooks are wanted for robbing several banks. Scooby is praised as the hero. The gang promises him the biggest, juiciest steak ever.

It was a lovely summer morning, but little Roo felt grumpy and did not know why. He did not want to play or smile. His mother asked what was wrong and said, "Everybody feels better when they smile." She tickled him, flipped him head over heels, and played with him in a hollow tree, but Roo still would not smile. Then she tossed dry leaves into the air, and they fell all over him. His mother laughed because he looked funny, but Roo said he was not smiling. At breakfast time, his mother carried him down the hill to find food. Roo said he was not hungry, though his mother was. She told him to hold on tight. On the way, she did silly hops and did not see a wide, muddy hole. They slipped into it, and mud covered Roo. His mother was soaking wet and slimy from her ears to her toes. When Roo saw her, he could not help smiling.

Gerald was a tall giraffe with a long, slim neck, crooked knees, and thin legs. He could stand still and munch tree shoots, but he buckled when he ran. At Africa’s yearly jungle dance, the animals danced while Gerald felt sad because he was bad at dancing. The lions and other animals laughed and called him clumsy, so Gerald froze and walked home feeling alone. In a clearing, Gerald admired the moon. A cricket told him that different creatures may need different songs and that everything makes music. The cricket played his violin, and Gerald began to shuffle, sway his neck, swish his tail, leap, and dance. “I am dancing!” Gerald cried. The animals came back and watched with wide eyes. They called him the best dancer they had ever seen and asked how he learned. Gerald bowed, looked at the moon, and said, “We all can dance when we find music that we love.”

It is lunchtime at Peppa's house, and Peppa asks to make pizza. George, Mommy Pig, and Daddy Pig all love pizza. First, everyone washes their hands with soap and water. They gather flour, tomatoes, cheese, and toppings. Peppa says George likes pineapple, and Daddy Pig jokes that pineapple on pizza is against the law. Mommy Pig mixes flour and water to make dough. She puts flour on the table, and Peppa and George knead the dough with clean hands. They make four balls, and Mommy Pig rolls them flat. Mommy Pig and Daddy Pig make tomato sauce, and Peppa and George spread it on the dough. Then everyone decorates pizzas with happy faces. Daddy Pig uses mushrooms and olives, Mommy Pig uses onions and basil, Peppa uses sweet corn and little tomatoes, and George uses pineapple and cheese. Mommy Pig bakes the pizzas. In the garden, the family eats them. Peppa says they are the best pizzas in the world, and everyone loves pizza.

In spring, a child waits to plant while Nana explains that the dirt must dry and warm. Under the soil, earthworms and insects are already digging, building, and stirring it. Together, the child and Nana clear old plants, remove weeds, and spread compost. They plant seeds and water them. Soon carrots sprout, peas bloom, bees gather pollen, and many creatures find food above and below ground. Rain soaks the soil, roots drink, and the child plays with Nana in the garden. They harvest beans, tomatoes, cucumbers, zucchini, and other food, while birds, bats, ladybugs, snakes, skunks, and spiders hunt. As September comes, pumpkins grow, sunflowers bow, and the garden house is made for reading. When cold weather nears, they harvest quickly and share with neighbors. Frost covers the leaves, and they cover the garden for winter. Beetles, ants, and earthworms hide down in the dirt. Under the snow, a whole new garden sleeps down in the dirt, waiting for spring, sunshine, blossoms, and new sprouts.

One day, Taylor built something new, special, and amazing. Taylor felt proud, but it came crashing down. The chicken came first and said, “Cluck, cluck,” asking Taylor to talk. Taylor did not want to talk, so the chicken left. The bear asked Taylor to shout about feeling angry, but Taylor did not want to shout. The elephant offered to fix things by remembering how they were, but Taylor did not want to remember. Then the hyena suggested laughing, the ostrich suggested hiding, the kangaroo suggested throwing everything away, and the snake suggested knocking down someone else’s things. Taylor did not want to do anything with anyone, so all the animals left. A rabbit quietly came close and sat beside Taylor. Taylor asked, “Please stay with me.” The rabbit listened while Taylor talked, shouted, remembered, laughed, and shared plans to hide, throw things away, and ruin things. The rabbit never left. Later, Taylor planned to build again and said, “I can’t wait. It’s going to be amazing.”

An egg proudly calls himself “a good egg” and tries to help everyone in his carton. Meg, Peg, Greg, CLE, Shell, Shelly, Sheldon, Shelby, Eggbert, Frank, and Other Frank ignore bedtime, eat sugary cereal, throw tantrums, and break things. The good egg tries to fix their behavior and keep peace, but the pressure makes cracks spread across his shell. His doctor says he is putting too much pressure on himself, so he leaves the carton. Traveling alone, he takes walks, reads, floats in a river, writes in his journal, breathes quietly, and paints. Little by little, his shell heals, and his head no longer feels scrambled. He decides to return because he misses his friends and understands he must care for himself too. The eggs welcome him home. Some are still a little bad, but they are not like before. The egg realizes the others are not perfect, and he does not have to be either. The solid dozen is together again.

Under a full moon in the Frigid far north, the animals hurry because visitors will soon arrive. Walrus bakes cookies, while man wraps gifts for their dear Southern friends, who are braving icebergs and drifts. Caribou decorates his antlers with bows, and Harp seal plants candy canes in the flows. Beluga and humpback bring up sea stars from deep below. Bald eagle dives and snowy owl soars to place festive mistletoe over the doors. Fox lights lanterns for the skaters, Hair wears snowshoes, and hot Tundra tea is brewed. Then polar bear cheers as penguins float into view, just in time for the tree-trimming party. When everyone cannot hang the star, narwhal flings it from afar. The animals gather to watch Northern Le add shimmering holiday magic to the night. The penguins return home to Antarctica. Wishes from the Arctic friends rise on the breeze and echo off icebergs: “Merry Christmas.”

One wonderful day, chimpanzee Jim awoke to find everything was wrong: the sun was too bright, the sky was too blue, and bananas were too sweet. Norman suggested Jim might be grumpy, but Jim insisted he was not. On his walk, Jim met Marabou, Lemur, and Snake. They said his hunched body, bunched eyebrows, and frown looked grumpy. Jim changed his posture, raised his eyebrows, and smiled, but he still did not feel happy. Birds, monkeys, zebras, peacocks, and others suggested singing, swinging, rolling, strolling, lying in grass, stomping, laughing, dancing, and more. Jim did not want any of it. He shouted, beat his chest, and stormed away. Then Jim apologized for shouting and admitted he was grumpy. He found Norman slumped, with bunched eyebrows and a frown, because dancing with a porcupine hurt him. Norman said he would probably feel better soon. Jim said he would too, but he needed to be grumpy for now. Norman called it a wonderful day to be grumpy, and Jim agreed, feeling a little better.

Every spring, Rebecca Estelle planted vegetables for winter but refused to plant pumpkins because, as a child, her family had eaten only pumpkins for a month. One autumn, a pumpkin fell from the pumpkin truck and smashed in her yard. She buried the pieces, but in spring pumpkin vines grew. Rebecca Estelle cut them down, yet they returned. She ignored them all summer, and by autumn the vines covered her yard with pumpkins. Unable to ignore them, she decided to give them away. Delivering them was too hard, so she made pies, tarts, muffins, cakes, bread, pudding, and cookies. Then she carved jack-o'-lanterns and lit them with candles to bring people to her house. Everyone in town came, enjoyed the pumpkin treats, and took home jack-o'-lanterns, seeds, and food. Rebecca Estelle enjoyed the gathering too. She gave away everything except a handful of seeds, which she saved for planting next spring.

Harry Potter begins an amazing magical adventure when Hagrid, a giant on a flying motorbike, takes him from the cupboard under the stairs, where he lives with the Dursleys. Uncle Vernon will not share Harry’s many letters, and Dudley, Harry’s cousin, is unkind. Hagrid takes Harry to Gringotts and Diagon Alley, where Harry buys a wand. At King’s Cross Station, Harry boards the train to Hogwarts and becomes friends with Hermione and Ron. He also meets Malfoy, a rude boy. The Sorting Hat places the new students into houses. Harry studies potions with Severus Snape, plays Quidditch, and sees his heart’s desire in a magical mirror. He learns about the Sorcerer’s Stone and faces a troll, a dangerous forest, a dragon, and Fluffy, a three-headed dog. Harry, Hermione, and Ron fall onto a spiny plant and play wizard chess. You-Know-Who wants the Stone, but Harry defeats him again. Then Harry goes to bed, hoping for dreams of magic.

Harry begins an amazing adventure. Hagrid, a giant on a flying motorbike, brought him home as a baby. Harry has lived in a cupboard under the stairs, while his cousin Dudley is not cuddly. Uncle Vernon will not share Harry’s many letters, but a friend takes Harry away on his birthday. Hagrid brings him to Gringotts and Diagon Alley, where Harry sees goblins, gold, a secret vault, and Ollivander’s wondrous wand shop. At King’s Cross Station, Harry boards the train from Platform Nine and Three-Quarters and meets Hermione and Ron. At Hogwarts, a singing hat chooses houses for nervous new students. Harry learns potions from bad-tempered Severus Snape and plays Quidditch. He sees a dragon, seeks the Sorcerer’s Stone, and faces a terrible troll, a strange forest journey, and Fluffy, a vicious three-headed dog. Harry and his friends fall onto a spiny plant and play chess. After Harry beats You-Know-Who again, it is time for bed, with dreams of magic.

Billions of honeybees have disappeared from their colonies and failed to return, causing colony collapse disorder (CCD). The disorder has reduced the U.S. honeybee population to about half its level 50 years ago and threatens food production because honeybees pollinate many crops. Scientists have considered overcrowded hives, lack of pollen, parasites, pesticides, a fungus, and a virus as possible causes. In Montana, researchers compared empty hives with healthy control hives and found the fungus and virus in every empty hive tested. Bees might survive either infection alone, but the combination was most certainly deadly. Other scientists are studying whether several factors weaken bees’ immune systems together. Pesticides may also harm bees: they can enter pollen, affect bees’ ability to find nectar, and cause them to become lost. Studies found many chemicals in affected hives but could not prove pesticides directly caused CCD. Investigations continue, and scientists must identify the cause before finding a cure; pesticide use should be cut back.

Billions of honeybees have disappeared from their colonies and do not return. This problem is called colony collapse disorder, or CCD, and it has greatly reduced the honeybee population. Because honeybees pollinate many crops, CCD could threaten fruits, vegetables, and other food production. Scientists have looked at overcrowded hives, lack of pollen, parasites, pesticides, a fungus, and a virus. In Montana, they compared empty hives with healthy control hives and found the fungus and virus in every empty hive. Bees might survive either infection alone, but the two together could kill them. Other scientists think several factors may weaken bees and cause infection. Pesticides are another suspect. They can enter pollen and affect how bees search for nectar. Sick bees may get lost and never return. Studies found many chemicals in hives affected by CCD, but they did not prove pesticides caused it. Scientists continue searching for the exact cause and a way to save the bees.

Before the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, organizers needed an attraction to surpass the Eiffel Tower. Mechanical engineer George Ferris designed a huge moving wheel made of strong, lightweight steel. His partner, William Gronau, helped measure the plans, but judges and lenders doubted the unusual idea. With little money, George gathered investors and ordered parts from steel mills. Workers dug through frozen ground and dangerous quicksand, then built a deep foundation and assembled more than 100,000 pieces. On June 21, 1893, the Ferris wheel opened. Its passenger cars rose 265 feet, giving riders views of Chicago, Lake Michigan, and distant states. Steam engines turned the wheel, which carried 1.5 million passengers during the fair and survived storms without repairs. At night, 3,000 electric bulbs made it glow. When the fair ended, George’s investors named the invention the Ferris wheel. Copies soon appeared around the world, and Ferris wheels remain popular rides at fairs and amusement parks.

Before the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, people wanted a new attraction to outshine the Eiffel Tower. George Ferris, a young engineer, designed a huge moving wheel with steel parts. The judges doubted him, and they gave him no money. George used his savings and found investors, then ordered parts from many steel mills. His workers dug through frozen ground and dangerous quicksand to build a strong foundation. They joined more than 100,000 parts and finished the great wheel just before the fair opened. On June 21, 1893, George blew a whistle, and the Ferris wheel began to turn. People rode in large cars with velvet seats and saw Chicago, Lake Michigan, and faraway states. The wheel was safe, and visitors came from around the world to ride it. It carried 1.5 million passengers and shone with 3,000 electric lights. When the fair ended, the wheel stopped, but Ferris wheels soon appeared around the world and are still loved today.

There was a cold lady who swallowed some snow. The story says, “I don't know why she swallowed some snow. Perhaps you know.” Then she swallowed a pipe, though she wasn't the type to gulp down a pipe, because she wanted to warm her ten toes that tickled and tingled from layers of snow. Next, she swallowed coal to keep her pipes glow. What was her goal? She swallowed a black-brimmed hat before she froze. Then she swallowed a long brown stick to push down the snow. Finally, she swallowed a long striped scarf because it was so cold, although she tried not to barf. The cold lady had quite enough, so she thought and thought and came up with a plan. She hiccupped twice: “Hiccup, hiccup!” All the stuff she swallowed popped out and became a snowman.

One night, the child finds a note saying Gabe, the monster under the bed, has gone fishing for a week. The child misses Gabe’s ragged breathing, nose whistling, uncut claws, and green ooze, and cannot sleep. The child knocks on the floorboards to call a substitute monster. Herbert arrives, but he has no claws and has never scared a child. Ralph has claws, but they are smooth and covered with nail polish. Cynthia has jagged claws and a slimy tail, but she is a girl monster, so the child sends her away. Max is a scruffy boy with excellent claws, but his tail is stumpy; his threat to lick the child makes the child laugh. Max says the child is too picky and leaves. Then Gabe returns because fishing was not challenging. He makes green drool, unfurls his spiked tail, and sharpens his claws. The child says no other monster can scare them like Gabe, then hides under the blanket. Gabe asks for a toe, but the child offers a pillow instead. With Gabe and his ooze back, everything is normal, and the child soon sleeps.

There was an old lady who swallowed a chick, but she did not get sick. Then she swallowed some straw to cover the chick. The chick looked in awe. Next, she swallowed an egg to Jazz up the straw. She swallowed some candy to sweeten the egg, because she knew the candy would come in handy. Then she swallowed a brightly colored basket to carry the candy. After that, she swallowed a bow to tie on the basket. Each time, she repeated, “I don't know why she swallowed that chick, but she didn't get sick.” When she finished, the old lady started to hop. She jumped up and down and would not stop. She skipped down the trail on a day that was sunny. Then she met the Easter bunny. The Easter bunny called, “Happy Easter!”

Every morning, Roger's Dalmatian, Pongo, helped him get ready in London. In the park, Roger read that a tiger had been killed for its beautiful belt. Pongo then met Perdita, Anita's Dalmatian, and their owners fell in love and married. Perdita had 15 puppies, but Cruella wanted them for a spotted coat. When Anita refused to sell them, Cruella fired her. Later, Horace and Jasper stole the puppies and took them to Manor DeVille, where Cruella kept 99 Dalmatians. Pongo sent a message through dogs across the country. Kipper and other animals made a rescue plan, while Pongo and Perdita hurried to the puppies. Kipper led the puppies out, and Horace and Jasper were stopped by the animals. The puppies escaped, but one was left behind. Pongo and Perdita found 98 puppies at a farm, and Kipper rescued the last one. Cruella fell into molasses, and the men were arrested. Roger made a successful video game about Cruella. The family moved to Manor DeVille with all the Dalmatians.

Mickey tells Pluto to get the yellow ball because it is time to play. Pluto gets the yellow ball and brings it to Mickey. Mickey throws the ball, and Pluto brings it back. Mickey throws the yellow ball again, and Pluto brings it back again. Then Mickey says, “I will throw it really far this time.” Mickey throws the yellow ball really far. Pluto does not see the yellow ball, so he comes back without it. Mickey asks, “Where’s the yellow ball?” Mickey and Pluto look for the yellow ball. Mickey asks, “Do you see it?” Pluto finds the yellow ball. Mickey says, “Good boy, you found it.” Then Mickey says, “Let’s take the yellow ball home.” Mickey and Pluto take the yellow ball home.

On a cold winter morning, Dexter and his twin sister Leah raced to be first to eat Mama’s bacon and cheese bread pudding. They argued about taking turns. Papa sent both twins to get eggs from their neighbor, Ms. Marvis. Her quiet house made Dexter wonder about her family. The twins invited Ms. Marvis to dinner. She shared stories from Poland and told them about punchki, jelly donuts made in winter. Ms. Marvis was happy but said she had not made them for years. Her children were grown and gone. The next day, Papa helped Dexter and Leah make blueberry punchki. They left some on Ms. Marvis’s porch. Later, they built a snow family in her yard. Ms. Marvis wrote that the donuts, dinner, and snow family made her feel special. Dexter and Leah felt thankful for each other. They hoped to keep making the new treats and tradition together.

Mr Incredible, a superhero, had a fan named Buddy, who wanted to be a super. After Mr Incredible said “Supers were born, not made,” he married Elastigirl. When supers were sued, the government made them hide, so Mr Incredible and Elastigirl became Bob and Helen Parr and raised Violet, Dash, and Jack Jack. Bob missed helping people. Mirage secretly sent him to fight the omnidroid on an island, and he defeated it. But Mirage’s boss was Buddy, now called Syndrome. Syndrome captured Bob and planned to use the omnidroid to look like a hero. Helen, Violet, and Dash followed Bob to the island, and Jack Jack was there too. Syndrome launched the omnidroid toward the city. The family escaped, freed Bob, and fought Syndrome’s guards. Violet freed them after Syndrome froze them with a ray. In the city, the omnidroid defeated Syndrome, but Mr Incredible, Elastigirl, Violet, Dash, and Frozone defeated the robot together. Syndrome later dropped Jack Jack, but the baby escaped and caused Syndrome to fall. The family returned to undercover life, ready to protect the world together.

Today, Mrs. Boot, Poppy, and Sam take a school outing on an old steam train. Rusty wants to go on the outing too. The train leaves, and the children look out of the windows until the engine breaks down near Farmer Dre’s farm. The driver says they must get help, so the children climb off and plan a picnic in a field. Their teacher stops them when she sees a bull, but Poppy explains that Buttercup is a nice cow. Farmer Dre arrives with Dolly, his horse, yet the teacher says a horse cannot replace an engine. The driver unhitches the broken engine, and the children climb back aboard. Farmer Dre has a long rope and tells Dolly to pull. Dolly pulls very slowly, and the train starts to move while Farmer Dre walks beside her. At last, they reach the station. Farmer Dre says, “Out by engine, back by horse.” Sam says it was a good outing.

Mr. Skinny was extremely thin and lived in Fatland, where people, animals, and even plants seemed fat. He ate very little: one cornflake for breakfast, one baked bean for lunch, nothing for tea, and the world's smallest sausage for supper. Wanting a bigger appetite, he visited Dr. Plump. The doctor offered a huge cream cake, donuts, and currant buns, but Mr. Skinny ate only a little, while Dr. Plump ate the rest. Dr. Plump decided that Mr. Skinny needed drastic measures, so he telephoned Mr. Greedy, who lived one hundred miles away. Mr. Greedy invited Mr. Skinny to stay with him and help build his appetite. After a month, Mr. Skinny returned home happy because he had a tummy, something he had always wanted. Feeling proud, he stopped to see Dr. Plump. The doctor congratulated him and said they should celebrate. Then Dr. Plump opened his desk drawer.

On Christmas Eve, Pig eagerly waited for Santa and hoped to receive the many presents on his list. His friend Trevor told him Santa would come while they slept, but Pig refused to go to bed. He stayed beside the stockings and gingerbread crumbs, determined to see Santa arrive. At 3:33, Pig heard a strange sound and saw a portly old gent with a bag of toys. Santa gave presents to Mark, Trevor, and Pig, then drank his milk. When Santa started to leave, Pig shouted that he wanted more because his pile was not enough. He nipped Santa’s behind and held onto him as Santa climbed up the chimney and reached the sleigh. Pig demanded all his presents, but the speedy reindeer pulled the sleigh away. Pig fell from the sleigh, while Trevor slept. Pig survived the great drop because a tree with an angel on top saved him.

WALL-E lived alone in a trailer on a rubbish-covered Earth with his pet cockroach. He collected treasures and found a plant, then met Eve, a flying robot sent from space. WALL-E wanted to be her friend, and he rescued her from a sandstorm. Eve took the plant and shut down, so WALL-E followed her onto the Axiom, a giant star liner. There, he learned that humans lived in hover chairs and that the plant could show Earth was safe to return to. Otto, the autopilot, tried to stop the ship from going home. WALL-E and Eve escaped danger, but Otto badly damaged WALL-E. The captain stood up for the first time, turned Otto off, and Eve put the plant in the holo-detector. The Axiom returned to Earth. Eve repaired WALL-E, but he did not remember her until an electric spark passed between them. WALL-E held Eve’s hand at last. Humans began caring for Earth, and the planet could become green again.

Once upon a time, a little old woman and a little old man lived happily on a farm, but they were sad because they had no children. The woman made a boy from gingerbread dough, gave him eyes, a mouth, and buttons, and baked him. When she opened the oven, the gingerbread man jumped out and ran away, singing, “Run, run as fast as you can. You can't catch me. I'm the gingerbread man.” He escaped from the little old woman and man, a horse, a cow, a farmer, and children, who all wanted to eat him. Then he reached a river, but he could not swim. A fox offered to carry him across. The gingerbread man climbed from the fox’s tail to his back and then his nose because the water was getting higher. But the fox snapped and ate him piece by piece. After several snaps, the gingerbread man was gone.

Arlo lived on a farm with his family at the base of Clawtooth Mountain. He wanted to help so he could earn his footprint on the family silo, but he was easily frightened. When Papa died, Arlo felt lost. While the family struggled to harvest crops before winter, Arlo chased a critter stealing food and fell into the river. He washed far from home, but remembered Papa saying he could follow the river home. The critter brought berries, and Arlo named him Spot. They became friends and traveled together, helping each other. Spot understood Arlo's sadness because he had lost his family too. Later, friendly T-Rexes praised Arlo for being brave after he and Spot helped save their longhorns from Raptors. Near home, pterodactyls took Spot, but Arlo scared them away and rescued Spot from a flood. When Arlo reached a human family, he let Spot stay because Spot belonged there. Arlo returned to his farm, knowing he had found his way home and earned his mark, making Papa proud.

Pete the Cat wakes up ready for school, but Mom says it is a snow day. Pete and his brother Bob put on warm clothes and go sledding. Pete throws snowballs, builds a snow cat, and invites Cy to join them. They climb Big Hill and sled down while Trey and Emma are at the top. On the way home, Pete and Bob enjoy hot chocolate at Trey's house. Pete plans to tell his class about the fun, but more snow keeps school closed. He builds a snow fort and snow dog, throws snowballs, and goes sledding. Then Mom asks him to shovel the walk, and he becomes too tired to play. Pete misses his teacher and classmates. When another snow day comes, Pete plows the streets, and other cats help clear them. The streets become safe, the bus runs, and school opens. During snow day Show and Tell, Pete shares his snowy adventures. He says he loves snow, but loves school best.

Big Bowl fire engines wait day and night at the station, ready to rescue people or fight a blazing fire. When a fire alarm sounds, the engine roars out with firefighters aboard. It speeds along with sirens screaming and bright lights flashing. The crew wears helmets, fireproof coats and trousers, and strong boots. At the fire, they jump out, unroll the hose, and bring out the gear. A nozzle sprays water onto the flames, while the engine’s pump pulls more water from pipes below the ground when the tank is empty. Smoke fills the air, so the firefighters put on masks. The ladder rises high, and sometimes its platform reaches a window. At last, the flames are extinguished. The crew rolls up the hose and returns to the station for a break. The fire engine stays wide awake, waiting for the next alarm.

Henry had no brothers, sisters, friends, or pets, and he wished for a brother, a new street, and a dog. His parents first said no, but after looking at their house, street, and Henry, they agreed to a dog. Henry searched for a dog that was not short, did not have curly fur, and had no pointed ears. He chose Mudge, a puppy with floppy ears and straight fur. Mudge grew huge, weighing 180 pounds, and became Henry’s companion. Before Mudge, Henry hurried to school, worrying about tornadoes, ghosts, biting dogs, and bullies. With Mudge, he felt happy and thought about vanilla ice cream, rain, rocks, and good dreams. Mudge loved Henry’s room and slept beside him. One day, Mudge wandered away and became lost. Henry cried, then realized Mudge must be lost because he loved Henry. Henry searched and called through roads, a field, a stream, and pine trees. Mudge heard him and came running. Afterward, Mudge never walked alone, and both stayed close, knowing they would not lose each other again.

Summer is over, and the crayons return to school. Blue and Beige wave goodbye to the beach, saying, “See you next year” and “Goodbye, beach. Later, dudes.” The night before the first day is exciting because the crayons choose what to wear. At school, they enjoy seeing old friends, who notice changes and say they look marvelous. They also make new friends: Chunky Toddler Crayon meets Husky Toddler Crayon, and both wonder if they are related because they share the same last name. Back in class, Purple Crayon enjoys math because it is neat. Black Crayon likes writing and starts with an outline. White Crayon loves reading. Yellow and Orange enjoy science when they see that Jupiter is yellow and orange, giving them something they can agree on. Everyone looks forward to art class, especially because making a mess is fun. When someone asks, “Did someone say mess?” the crayons are ready for art.

This is Unicorn and Horse. Unicorn has a sapphire horn, a silver coat, a rainbow mane, and perfect white teeth. He eats pink cupcakes, makes rainbows, and dances, so the animals love him. Horse has none of these things and sits grumpy because he wishes he were Unicorn. One night, two men sneak into Unicorn’s paddock, tie him up, and carry him away in a truck because a rainbow-dancing unicorn who eats cupcakes for breakfast could make someone a lot of money. The animals hear the truck, but Squirrel cannot run fast enough, Bird cannot fly fast enough, Fox cannot run on the road, and Turtle cannot run at all. Horse is the only animal who can help. He runs after the truck and frees Unicorn with six great chomps of his large teeth. Unicorn thanks Horse. Afterward, sometimes Horse eats cupcakes and makes rainbows, while Unicorn eats hay and does not make rainbows. Horse likes races, and Unicorn likes ring toss. Most of all, they like each other, which is better than pink cupcakes.

Good Night Gorilla begins with “Good night, elephant.” Then the story says, “Good night, lion,” “Good night, hyena,” “Good night, giraffe,” and “Good night, armadillo.” Next are the words, “Good night, dear. Good night.” “Good night” is said many more times. Then comes the question, “Huh?” After that, the story says, “Good night, Sue. Good night, dear. Good night.” The story ends with “Good Night Gorilla.” In order, the goodnights name elephant, lion, hyena, giraffe, armadillo, and Sue. The words also say “dear” twice. “Good night” is repeated many times between the names. The question “Huh?” comes after the first group of goodnights and before the goodnights with Sue. The final words are “Good Night Gorilla,” after all the other goodnights.

Little Nut Brown Harry is going to bed and holds on tight to Big Nut Brown Harry’s long ears. He asks, “Guess how much I love you?” Little Nut Brown Harry stretches his arms wide, reaches high, turns upside down to reach with his toes, and hops high. Each time, Big Nut Brown Harry shows that he can reach even farther, swing Little Nut Brown Harry over his head, or hop so high that his ears touch the branches.
