Little Nut Brown Harry thinks these things are very big and wishes he could do them too. He says he loves Big Nut Brown Harry down the lane to the river, but Big Nut Brown Harry loves him across the river and over the hills. Soon Little Nut Brown Harry is very sleepy. Looking into the big dark night, he says he loves Big Nut Brown Harry right up to the moon. Big Nut Brown Harry settles him into his bed of leaves, kisses him good night, and lies down close by. He whispers, “I love you. Right up to the moon and back.”

Bruce was a bear who disliked holidays and usually slept through winter. This year, his family stayed awake for a cozy snow field Christmas, so Bruce wore long underwear and a warm hat. Then forest animals mistook him for Santa. Bruce tried to ignore them, but more animals arrived and asked for Christmas gifts, including balloons, world peace, a race car, and a power compound miter saw. When they left, Thistle announced that Santa Bruce would deliver presents, even though Bruce said, “Bah humbug,” and refused. The mice and geese persuaded him to sit in a sled, and the forest prepared boxes of crackers. Bruce finally agreed to go for one night. Delivering presents was difficult, but he finished before morning. The animals woke to gifts and thanked him for spreading Christmas happiness. Bruce still liked sleeping more than happiness, but he said he would sleep through next Christmas, while everyone else wanted to do it every year.

It is good to give thanks to the Lord. Friends and family arrive, and everyone shares hugs, kisses, hellos, and laughter on a bright, cool day. Outside, the family climbs over piles of red, yellow, and golden-brown leaves, then laughs and rolls back down. When a gusty autumn storm begins, they go inside for warm cider. The house fills with smells of turkey, stuffing, and pies. When the meal is ready, Mama cries, and everyone sits, joins hands, bows their heads, and says grace, giving praise to God. They enjoy the food and family God has given them. The child eats pumpkin pie, while Grandpa Love laughs and says, “Oh my, I can’t eat more.” After the wondrous meal, everyone chats, laughs, and shares jokes and tales. The child yawns as the family says goodbye. At bedtime, the child whispers prayers, receives a good-night kiss, and shuts their eyes, thankful to give thanks to the Lord.

The narrator calls his six-year-old brother “the pain” because he needs help getting ready, cries when left behind, and receives special attention. He eats poorly, makes a mess in the bathroom, and stays up late. When their parents let the narrator stay up later, he finds it boring without his brother. The next day, the brother interrupts a phone call, knocks down block buildings, and the narrator thinks his brother gets the love he wants. He thinks Mom and Daddy love his brother better because they call him lovable and say he is what they always wanted. The brother calls his older sister “the great one” and complains that she plays piano, feeds the cat, cares for the baby, remembers phone numbers, and builds block cities. He wants to be the garbage man and knocks down her buildings. When he plays with the blocks alone, he discovers it is not fun. At swimming, she can swim and dive while he is afraid to put his face in the water, so he spits water, pulls her hair, and pinches her. After their parents praise and hug her, he thinks they love her better than him.

The older sister calls her little brother “the pain.” He is six and slow to get ready, so Mom and Daddy help him. He cries when she leaves, gets praise for his schoolwork, dessert, and a late bedtime. She thinks Mom and Daddy love him better. When she stays up later without him, she finds there is nothing to do. The next day, he sings during her phone call, knocks down her block buildings, and sleeps with the cat. Then the little brother calls his older sister “the great one.” She plays piano, feeds the cat, remembers phone numbers, and builds cities with friends. He wants to be the garbage man and knocks down her buildings. When he plays blocks alone, it is not fun. At swimming, she swims and dives, but he is scared, so he spits water, pulls her hair, and pinches her. Mom and Daddy hug and praise each child. Both children think their parents love the other better.

One day, Macy decided to go camping, and all her friends came along. They found the perfect place to make a camp and worked together to pitch a tent. Pitching a tent was not easy, and the tent fell down. They tried again and again until the tent stayed up. “Good job, everyone!” That night, they sang around the campfire. When bedtime came, Thyro went into the tent first with his flashlight. Charlie came next and warned everyone to watch the pegs. Tula came third, and Macy came fourth. Eddie came too, so five campers were in the tent. It was a squash, a squeeze, and a squeezy Squish Squash! After the campers said good night, Cyel popped out, then Tula, Charlie, and Macy popped out. At last, one camper was in the tent, and four campers were under the stars. “Sleep tight, campers.” “Hoot hoot.”

Long ago, God promised to send a new king who would rescue his people and rule forever. An angel told Mary that her baby would be the forever king. Another angel told Joseph that Mary’s baby would be the rescuing king. Mary and Joseph traveled to Bethlehem, where the busy city had no room for them. Jesus was born there and slept in a manger, which usually held food for animals. That night, an angel told frightened shepherds that God’s chosen king had been born. Many angels celebrated, and the shepherds hurried to Bethlehem. They found the baby lying in the manger, just as the angel had said. Far away, wise men saw a new star and understood that the promised king had been born. They traveled a long way and found him. Everything God promised came true. God had sent the greatest king of all: Jesus, the new king, the rescuing king, and the forever king.

I know an old lady who swallowed a dry Thanksgiving pie. Then she swallowed cider to moisten it, but it rumbled, mumbled, and grumbled inside her. Next, she swallowed a whole roll to go with the cider, followed by a fat yellow squash. She swallowed a salad to go with the squash, and looked quite pallid. Then she swallowed a turkey, though the future looked murky. She swallowed a pot to go with the turkey, and a ten-layer cake to go with the pot. Each new food was added to go with the food before it, making a long chain inside her. After the cake, people tied rope to her feet. The old lady then swallowed some bread. She said, “Hmm, I’m full,” and wished everyone “Happy Thanksgiving.” The repeated words “Perhaps she’ll die” appear after the foods, but the story ends with her saying she is full, not with her dying.

On Valentine’s Day, Splat the cat gets ready carefully because he has made cards for his class and a special card for Kitten, a cat he likes. He puts Kitten’s red envelope in his bag and goes to school, but every time he sees her, he becomes nervous. Kitten pulls his ears, pokes his belly, ties his tail, and calls him smelly before running away. During the Valentine exchange, Splat waits to give her his card. At recess, Spike grabs the envelope and boasts that he likes Kitten more. He draws a huge heart, making Splat’s card seem tiny, so Splat throws it in the trash. Kitten opens Spike’s card, then takes Splat’s card from the trash without Splat seeing. It says, “I like you.” Kitten gives Splat a pink envelope. Her card says his fur is soft, his belly noise is silly, his tail is bendy, and he smells nice after a bath. It also says, “I like you.” Splat gets a special Valentine back from Kitten.

One night, the narrator finds a note saying Gabe, their monster, has left because someone needs him more. That someone is little sister Emma, who keeps climbing out of her toddler bed. The narrator goes to Emma's room and promises to get Emma asleep, but Gabe allows only three chances. The narrator summons Agatha, a slime-covered monster, but Emma laughs and wipes her noses. Cynthia has claws, yet Emma decorates her tail and dances. Vladimir, a tentacled monster, also fails because Emma treats his tentacles like jump ropes. Gabe returns and orders Emma into bed, but she calls him “Fuzzy” and is not afraid. Gabe says he must stay with Emma, leaving the narrator worried about sleeping alone. Then Gabe’s little sister Stella arrives with his snack. Her hiccups and love of toes scare Emma into bed. Gabe says Stella is the perfect monster for Emma. The narrator returns to bed with Gabe, while Emma stays with Stella, so everything is back to normal.

Danny and Dinosaur are bored because they have no games to play. Danny suggests chores or a trip to space, but Mummy reminds them to take lunch. They pack a lunch and visit the science museum, where they find a rocket ready to launch. Ignoring warnings, they press buttons and fly into space. Danny discovers they left their lunches at home, so hungry Dinosaur eats the rocket’s gadgets, controls, fuel, the moon, Martians, satellites, Saturn, and space rovers. The rocket disappears, leaving them stranded. Danny cries, so Dinosaur makes a plan to use poop as rocket fuel. As it flies, it poops out everything it ate, creating a trail back to Earth. They orbit Earth, pass over their town, and land safely. The returned objects form a poop planet beside the moon. Danny promises to listen to Mummy because “fun is not fun without food for your tummy.” A Mars cat finally pops out of Dinosaur’s bottom.

Barbie lives by the ocean and loves swimming and riding her fast jet ski. At the lagoon, she hears "squeak, squeak" and finds a lost baby dolphin. Barbie comforts him and searches with him, but they see only fish, birds, and seaweed. When it gets dark, the dolphin follows Barbie home because he cannot find his family. Barbie calls a dolphin expert, feeds him from a bottle, and sets up a tent so she can watch him. She pats his head and says, "Good night." The next day, Barbie's friends play with the dolphin, but he still misses his family. Together, they ride jet skis and search near the lagoon and a cove. Then they hear "squeak, squeak": the baby dolphin's family has found him. The dolphins jump, splash, and play together. They thank Barbie, and she waves goodbye, happy to have a new friend.

Barbie lives by the ocean and loves to swim and ride her jet ski fast. She rides to the lagoon and hears, “squeak, squeak.” A baby dolphin is swimming there. He is lost and cannot find his family. Barbie comforts him and helps him search. They see fish, birds, and seaweed, but no family. When it gets dark, Barbie goes home, and the baby dolphin follows her. Barbie calls a dolphin expert, feeds him from a bottle, and makes a tent to watch him. She pats him and says, “Good night.” The next day, Barbie’s friends play with the dolphin, but he misses his family. Barbie, her friends, and the dolphin ride jet skis and search near the lagoon and a cove. They hear, “squeak, squeak.” The baby dolphin’s family found him. They jump, splash, and play together. The dolphins thank Barbie. Barbie waves goodbye, happy to have a new friend.

The child takes walks with his father and their old dog, Major. They walk quietly, and the child calls this a listening walk because he keeps still and listens to many sounds. He hears Major’s long toenails scratch the sidewalk, his father’s slow shoes, lawn mowers, sprinklers, cars, a bicycle bell, a crying baby, a jet, a basketball, high heels, a bus, and a loud jackhammer. The jackhammer hurts his ears, so he covers them. Sometimes they take Major to the park, where it is quieter. The child hears his father’s shoes, pigeons, ducks, a woodpecker, crickets, wind, and bees. Pigeons and small ducks come close because they want food, while big ducks stay back. The child says listening walks are fun and can happen around a block or yard. Even without walking, sounds are everywhere. He tells the reader to close the book, listen, and count how many sounds can be heard.

Sophia and Maddie play at a park, but Sophia cannot climb as high as Maddie. When Sophia discovers that Maddie and her little brother Ryan have only bread and milk because their family lacks money, she promises not to tell. At home, Sophia sees her family has plenty of food, so she tries to help by packing fish, eggs, and then burritos for Maddie. The fish and eggs are bad for backpacks, but the burritos work, and Maddie helps Sophia reach the top of the climbing wall. Sophia thanks her friend, saying, “That's what friends are for.” Later, Sophia sees that Maddie's refrigerator is still nearly empty. She tells Mom, even though it breaks her promise, because she cannot help Maddie alone. Mom, Louis, and Sophia bring groceries to Maddie's family, and Louis gives away his cheesy pizza bombs for a treat. Maddie says a promise is important, but Sophia explains that Maddie is more important than the promise. They remain friends and race upstairs together.

Sophia and Maddie played at the park. Maddie climbed the climbing wall, but Sophia could not reach the top. Sophia was hungry, so she went to Maddie's home for a snack. Maddie had only bread and milk, and she saved the milk for little Ryan because her family had little money. Sophia promised not to tell. At home, Sophia saw that her fridge was full. She tried to help by packing fish and eggs, but they were yucky in backpacks. She packed burritos, too. Burritos were good for kids and backpacks. Then Maddie helped Sophia climb to the top. Sophia thanked her. Maddie said, “That's what friends are for.” Sophia saw that Maddie and Ryan still needed food. She told Mom, even though it broke her promise. Mom brought groceries, and Louis gave them cheesy pizza bombs for a treat. Maddie smiled. She said, “Always,” when Sophia asked if they were still friends. They ran home together. “That's what friends are for.”

Arthur loves new puppy Pal and promises to train him, but Pal dislikes the garage, makes messes, runs from his leash, and wakes the family at night. Mother lets Pal stay inside briefly, yet he destroys the living room, so the family decides he must move to the garage. The garage key disappears, allowing Pal one more night in the house. Arthur worries Pal may be sent away, especially after hearing about other problem puppies. He trains Pal with love, practicing sit, down, stay, and tricks in a backyard training school. At a puppy show, Pal obeys Arthur and impresses the family, so they decide he can stay in the house and does not need the garage or a farm. Later, Pal returns from behind the rose bushes with the missing garage key. Arthur gives him a special dinner, then cannot find his leash. While everyone searches, Pal again runs behind the rose bushes.

Once there was a boy who loved Stars very much. Every night, the boy watched the stars from his window and wished for one of his own. He dreamed that the star would be his friend, and they would play hide and go seek and take long walks together. The boy decided to catch one. He set out at sunrise, but he could not see a star, so he waited all day. Finally, just before the sun went away, he saw one. He jumped and climbed the tallest tree, but the star was still Way Out Of Reach. A life preserver was too heavy, his paper spaceship did not fly well, and a seagull would not help. Then he saw a baby star floating in the water. He reached for it, but it rippled through his fingers. The boy was sad, but while walking home, he saw a star washed onto the bright golden sand. He had caught a star of his very own.

Sarah Hartwell does not want to get out of bed for her first day at a new school. She says she hates it because she does not know anyone and thinks starting over will be hard. Her father, Mr. Hartwell, tells her she must go, gives her toast and her lunchbox, and drives her there. Sarah's hands are cold and clammy; she says she cannot breathe and feels sick. At the school, Principal Mrs. Burton welcomes Sarah and leads her through the crowded hallways. She tells Sarah that everyone is nervous on the first day. In the classroom, most of the children are already in their seats and look up when Mrs. Burton asks for attention. She brings Sarah to the front and introduces her to the class as their new teacher, Mrs. Sarah Jane Hartwell.

One morning, Mr. Hartwell woke Sarah for her first day at a new school. Sarah hid under the covers and said, “I'm not going.” She did not want to start over because she did not know anyone. Mr. Hartwell told her to get ready. Sarah got dressed, ate toast, took her lunchbox, and rode with him in the car. Her hands were cold and clammy, and she said, “I feel sick.” At school, Principal Mrs. Burton came to the car and led Sarah through the crowded hallways. She said, “Don't worry. Everyone is nervous the first day.” In the classroom, most children were already in their seats. They looked up when Mrs. Burton brought Sarah to the front of the room. Then Mrs. Burton said, “Class, I would like you to meet your new teacher, Mrs. Sarah Jane Hartwell.” Sarah was the new teacher at the school.

At first, all the beans at school were one mixed group, but later some became the famous “cool beans.” The cool beans could play guitar, draw superheroes, or jump high, while the narrator felt ordinary and uncool. The narrator wore sunglasses that were too big, swaggered, was picked last, and stopped trying to compete. The cool beans and the narrator grew apart. Then, in one day, three cool beans showed kindness. One helped clean lunch from the narrator’s loafers, another dusted off a scraped knee, and a third whispered, “The teacher asked you to read from page 32,” after classmates laughed. These small actions gave the narrator confidence and showed that somebody had the narrator’s back. The narrator began spending time with the cool beans again at lunch, after school, and on weekends. The narrator realized that being cool is not about looks or special skills. It is about a wink, nod, or smile, helping someone up, pointing them in the right direction, and asking, “You need a hand?” “Yes, please.” Now that’s cool.

Penny felt lonely like a stray and wished for friendship and a home. A girl found her and carried her to a fountain, where Penny helped make the girl happy when she wished for ice cream. An older man picked Penny up to check a tire and then spent her with other coins. A boy got a ball and bone for his dog. Soon, Penny became change in a purse and felt sad because she did not understand why she mattered. Bumping and bouncing carried her with other change. Later, a child needed Penny for a tooth, so Penny was tucked into a snug place. The next morning, another child found her and said she belonged in the perfect place. Penny was happy because she was wanted, loved, and finally had a home. She would never forget the people and animals she had helped along the way.

Mickey sees blue sky and sunshine at the clubhouse, so he checks the weather and calls Minnie about a hike. Minnie calls Daisy and buys strawberries. Daisy invites her music, while Donald says he will get his gear and be ready in half an hour. Goofy does not answer Mickey’s calls. Minnie, Daisy, and Donald meet Mickey, but it is getting late. They look toward Goofy’s quiet house with the telescope and decide to investigate. At Goofy’s house, Nikki finds his missing friend fast asleep. The friends need Goofy for the hike, so they try to wake him. Minnie calls his name, Daisy plays music, and Donald uses the silly button on his phone, but Goofy keeps sleeping and snoring. Mickey calls to him too. Pluto licks Goofy’s face, and Goofy wakes up. Everyone gets in the car, and Mickey checks his phone to make sure they are going in the right direction. They all make it. “Hot dog!” says Mickey. “It’s going to be a great afternoon.”

Pig was a pug whose passport listed no age, and he was a terrible traveler. Whenever he went on vacation, he ruined careful plans and caused great dismay. He broke rules, ignored traditions, and acted without respect for local people or ancient taboos. At parties, parades, processions, and even wild celebrations, Pig created chaos and devastation. His insensitive antics spoiled holidays, so locals gathered and shouted, “Go away!” Pig did not stop. He kept rocking and rolling until his rough play spun out of control. His need to offend seemed huge, but every wild party eventually ended. When travelers treat locals with little regard, the locals may come back to bite them hard. These days, Pig has learned not to ruin a whole holiday. However, the truth remains that Pig does not travel well, even though he might try.

On an autumn hike with friends, you see lizards, squirrels, butterflies, and deer. Then you turn around and find a turkey at your feet. You try to send him home, but he refuses to go, so you must hide him because you cannot keep a turkey. You sneak him through the gate, feed him acorns, and take him into the fort when the coast is clear. You make turkey masks with paper, scissors, glue, tape, and string. You also make a Feathered Tail from hand-shaped paper. Everyone stretches their necks, puffs up, clucks “gobble,” and flaps like turkeys. Hats and sunglasses finish the disguises, so you can take the turkey out to play. Later, the turkey will not go home, even when you call or gently nudge him. His flock is waiting in the valley below. He was lost, but now he has found his way back. You wave goodbye and wish him well. Everyone deserves to be with loved ones, and friendships can last all year.

Sam-I-am introduces himself and repeatedly asks another character to try green eggs and ham. The character refuses each offer and says he will not eat them anywhere, including a house, box, car, tree, train, dark, rain, or boat, or with a mouse, fox, or goat. Sam-I-am keeps offering the food in new places and with different animals, but the character continues to say no. At last, Sam-I-am says, “Try them, and you may,” and the character agrees to try them if Sam-I-am will let him be. After trying the green eggs and ham, the character says, “I like green eggs and ham.” He discovers that he likes them in every place and with every animal named, because they are “so good.” He eats them in a box, with a fox, in a house, with a mouse, and anywhere else. At the end, he says he likes green eggs and ham and thanks Sam-I-am.

On Market Day, Mrs. Boot puts a trailer on the car, and Poppy and Sam put a wire crate inside it. They drive to the market and walk past cows, sheep, and pigs to a shed full of bird cages. Mrs. Boot chooses four young white geese and pays a woman for them. Poppy sees a lonely duck and buys it with her own money. When they return, Mrs. Boot brings the crate, and the woman puts the geese inside. Before Sam shuts the door, one goose jumps out and runs from the shed. The three of them chase it. The goose jumps through an open car door, but it escapes when another woman opens the door on the other side. It runs into the plant tent, where Sam catches it. Then they go home with the four geese and Poppy’s duck. Sam says, “Markets are fun.”

New cars are coming to Radiator Springs to see Lightning McQueen, so the town gets ready. McQueen paves a smooth road for his fans. Ramone gives himself fresh paint and plans to paint the visiting cars. Sarge leads boot camp to get visiting 4x4s into good shape. Filmore makes fuel for thirsty fans. Luigi has new tires at Casadella Tires, and Guido helps McQueen try them on. Flo prepares her diner, where cars can sip oil with friends. Red waters flowers, while Sally fixes her motel for resting guests. Frank cuts and harvests grain, and Mater makes him work extra hard. Sheriff puts up signs so cars will not speed. Doc is ready to give tired cars a tune-up. Lizzy gets bumper stickers to sell. Corey reports the latest news, and How of the Lightyear blimp flies overhead to announce visitors. The work is done, so the cars go out and have fun.

When snow falls to the ground and all the trees are bare, everyone knows it is winter, including the rabbit. In winter, some animals fly away from the cold, while others stay where they live. Some have a long, cozy sleep where they live. Some swim to warmer waters, while some have a thick, woolly coat and can stay in the snow. Some gather extra food for winter, while some travel far to find things to eat. Some stay very still, while some keep busy, moving fast and staying warm. The animals spend winter in different ways: some leave, some sleep, some swim, some stay in the snow, some gather food, some travel far, and some keep moving. When the snow has melted and the trees are in bloom, everyone knows it is spring, including the rabbit.

On the night before Valentine’s Day, children in town quietly gathered paper, glue, scissors, and paint to make cards for their friends. They decorated giant hearts, wrote names on envelopes, and went to bed hoping their friends had made cards too. The next morning, the classroom was bright with red, pink, and white decorations. A giant bouquet arrived for the teacher from a secret admirer, whom everyone knew was Mr. O’Meyer. The children played pin the heart, won silly prizes, and had their faces painted with hearts. Girls ran away from kissy face boys. Then the children delivered and opened cards, laughing at the wild messages. They ate cherries and grapes, drank fruit punch with heart-shaped ice cubes, and thought the party was over. At quarter past one, the principal appeared dressed as Cupid. He quickly left a present and a note that said, “Happy Valentine’s Day to one and to all.”

Christopher Robin had stuffed animals, and Winnie the Pooh was his favorite bear. They played in the Hundred Acre Wood. One morning, Pooh woke in his tree house with a very hungry tummy, but every honey pot was empty. He went outside to find honey. Pooh tried to fool bees with a branch, but they chased him, so he hid. Then he asked Eeyore for honey, but found none. Eeyore noticed that Pooh had lost his tail and promised to help find it. Owl said they should offer a reward for a replacement tail, but Pooh misunderstood “issue” as a sneeze and thought they needed honey. Christopher Robin made signs saying “A very important thing to do,” and Pooh posted them. Tigger pounced on Balloon and wrestled with him, then went to be a hero. At a meeting, Christopher Robin announced a contest to find Eeyore a new tail. Pooh drew a honey pot, so the prize would be honey, and the contest began.

One sunny spring morning, Winnie-the-Pooh was hungry and had no honey. He went to Rabbit’s tidy house and learned that bees need flowers and gardens to make honey. Pooh thought this meant gardens grow honey, so he told Piglet about a secret garden. Tigger found a good spot, and the friends asked Owl how to plant it. Owl said they needed seeds, and Rabbit gave them some. Pooh, Piglet, Tigger, Owl, Kanga, and Roo planted the seeds. They waited while plants grew and bees buzzed, but no honey appeared. Pooh found a tomato instead and wished the garden would grow honey. Rabbit came with Roo and said there was no secret: they only had to follow a bee to its hive. The bee flew into a stump, where Pooh found honey. The secret garden was not secret anymore. Pooh’s friends picked vegetables, while Pooh happily collected honey and became sticky.

Everyone in town knew Edua, a dinosaur who played with neighborhood kids, helped little old ladies cross the street, and baked chocolate chip cookies. Everybody loved her except Reginald Bon Hoopy Dooby, who knew almost everything and liked giving class reports. He planned to report that dinosaurs were totally extinct. During his report, Beth Mcer, Tommy Briter, and Miss Mink pointed out that Edua was a dinosaur who was still helping people and baking cookies. Everyone went outside to eat cookies, so Reginald thought no one listened to him. He decided to prove dinosaurs were extinct and make Edua disappear. The next morning, his flyers and protests failed, and nobody listened. Reginald finally cried. Edua offered to listen, so he took her to his classroom and explained the truth about dinosaurs. His convincing talk made Edua believe she was extinct. However, she did not care, and Reginald no longer cared either.

At 13 Go Away Lane, Bruce the bear received a fun letter about a visit from Cousin Proof, but he ate it because he disliked fun. He said no to his family’s playful ideas so often that Thistle, Rupert, Nibs, and the geese made secret wishes for him to change. The next morning, Bruce left for a fishing trip while Kevin arrived. Their wishes seemed to replace grumpy Bruce with cheerful, adventurous, pizzazz-filled Kevin, who brought sandwiches and loved fun. Everyone enjoyed candy fights, huge pizza orders, shouting, and an indoor pool until fun became too much. The family wished for regular Bruce to return, while Kevin wished for more fun and left on a fun bus. Bruce came home, saw his unhappy family, and agreed to try fun. However, when he saw the mess in his house, he became grumpy again. Everything returned to normal: the mice hugged Bruce, Bruce wanted the day to end, and the geese received 26 pizzas instead of sandwiches.

“Kiki Ricky,” crowed the rooster, and Jack woke wanting a big pancake. His busy mother said he must help. Jack cut wheat with a sickle, carried it on the donkey to the mill, and helped the miller thresh it. The miller used the water wheel and millstone to grind the grain into flour. Jack then gathered the other ingredients: he fed grain to the black hen, who laid an egg; milked the spotted cow; churned cream into butter; brought firewood; and fetched strawberry jam from the cellar. In the kitchen, his mother told him how to mix flour, egg, and milk until the batter was smooth. She heated butter in a frying pan and poured in the batter. When the pancake was golden brown underneath, she flipped it into the air and cooked the other side. She put it on a plate and spread jam on top. Jack said he knew what to do now.

Martin Luther King Jr. was born in 1929 in Atlanta, Georgia. As a child, he learned that Black people faced unfair treatment and white-only places because of segregation. He read about Black leaders, became an excellent student, and decided to become a minister. After studying at Morehouse College and Boston University, he married Ketta Scott and became a pastor in Montgomery, Alabama.

When Rosa Parks was arrested, Dr. King led a peaceful bus protest. He told angry followers, “We must meet hate with love.” After almost a year, buses no longer had white-only sections. In Atlanta, he led protests and the 1963 March on Washington, where he gave his “I have a dream” speech. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964, and new laws ended legal segregation. In 1968, James Earl Ray shot Dr. King in Memphis while Dr. King supported equal pay for Black and white garbage workers. Dr. King died, dreaming of a world free of hate, prejudice, and violence.

Martin Luther King Jr. was born in Atlanta, Georgia. As a child, he played, sang in his father’s church, and read books about Black leaders. He cried when white friends could not play with him. His mother explained that Black people were not always treated fairly. Martin became a minister and married Ketta Scott. In Montgomery, Rosa Parks was told to give up her bus seat. She refused, and Dr. King led a peaceful bus protest. He told people, “We must meet hate with love.” The protest ended white-only bus sections. Dr. King then led peaceful protests and marches in Atlanta. In 1963, more than 200,000 people joined him at the March on Washington. He said, “I have a dream” of a fair nation. In 1964, he won the Nobel Peace Prize. New laws ended many white-only places. In 1968, James Earl Ray shot Dr. King in Memphis. Dr. King dreamed of a world free of hate, prejudice, and violence.

Since he hatched, Al the owl wished to become a knight. He imagined being brave, clever, and surrounded by friends. When Knights began disappearing from the castle, Al applied to night school and was accepted. He struggled with swords and shields and often nodded off during the day, but he worked hard and graduated with honor. Al became part of the Night Watch and guarded the castle walls while the other Knights slept. One very dark, quiet night, he heard a Dragon’s wings. The hungry Dragon wanted to eat him because Al looked like a midnight snack. Al was afraid, but he puffed out his feathers and said he was a knight. Then he cleverly explained that he was too small and suggested pizza instead. The Dragon loved pizza. They discovered they both hatched from eggs and liked the night, so they became friends. Afterward, no Knights disappeared, and Al proudly patrolled the walls, brave, clever, and with many friends.

Jack hides model plane because Nancy always wants to help. She finds him and offers to glue the wings, but he says he must meet Angie and Melton for the Shady Woods snowman contest. Nancy joins them, but the rules allow only three team members, so she builds her own snowman. Clyde and his friends make fun of it and ruin it while pretending to help. Jack tells them to leave Nancy alone, then decides to help fix the snowman. Angie and Melton return to their team, while Jack and Nancy work together. Nancy shapes the snowman, and Jack discovers that helping can be fun. Her regular, midsized snowman does not win; Angie and Melton win the trophy. Jack feels sad for a moment, but he joins Nancy in celebrating them. On the way home, he tells Nancy she is good at making snowmen. After dinner, Jack learns she is also good at making trophies.

One small snowflake falls, but making a snowman needs billions of snowflakes. They pile into a mound, and the snowflakes are patted, packed, and rolled into one big ball. A middle-size ball and a small ball are made for the top, and the three balls are stacked. A short, flat hat or a tall hat goes on top, and two bottle caps become the snowman's eyes. A carrot can fill the empty space in the middle of his face. Five walnut buttons in a row, a belt, boots, a big wool scarf, a broom, mittens, earmuffs, a fanny pack, and something to read complete his clothes and things to hold. That's absolutely all you need for a snowman. Then one small snowflake falls again. Soon soft white snowflakes fill the sky, float down everywhere, and pile up high. And that's all you need for a snowman's friend.

Easter morning, Bonnie finds an Easter basket filled with candy, eggs, and jelly beans. Inside, the toys see a bunny and think it is a new toy. Woody says, “Howdy,” but the bunny does not say hello. Mr. Potato Head makes a funny face, but the bunny does not giggle. Mr. Prickle Pants sings and dances, but the bunny does not clap or cheer. Rex and Trixie play a game, yet the bunny does not play alone. Dolly has a tea party, but the bunny does not sip tea. Buzz sounds his laser, but the bunny does not wake up. The toys wonder why the bunny does not want to play. Bonnie comes and bites the bunny’s ear, shocking the toys. Then they discover that the bunny is not a toy. It is a chocolate bunny. Everyone laughs, and this Easter is full of surprises.

A five-year-old child becomes frightened when pieces of hair appear in a comb, fuzz comes out of the child's body, skin peels from the toes, and a gray, wet chunk falls from the nose. The child thinks the stuffing, skin, and even a little brain are coming out and worries about falling apart. While reading Dr. Seuss, the child discovers a loose tooth and fears being unable to eat. The child decides the glue holding everything together is failing and imagines losing ears, eyeballs, an arm, or a head, ending as a shapeless pile. The child is thankful that Dad has lots of masking tape. Dad explains that losing baby teeth is normal because new teeth will grow, and says there is nothing to fear about the child's hair, skin, and everything else. The child feels relieved, then asks what the yellow stuff from the ear is.

George visited a Christmas tree farm with the Man with the Yellow Hat to choose a tree. Although George promised to stay close, he climbed the tallest tree to see all the trees. Two men cut down that tree and carried George away on a truck. The truck stopped at a hospital, where George explored, played, and found his tree. He decorated it with things he found, including an x-ray and a balloon, and mixed up some gifts. The nurse wanted to remove him, but the sick children laughed at his funny tree and asked him to stay. The nurse agreed if George helped fix it. The children returned his decorations and gave him real ornaments, while George hung lights and tinsel. Then George helped open gifts and made the children laugh. The Man with the Yellow Hat arrived after following the truck, and George was reunited with him. Santa Claus came with a golden star. At the children’s request, George placed it on top of the tree.

A boy named Buzz had a pet fly, Fly Guy, who could say “Buzz.” Fly Guy joined Buzz at football practice. Coach needed one more player, but laughed when Buzz said Fly Guy could play. Fly Guy kicked the ball, went out for a pass, and tried to tackle Buzz. Coach said flies could not play football, but Fly Guy could come to the game. Before the game, Buzz made Fly Guy a helmet. They practiced, planned a secret play, and created a touchdown dance. At the game, Fly Guy sat on the bench while teams scored. With one second left, the Go-Getters were behind 14–17, the other team was about to score, and a player was hurt. Coach let Fly Guy play because the game seemed lost. Buzz said it was time for their secret play. Fly Guy flew up the quarterback’s nose, so the quarterback dropped the ball. Buzz picked it up and scored. Fly Guy and Buzz did their dance, and the team cheered, “We won! Hooray for Fly Guy!”

A boy named Buzz had a pet fly named Fly Guy. Fly Guy could say, "Buzz." Fly Guy went with Buzz to play football. Coach said they needed one more player, but he laughed when Buzz said Fly Guy could play. Fly Guy kicked the ball, went out for a pass, and tried to tackle Buzz. Coach said flies could not play football, but Fly Guy could come to the game. Before the game, Buzz made Fly Guy a helmet. They practiced, planned a secret play, and made a touchdown dance. At the big game, Fly Guy sat on the bench. The Go-Getters were behind, 14 to 17, with one second left. A player was hurt, so Coach let Fly Guy play. Fly Guy flew up the quarterback's nose, and the boy dropped the ball. Buzz picked it up and scored. Fly Guy and Buzz did their touchdown dance. The team cheered, "We won! Hooray for Fly Guy!"

Mr. Silly lives in Nonsense Land, where red trees, blue grass, hat-wearing dogs, and backward-flying birds make everything silly. He lives in a house with its upstairs in the wrong place and dreams of winning the Nonsense Cup. While eating a silly breakfast, he remembers past winners: Mr. Ridiculous wallpapered the outside of his house, and Mr. Foolish invented a car with square wheels. Mr. Silly cannot think of an idea, so he walks outside and meets animals wearing unusual clothes and making the wrong sounds. Then he gets a beautiful, silly idea. He buys paint and a paintbrush. At the cup ceremony, Mr. Muddle shows a square apple, and Miss Ninkmp presents a very silly teapot. Before the king can announce the winner, he notices that the city tree has green leaves instead of red ones. Mr. Silly says he painted them green while everyone slept. The crowd cheers, and the king gives Mr. Silly the Nonsense Cup for the silliest idea. A bird says “Woof” and flies away backwards.

Our class wants to learn what a doctor does, so we talk to Dr. Zambiel, a pediatrician who treats children. He works in a clinic and sees about 20 patients each day. He finds out what is wrong, then patients may need medicine, rest, or a hospital visit. Doctors write prescriptions for medicine. Children may see specialists who treat one part of the body. Dr. Zambiel says children should have yearly checkups. He examines their ears, listens to their hearts, and asks about healthy food and exercise. An otoscope helps doctors look in ears, and a stethoscope helps them listen to hearts. Nurses give shots that protect children from diseases such as measles. Dr. Zambiel studied for 24 years, then had more training as a resident and fellow. He also teaches medical students at the hospital, where they learn by seeing real patients. After Laney tells about breaking her arm and getting an x-ray, the class goes to recess. Running keeps them healthy, so they thank Dr. Zambiel for helping them feel their best.

One morning, somebody put a chocolate chicken in the bird bath. Max said, “I love you,” but Ruby said they must first have an egg hunt. Whoever found the most eggs would get the chocolate chicken. Max searched, but he found only a mud puddle, acorns, and a spoon. He said, “No eggs, no chicken.” Ruby found many colorful eggs: yellow, blue, red, gold, turquoise, and lavender. Ruby told Max to pull himself together, so he searched with her. Max bound some ants and made ant and acorn pancakes, while Ruby kept finding eggs. Ruby counted her eggs and said she would get the chicken. Max hid because he had found no eggs. Ruby looked for him. While hiding, Max ate the chocolate chicken’s tail, head, and wings. Ruby offered him half the chicken, but Max came out after eating it. Ruby asked how he could do this to her. Max said, “I love you.”

When you lose front teeth, new people teeth grow in. The story asks what it would be like to have animal teeth. Beaver teeth are strong, orange, and keep growing for cutting trees. Great white shark teeth are sharp, and new teeth slide in when old ones fall out. A narwhal has one long tooth called a tusk. Elephant tusks can dig, pull roots, and lift heavy things. Rattlesnake fangs inject venom. Naked mole rat teeth dig tunnels and can move like chopsticks. Vampire bat teeth stay sharp for biting skin. Hippo teeth scare enemies and stay white. Bengal tiger teeth hold heavy things, while crocodile teeth change and birds clean them. Camel teeth bite thorny plants but wear down. Animal teeth could be cool, but people use front teeth to eat, talk, and smile. The teeth that replace lost teeth will be people teeth.

Martin Luther King Jr. was a boy who fell many times, but he always got back up. He loved books and big words. When he was six, his white friend could no longer play with him because Martin was black. Martin learned that people were treated unfairly because of skin color, but his parents taught him to answer hurt with love. He became a minister and learned about peaceful change from Gandhi. After Rosa Parks was arrested, Martin helped lead a bus boycott in Montgomery, Alabama. Black people and some white people stopped riding buses for more than a year, and the rules changed. Martin led more peaceful protests, including marches in Birmingham and Washington, where he shared his dream of freedom. Children joined the protests too. In Selma, marchers were attacked, but they stayed peaceful and kept going until they reached Montgomery. Laws changed. Martin taught that people must stand together, choose peace, and keep moving forward for justice and freedom.

Ariel hides a shell for Flounder to find, but he searches in the wrong places. He pulls up a strange, shiny, smooth, long object with a round end. Ariel imagines it comes from the human world and guesses it could be a key, a music tool, or a magic wand. Sebastian says it is a spoon used by humans to eat, and warns Ariel to throw it away because her father dislikes the surface. Ariel shows the spoon to her sisters and finds more human objects. Her sisters say humans might use them to capture mermaids, smash fish, or summon witches. Ariel's father warns her that humans are dangerous and tells her never to visit the surface or collect their things. Still, Ariel and Flounder search for a hiding place and discover a secret grotto. There they find a necklace with a pearl. Ariel thinks humans admire her world, so they may not be terrible, and hopes to learn about them someday.

Jack and Annie go to the magic treehouse in Frog Creek Woods. They find a green silk bookmark in the Egypt book. They wish to visit ancient Egypt. A black cat with yellow eyes appears, and the treehouse carries them to a desert. They follow a funeral parade to a pyramid, but the parade vanishes. Inside, they meet Hutapy, the ghost Queen of the Nile. She needs her book of the dead to travel to the next life. Jack reads hieroglyphs, and they find the book hidden in a jug inside a boat. Jack puts it by Hutapy’s mummy. Then Jack and Annie get lost in a false passage. They follow the cat’s meow and escape. Back in the treehouse, they wish to return to Frog Creek. They see an M on the floor and wonder about M. They promise to bring back the medallion and bookmark. Their mom is making peanut butter and jelly sandwiches.

One day, Daisy tells Minnie about a contest for the funniest photo. Minnie decides to enter, so she takes her camera to find funny things. First, she photographs Donald using a watering can in the clubhouse garden. Her camera goes, “Snap, snap.” Then she photographs Goofy stuck in a tight spot. She photographs Daisy wearing a silly costume. She photographs Pluto with fine, feathered, and furry friends by the lake. Professor von Drake waves hello. Then he slips, and Minnie takes his picture too. At last, Minnie sees a frog riding Mickey’s bicycle. Mickey says, “Hey!” and the frog says, “Ribbit.” Minnie enters all her photos in the contest. The judges laugh most at the photo of the frog riding the bicycle. Therefore, Minnie wins first prize. When Minnie looks at her pictures, she starts to giggle. She sure has some funny friends.

The story describes several kinds of snow. Snow that falls softly at night feels like a shy friend and brings peace. Snow that falls in cheerful flakes while people are at school or work promises to send them home over slippery white roads to the rooms they love. Light snow shows delicate tree branches, lamppost light, and a sparrow’s feet, while heavy snow buries cars, bends evergreens, and keeps kitties curled up. Children love snow, so they put on red boots and mittens, catch flakes on their tongues, and roll down hills. Snow gives them angels and new friends. While it stays, it reminds people that nothing lasts forever except memories. They can walk through the beautiful world, then return to quiet white homes for a warm drink, reading, a game, or conversation. As flowers, the sun, and green gardens sleep, it is the snow’s turn to fall, and everyone will watch it.

At the Great Barrier Reef, Coral and Marlin expected babies. A barracuda killed Coral and all but one egg. Marlin promised to protect Nemo. When Nemo touched a boat, a diver took him to Sydney. Marlin met Dory and followed clues from the scuba mask. Nemo was in a dentist’s tank, where Gil and the tank gang planned an escape before Darla got Nemo as a birthday gift. Marlin and Dory survived dangers and reached Sydney with help from turtles and a whale. Nemo jammed the filter and escaped down a drain. Dory found him, but Marlin thought he was gone. They reunited and followed Marlin’s words, “Just keep swimming, swimming,” to save Dory and other fish from a net. Marlin and Nemo returned home. Marlin let Nemo go to school and have an adventure. In Sydney, the tank gang escaped and planned their next move.

Spookley was a strange little pumpkin who was square instead of round. The other pumpkins teased him, and he wished he could roll like them. One night before Halloween, a mighty storm tossed the round pumpkins around and broke the fence. Three pumpkins rolled toward the bay, so Spookley tipped, flipped, and blocked the hole with his body. More pumpkins crashed into him, but he stayed in place and saved the patch. At dawn, the farmer found Spookley bruised but strong against the broken fence. He saved Spookley's special seeds and planted them the next year. Soon the garden had hundreds of pumpkins in many shapes and colors, including squares, cubes, rectangles, triangles, blue pumpkins, and polka-dot pumpkins. Every Halloween, people visited Spookley's patch and chose pumpkins of different shapes. At the end, the story says you cannot judge a book or a pumpkin by its cover.

T-Rexes can't tie their shoes. The narrator says that being small can make it hard to reach a shelf or get dressed by yourself. The narrator also says, "You're not alone, my dear friend," because animals have hard things to do, too. A long list shows what animals cannot do: alligators can't pick apples, bees can't ride bicycles, Cheetas can't chew bubblegum, dogs can't wash dishes, elephants can't fit in elevators, foxes can't flip pancakes, giraffes can't do gymnastics, and horses can't play hopscotch. It also says that kangaroos can't practice Kung Fu, monkeys can't do magic tricks, narwhals can't eat nachos, owls can't fold origami, penguins can't play pingpong, and seahorses can't sing. Urchins can't open umbrellas, vampire bats can't vacuum, walruses can't make waffles, xenops can't play xylophones, yaks can't throw yo-yos, and zebras can't go ziplining. The animals can have a lot of fun trying.

Whenever trouble happens in Adventure Bay, Ryder calls the PAW Patrol to the lookout. The six pups report for a mission, and Ryder chooses the best pups for the job. Chase, the organized police pup, can direct traffic and solve mysteries. Marshall is a fire dog who uses his hose, though he sometimes trips. Rubble digs and builds with his construction tools. Skye flies her helicopter and helps from the air. Rocky reuses old things with his tools and mechanical claw. Zuma dives underwater with his hovercraft. Their pup houses change into special vehicles, and their Pup Packs hold useful tools. After getting the mission, the pups roll out to help. They use their special skills and work together because no job is too big and no pup is too small. When the work is done, Ryder gives them pup treats. Then Ryder and the pups play at the pup park while the citizens of Adventure Bay stay safe.

Long ago, Hamato Yoshi bought four turtles. Green goo made the turtles human-sized and changed Hamato into a human rat. He became Splinter. For 15 years, he lived in a sewer with the turtles, teaching them ninja skills. Leonardo was brave. Michelangelo loved fun. Donatello was smart. Raphael was tough. On their 15th birthday, Splinter let them visit the surface. They explored the city, found pizza, and saw April being taken with her dad. The turtles tried to help, but they could not work as a team, so the Krang got away. Splinter chose Leonardo as their leader. The turtles returned and followed the van. They learned that the Krang were alien robots with brains and were capturing scientists. At the hideout, the Krang took April and her dad. Snake became the giant weed Snakeweed after green goo covered him. The turtles saved April when she fell from a helicopter and escaped Snakeweed when a generator exploded. April's dad was still held by the Krang, so the turtles promised to help. Now they were a team.

George’s mother asks him to bark, but George always says, “No.” She tells him that cats say “Wow,” ducks say “Quack quack,” pigs say “Oink oink,” and dogs say “Arf!” Each time she asks him to bark again, George says, “No.” Since George will not bark, his mother takes him to the vet. The vet says he will find the problem and asks George to bark. Instead, he reaches inside George and pulls out a cat. He asks George to bark again, but George says, “No.” The vet reaches deeper and pulls out a duck, then reaches even deeper and pulls out a pig. George still says, “No.” Finally, the vet reaches very deep and pulls out bark, but George still says, “No.” George’s mother is thrilled. She kisses the vet, the cat, the duck, the pig, and the cow. On the way home, she wants to show George to everyone in the street. She says, “Bark, George!” But George surprises her by saying, “Hello.”

An egg rolled through the trees, across a meadow, and down a hill into Mother Duck’s nest. Mother Duck was reading and did not notice. Four ducklings hatched: Crayon had blue spots, Zebra had brown stripes, Moonlight was yellow, and the odd-looking GUI GUI said, “GUI GUI.” Mother Duck taught them to swim, dive, and waddle. GUI GUI learned fastest and grew bigger and stronger, but Mother Duck loved all four equally. One day, three crocodiles came from the lake. They said GUI GUI looked like them and told him to take the ducks to the bridge, where they would eat them. GUI GUI felt worried, but decided to protect his family. The next day, he brought the ducks to the bridge for diving practice. Instead of ducks, three big rocks fell onto the crocodiles’ teeth. Crack, crack, crack! The crocodiles ran away. GUI GUI saved the ducks, so everyone celebrated. He stayed with his family and became a stronger, happier crocoduck.

Mowgli was left alone as a baby, but Bagheera the panther took him to a wolf family. Mowgli grew up with the wolves and loved them as brothers. When Shere Khan the tiger returned, Akela said Mowgli must leave because the pack could not protect him. Bagheera led Mowgli toward the man village, but Mowgli ran away because he wanted to stay in the jungle. He marched with elephants, then met Baloo the bear. Bagheera found him, but Mowgli refused to go, so Bagheera left him. Monkeys carried Mowgli to the ruined city, where King Louie wanted the secret of man's red fire. Baloo and Bagheera rescued him, but Mowgli ran away again. Shere Khan found him, and Mowgli scared the tiger away with a burning branch. Mowgli then understood that the jungle was dangerous. He went with Baloo and Bagheera to the man village. A girl's song drew Mowgli inside, while his friends returned to the jungle.

A queen wished for a daughter with lips red as blood, skin white as snow, and hair black as ebony. Snow White was born, but her mother died. Her father, the king, married a beautiful but cruel queen who loved her magic mirror. When the mirror said Snow White was fairest, the queen ordered a huntsman to kill her. The huntsman spared Snow White, so she hid in the forest and found the home of the Seven Dwarfs. She cleaned their house, and they let her stay with them. The queen learned Snow White was alive and disguised herself as an old woman. She gave Snow White a poisoned apple, and Snow White fell lifeless. The queen escaped but fell into a chasm. The dwarfs kept watch over Snow White. A prince found her and kissed her, and she awoke. Then the Seven Dwarfs rejoiced, and the prince carried Snow White to his castle in the clouds.

An old sow sent her three little pigs into the world to seek their fortunes and told them to write because she loved them. The first pig built a house of straw, and the second built one of sticks. A hungry wolf huffed and puffed both houses in and gobbled up both pigs. The third pig built a strong brick house, saying, “Nice and solid.” The wolf asked to enter, but the third pig refused. The wolf could not blow it down, so he tried tricks. The pig gathered turnips and apples before the wolf arrived, then escaped from him at the fair by hiding in a butter churn. The frightened wolf ran home, but later climbed onto the pig’s roof. The pig quickly heated a big iron pot. When the wolf came down, the pig cooked him and gobbled him up.

The first people in America were Indians, who came from Asia thousands of years ago. When Columbus arrived in 1492, he called the people Indians, although each tribe had its own name and language. European settlers moved west, sometimes sharing knowledge with tribes but often fighting them for land, until Indians lost most of their land. Different tribes adapted to their regions. Algonquian and Wampanoag people lived near the Atlantic and taught settlers to grow corn and squash. Seminoles escaped to Florida swamps, while Iroquois lived in long houses. Plains tribes followed buffalo, especially after horses arrived, using nearly every part of the animal for food, clothing, tools, and homes. Pueblo peoples farmed dry lands, built adobe homes, and held dances and meetings in kivas. Navajos raised sheep and wove blankets. Northwest Coast tribes fished, hunted whales, carved totem poles, and held potlatches. Tribes also used sign language and smoke signals to communicate across distances.

Long ago, Indians came to America from Asia. Many tribes lived in different places and spoke different languages. Columbus called them Indians. European settlers came later and moved west. Sometimes settlers and Indians helped each other, but often they fought over land, and the Indians lost most of their land. Different tribes lived in different ways. Algonquian people hunted and fished and lived in wigwams. The Wampanoag taught settlers to grow corn and squash. Seminoles ran away to Florida. Iroquois people lived in long houses. Plains Indians hunted buffalo. Horses helped tribes follow buffalo herds. They used buffalo meat, hides, bones, horns, and hoofs for many things. Pueblo Indians farmed in dry places and lived in pueblos. They made pottery, baskets, and cloth, and danced for rain and crops. Northwest Coast Indians fished, hunted whales, built canoes, and carved totem poles. Indian languages gave names to many places. Tribes used sign language and smoke signals to send messages.

It is autumn, and a strong wind carries flower seeds across the land. The Tiny Seed is smaller and slower than the others, but it survives dangers: the sun burns one seed, ice traps another, and other seeds drown, dry out, or are eaten. In winter, snow covers the seeds, while a Hungry Mouse eats one; the Tiny Seed stays still and survives. In spring, the seeds become plants. A weed blocks sunlight from one plant, and a child breaks another. The Tiny Seed finally grows, but a faster plant blooms first until a boy picks its flower. In summer, the Tiny Seed’s plant grows taller than people, trees, and houses. It becomes a giant flower that attracts birds, bees, butterflies, and many visitors. In autumn, its petals fall, and stronger wind shakes open the flower’s seed pod. Many tiny seeds fly away across the land, beginning the journey again.

On January 6, bored twelve-year-old Ben Ripley finds CIA agent Alexander Hale in his home. Hale says the CIA has watched Ben because of his excellent grades, language skills, mathematics, electronics ability, and STIQ results, and accepts him immediately into its secret Academy of Espionage. Ben leaves without telling his parents, who think he is attending St. Smithen’s Science Academy, because he wants to become a spy like Hale. On January 16, Hale brings Ben to the academy in Washington, D.C., a gloomy school hidden behind a wall. Soon after Ben arrives, gunfire erupts. He reaches the dormitory and is tackled by a masked girl, who reveals herself as a skilled student. She gives Ben a taser and explains that enemies have infiltrated the campus, taken the students and faculty hostage, and jammed communications. She reports that forty-one heavily armed enemies are nearby. The girl says, “Welcome to spy school.”

Ben Ripley is an ordinary middle school boy who dreams of becoming a spy. Alexander Hale, a CIA agent, arrives at Ben’s home and says Ben has been accepted into the secret Academy of Espionage. Ben learns that his excellent grades, mathematical gift, languages, electronics skills, and hidden CIA test answers helped him get in. He agrees to leave home at once, hide the academy from everyone, and live there for six years. At the academy in Washington, D.C., Ben sees no students. Alexander suddenly tells him to run while he shoots at attackers. Ben reaches the dormitory and is tackled by a masked girl. She reveals herself as a skilled student, gives Ben a taser, and leads him through the building. She explains that enemies have captured the students and teachers during an assembly. There are forty-one dangerous commandos, and their messages are blocked. The girl smiles and says, “Welcome to spy school.”

The speaker asks if you wake up with a wiggle and wiggle out of it. If you wiggle with breakfast, it might wind up on your head. You can wiggle where your tail would be, wiggle all your hair, feel extra silly, and wiggle in your underwear. You can also wiggle with your shadow and toys, and wonder if gorillas make a wiggle noise. In the water, you can wiggle one fin on each side or wiggle like a crocodile, open big and wide. When you wiggle where your wings would be, wiggles fill the sky. You should wiggle slowly near polar bears because they are very wiggle shy. Snakes are one big wiggle, with no wings, no tails, and no feet. Some wiggles are worth waiting for, followed by “Wiggle, wiggle, tweet.” The speaker asks you to join a wiggle and wonders if you would wiggle on the moon. At the end, the speaker says, “I think we're all the wiggles now,” and, “See you wiggles soon.”

Dead Eye, a seven-foot supervillain, and his henchmen, the Dead Boys, chase a skinny boy into Mr. Lee’s Deli. When Marco Jackson gets scared, he gets mad and changes into Toothpick, a superhero with finger spears. Toothpick defeats Dead Eye, but the scene is Marco’s comic drawing. JR visits Marco, asking about Tyrell’s attack and inviting him to play Army of the Undead 3. Marco agrees despite his father’s rule and plays for three hours before Dad comes home, takes the game box, and tells him to go cold turkey. Dad then enrolls Marcus in an after-school program; study lab is full, and Marcus refuses sports, so he chooses filmmaking. In class, he meets Jasmine, Khalid, Amari, and Sierra, whose insults make him angry. The teachers ask the group to create Sierra’s screenplay, Phone Zombies, for the fall arts showcase. Marcus wants Toothpick to be the big movie instead, so he promises to bring his own screenplays, believing his movie will crush hers.

Dead Eye, a supervillain, chases skinny Marco Jackson into Mr. Lee’s Deli, but Marco gets scared and becomes Toothpick, the world’s greatest superhero. Toothpick defeats Dead Eye and the Dead Boys. In real life, Marcus is drawing this comic when JR arrives. JR says Tyrell’s crew chased Marcus from the bus stop to the deli, but Marcus denies it. They play Army of the Undead 3, even though Dad forbids gaming on school days. Dad comes home, takes the game box, and tells Marcus to go cold turkey. After dinner, Dad signs Marcus up for filmmaking because art class has too many rules and study lab is full. In class, Marcus meets Jasmine, Khalid, Amari, Sierra, Darren, and Trish. Sierra argues with Marcus, and he gets angry. Darren asks Marcus to make a superhero movie, so Marcus dreams of making a Toothpick movie starring himself. But the class chooses Sierra’s screenplay, Phone Zombies, for its big project. Marcus says he has screenplays and promises to bring them tomorrow, planning to use his Toothpick comics.

EB worked with his peeps and crew to make Easter eggs, and he brings them to children. His real name is secret because his job requires him to hide his identity, but he says he is the Easter Bunny. He comes to homes when people have Easter spirit. Children try to catch him with carrots, but he is too fast. A rug covering a hole cannot stop him because burrowing is his life. He dances on a lit floor and escapes behind a door. He avoids a clever trap because his supersonic ears help him. He dodges flying fish and cherry yogurt pops, changes from two feet tall to small and gray, and escapes the Bunny Tumbler 2.0 with his lucky rabbit’s feet. He leaves Easter treats so no children are sad, though they are hopping mad when he escapes. After delivering treats to children big and small, EB visits his favorite kid and says he will return next year.

Vikram and I spend bedtime in Nana’s grand room, playing a good night game. We greet Ganesha by the window, marigolds, the milk moon, planes, curtains, a breeze, and a shy baby gecko. We also say good night to the dew-covered mantle and the golden idols Brahma, Shiva, and Vishnu. When Nana says it is bedtime, we brush our teeth while Tata kisses our hands and tickles our feet. Tata tells stories, then falls asleep in bed. In the Puja room, we prepare a round tray, light the deepam, smell flowers and perfume, and press our palms together. Though we want to keep playing, we whisper that we must end the day, and Tata’s loud snore scares sleep away. After one more peacock tale, Nana hums while drinking spicy chai. We yawn, hug Nana, and lie down. We snuggle with our bear as Nana caresses our hair. Ganesha watches as sleep wins, and we say good night to family, love, and the stars.

Every St Patrick's Day, Mr. Fish dresses as a leprechaun with a tall hat, whiskers, and a pot of gold. This year, his pot is empty, and he loses his cheer. Mrs. Squid tells everyone about the missing treasure. Mr. Eight leads the search. They swim up and down, over and under, while Pout-Pout Fish leads the parade. They look in the big, big dark, visit oysters near the Shamrock, and search a sunken pirate ship. They find pearls and golden coins, but not Mr. Fish's treasure. Some Searchers leave. Then Mr. Fish has an idea and swims to a hidden hollow at Rainbow Reef. There he finds shimmering yellow butterfly fish. “We found the gold at the end of the rainbow,” says Mr. Eight. The golden fish swim into Mr. Fish's pot and complete his costume. Everyone happily parades home. “What a lucky day,” says Mr. Fish. “Happy St Patrick's Day to one and all!”

It's a great day when Pete the Cat goes to space camp and meets his bunkmate, Glenn. After an announcement, Pete and Glenn put on uniforms and hurry to class. Astronauts Tom and Chris teach the campers about space, and the campers practice being astronauts in a zero-gravity chamber, rovers, and rockets. Pete's rocket flies very far, and Glenn cheers for him. At mission control, Tom announces that a flight to the moon leaves that day. Sally asks Pete to join, and Pete agrees. Pete buckles into the space capsule and blasts off with Tom and Sally. They pass a satellite, see a comet, and Pete plays his guitar in space. On the moon, they collect rocks and map its surface. Pete wears a jetpack to take pictures near Mars, but loses track of time. He rushes back before the ship leaves. The astronauts return home, and Pete plays more tunes, happy to stand on solid ground.

Lucas is an ordinary boy whose favorite toy is Teddy. He makes a rude mistake when he teases Lisa about her glasses and makes her cry. At home, Mom tells him Lisa is sad, what he did was wrong, and he needs to be kind. She explains that kindness means gentle words, respect for older and younger people, and help for anyone in need. Lucas decides to become kind in the morning. He thanks Mom, puts away his toys, and makes his bed. On the bus, he offers the new boy a seat and helps him find his classroom. He shares with friends and apologizes to Lisa, who says, “It’s okay.” Lucas waits for the slide, helps find a lost ball, picks up trash, holds a store door, and helps an old lady cross the street. At home, he helps Dad, his sister, and his neighbor. Lucas stops teasing and selfish behavior and learns that kindness comes back when people help without asking for anything.

Once, a city had no gardens, trees, or greenery. Most people stayed indoors, and the city was dreary. Liam was the one boy who loved being outside, even on drizzly days. One morning, he found a dark stairwell near the old railway. He climbed to the tracks. There he discovered dying wild flowers and plants, so he returned the next day and began caring for them. At first, he nearly drowned the flowers and had pruning problems, but he learned, and the plants grew into a garden. The garden spread along the railway and explored it with Liam. Winter snow kept Liam away, so he prepared tools and plans for spring. When the snow melted, Liam helped the garden wake up and spread into the city. Weeds and mosses moved first, followed by delicate plants. New gardeners appeared, and many years later the whole city had blossomed. Liam’s favorite garden was still the place where it all began.

Luca lived in a mountain village in Mexico with Mama, Papa, Paco, and Lupe. Every day, she helped at home and cared for the burro Papito. Near Christmas, Padre Alvarez asked Mama and Luca to weave a new blanket for baby Jesus. They chose bright rainbow yarn. But Mama became sick, and Papa took her to town. Luca cared for Paco and Lupe. She tried to finish the blanket, but the yarn tangled. She felt sad and hid during the Christmas procession because she had no gift. An old woman told her Mama would be fine and Papa would bring her home soon. She said any gift given with love was beautiful. Luca picked green weeds and brought them to the church. She placed them by the manger and prayed. The weeds changed into green branches with shining red stars. People called them the flower of the Holy Night, the poinsettia.

On Grandparents Day, Spider brings Grandpa to school, where he teaches that spiders are not insects, spiders help stop insects taking over the world, and butterflies taste better with barbecue sauce. Spider learns to travel by wind: climb high, release silk, and catch wind, while Fly simply says, “fly.” Spider and his sister make a web on a water fountain and learn to stop, drop, and run from vacuums. Spider molts, brings the old skin to show-and-tell, and sleeps at Worm’s house. When Daddy Longlegs makes fun of Fly, Spider gives him lunch instead of “a piece of my mind.” Fly’s treehouse and Grandpa blow away in the wind. Grandpa travels to Paris, then admits he caught a breeze to the airport and napped in first class. Fly gets stuck in Spider’s web, so they play at her house. Spider learns never to fall asleep in a shoe and lists fears, including vacuums and big feet. Spider wishes people would get to know spiders, just as Spider and Fly do.

The racing season was going well for Lightning McQueen until a rookie named Jackson Storm won a race. Storm kept beating Lightning and was part of the next generation of Hightech Racers. He trained for hours and ignored a young fan who wanted an autograph.

Lightning went to Thomasville, Doc Hudson’s hometown, to train with Smokey and Cruz Ramirez. Cruz helped him practice while Smokey released tractors. Storm’s Igniter commercial made Lightning cringe.

At the Florida 500, Storm said he would win easily. During the race, cars crashed, and a yellow flag came out. Lightning went to the pit and asked Cruz to finish the race. Cruz felt nervous, but Lightning reminded her about their training. She caught Storm. When he pushed her toward the wall, Cruz drove up the wall and flipped over him. She landed in first place and won. Storm was shocked, while Cruz and Lightning celebrated. In Victory Lane, Cruz said, “I learned from the best,” and smiled at Lightning.

In October, an ugly pumpkin waits to be picked among 100,000 pumpkins, but each time things start looking up, the pumpkin is tricked. One bright, crispy day, a skeleton comes for pumpkins. The pumpkin asks for a ride, but the skeleton laughs and says, “No way!” The pumpkin says it is getting late and has no home, but the skeleton rolls his eye, says goodbye, and leaves it alone. In November, the pumpkin comes upon some trees and asks if it may stay, saying please. The trees smile, and one says, “Take off your boots and spread your roots.” The pumpkin realizes this is another cruel joke, shouts that it is ugly, and cries when rain begins. It takes shelter in a garden overrun with squash. There, it notices something very odd and thinks, “Oh my gosh! I’m a squash at last.” On Thanksgiving, the pumpkin finds where it fits in, and the feast can begin.

When Horus turned 11 on 11th November, he invited friends to a fancy-dress party and planned eleven foods and games. Guests arrived in costumes, including a pink admiral, zebra punk, rhino astronaut, swan Princess Pure, mouse musketeer, cat Cleopatra, crocodile judge, and giraffe twins dressed as angels. Horus served a magnificent banquet but told everyone to wait until the 11th hour. The chair game ended in a draw, and no one won snakes and ladders because Thomas ate the dice. During the games, Kilroy won the sack race, Oliver seemed to cheat at cards, Maxwell caught boastful Oliver out at cricket, and Horus was hit by a tennis ball. The guests finished tug-of-war and rushed to eat, but the feast had vanished. They denied stealing it, yet could not discover the thief. Horus cheered everyone with wholemeal sandwiches and revealed the birthday cake he had hidden. They ate on the lawn until evening and left satisfied, while the mystery remained unsolved.

Horus turned 11 on 11th November and planned a fancy-dress party for his friends. He sent invitations, made eleven kinds of food, and prepared eleven games. The guests came in wonderful costumes: a pink admiral, a punk zebra, an astronaut rhino, Princess Pure the swan, a tiger, a musketeer mouse, Cleopatra the cat, Sam the crocodile, and two giraffe angels. Horus welcomed them to his grand hall, but said they must wait until the 11th hour to eat. They played games, including races, cards, snakes and ladders, cricket, tennis, and tug-of-war. At last, the feast was gone! The guests said they did not steal it. Horus made healthy sandwiches and then showed them the birthday cake, which he had hidden in the kitchen. Everyone ate on the lawn and went home happy, but nobody discovered who stole the feast.

Minnie is happy because it is summer. She asks her friends what they want to do. Mickey wants to swim, Goofy wants to fish, Daisy wants to swing, Pluto wants to dig, Donald wants to hike, and Minnie wants to take pictures. Minnie knows they can go to Star Lake. At Star Lake, Goofy can fish and Mickey can swim. Daisy cannot swing at first, so Minnie calls Toodles. Toodles can help. Now Daisy can swing. Pluto wants to dig for a bone, but he cannot dig at first. Minnie calls Toodles again, and Toodles brings a map. Now Pluto can dig. Donald can hike up a hill. Then Pluto digs and finds a bone. Daisy swings, Goofy fishes, and Mickey swims. Minnie takes pictures. Happy summer!

There was a cat and a dog. The dog was not scary. The cat was there, right? Yes. The dog was wide awake, right? No. The cat saw a mouse, right? Yes. The dog knew something was up, right? No. The cat crept across the floor, right? Yes. The cat skittered after the mouse, right? Yes. The dog opened one eye, right? No. The cat skidded into the wall, right? Yes. The dog leaped off the couch, right? No. The dog still did nothing, right? No. Finally, the dog woke up and barked and barked. The cat and the dog lay side by side with their noses to the mouse hole. Then the mouse came out to say hi. What do you think?

Anne Frank was born in Germany and loved games, movies, writing, and her diary. Because Adolf Hitler and the Nazis persecuted Jewish people, her family moved to Amsterdam, but Germany invaded the Netherlands in 1940. New laws took away Jewish people's freedoms, and Anne's sister Margot received a call-up notice for a concentration camp. Soon after, Anne's family hid with the Van Pelses and Fritz Pfeffer in the Secret Annex, behind a bookcase in her father's office. They stayed there for two years and one month, living quietly, studying, and depending on helpers such as Miep, Johannes Kleiman, and Johan Voskuijl. Anne wrote to "Kitty," decorated her room, and found hope in the sky and a chestnut tree. The Nazis were defeated, but six million Jews, including Anne, were killed in the Holocaust. Miep gave Anne's diary to her father, and it became famous. Anne's story asks people to help others, oppose unfairness, and remember that people can be good at heart.

Anne was a Jewish girl born in Germany. Nazis hated Jewish people, so her family moved to Amsterdam. When Nazis came there, Jews lost rights and had to wear yellow stars. On her birthday, Anne got a diary and called it Kitty. Soon, her sister Margot received a call-up notice. The family hid in the Secret Annex with the Van Pelses and Fritz Pfeffer. They stayed quiet, studied, and shared little food while helpers brought supplies and books. Anne wrote, decorated her room, and looked at the sky and a chestnut tree from the attic. She hoped for goodness and believed people were truly good at heart. After two years and one month, Anne and six million other Jews were killed in the Holocaust. Miep found Anne’s diary and gave it to her father. It became a famous book. Anne’s story teaches people to help others, speak against unfairness, and keep hope alive.

On All Hallows' Eve, Pinocchio and Jiminy Cricket went shopping in town. Pinocchio heard a story about the Witch of Wal Dunkle Way, who lived in a dark cave and came to town to find a new animal friend. When they got home, the house was still and silent. Geppetto and Figaro were missing. Pinocchio worried that the witch had taken Figaro, but Jiminy said the witch was only a story. Then Jiminy became worried too, so Pinocchio led him up a twisted trail to the witch’s cave. A deer jumped in front of them, and an owl flew over them, but neither was the witch. At the cave, lots and lots of bats flew at them while Jiminy lit a match. They found no witch or Figaro and returned home. Geppetto was waiting by the cottage with Figaro beside him. Figaro was safe. Everyone hurried inside, just in case.

Wendy, John, and Michael Darling practiced flying, but Wendy got scared and fell because she thought she saw a ghost. Wendy explained that All Hallows' Eve was a holiday with ghosts, spooky things, turnips with faces, tricks, and spooky stories. Peter Pan decided to trick Captain Hook with an old white sheet and a pirate hat, pretending to be the ghost of Old Sea Dog, a scary story pirates told. Tinker Bell sprinkled the children with Pixie Dust, and they flew to Hook's ship. Something tapped Hook's shoulder, but it was only Smee. Peter softly called himself the old sea dog and flew at Hook, so the scared captain ran away. Wendy and her brothers laughed, then Wendy said they should go home. In the woods, a spooky glow appeared. Someone yelled, “Boo!” and Wendy gasped when she saw a floating turnip. Peter floated from the shadows and said, “That was the idea,” after Wendy said he scared her.

Mickey prepares a Halloween party with spooky decorations, snacks, and an old pirate costume. He hears noises, but a coat rack and a plastic skeleton scare him in the dark attic. During a thunderstorm, he carries the trunk downstairs and gets dressed. Outside, Pluto runs under a clothesline, and a sheet covers him. Rain makes the sheet stick to him, so he cannot see. Donald, Goofy, Minnie, and Daisy arrive, but Mickey does not answer. The lights go out, and strange noises come from upstairs. Mickey’s friends think they are in a haunted house and believe a monster is coming when they see something near the window and hear footsteps and rattling bones. The lights come back on, and they discover Mickey covered in spider webs. Then Pluto runs in wearing the wet sheet, and Minnie thinks the ghost has returned. Mickey reveals that the ghost is Pluto. He says Halloween is good for a scare, but friends are good for a laugh.

“Yeehaw!” Mater the tow truck built a junkyard jukebox, but it was missing one last tire. He tried to show Ramone, Lightning McQueen, Luigi, and Sheriff, but everyone was busy catching the little tractors. The tractors were loose all over Radiator Springs and caused trouble.
