They ruined Red’s flowers, and Luigi’s leaning tower of tires became a pile. Mater decided to put away his jukebox so he could help his friends. On the way, he turned on the jukebox and sang along. One tractor followed the music, and soon many others followed too. Mater made the music louder and learned that the tractors wanted to listen and dance. He towed the jukebox into his junkyard, and the tractors danced inside. Mater’s friends saw that he had rounded up the tractors and cheered, “Hip hip hooray for Mater!” With the tractors safe, everyone enjoyed the music. Mater said his jukebox had saved the day, and the little tractors returned whenever he played it.

Mr. Peanuts is an unusual squirrel who loves Christmas and checks his mailbox for cards. One day, cousin squirrel invites him to spend the holidays together. Mr. Peanuts packs his Christmas sweaters, clears a path with his snowblower, and drives his convertible through the snow. Cousin squirrel welcomes him and brews a hazelnut latte. They enjoy snowshoes and sledding, then build an igloo for hiding acorns. They also make a fashionable snowman and a gingerbread train, though Mr. Peanuts would rather eat it than ride it. They build a campfire for roasting chestnuts and sing carols. On Christmas Eve, they wrap presents, read by the fire, and try to wait for Santa, but fall asleep. On Christmas morning, they find lots of presents under the tree. Cousin squirrel gives Mr. Peanuts a gift, and Mr. Peanuts gives cousin squirrel peanuts. Cousin squirrel calls his gift the best present a squirrel could ask for, and Mr. Peanuts says his gift is just what he wanted.

Mama Duck lived in a soft nest with her five ducklings: Whittle, Waddle, Paddle, Puddle, and Little Quack. One day, she said it was time to leave the nest and invited them to paddle on the pond. The ducklings were scared, but Mama said, “You can do it. I know you can.” Whittle jumped into the pond, and Waddle followed. Then Paddle wiggled into the water, and Puddle leaped in too. Each duckling felt brave after seeing the others. Little Quack was still alone in the nest. He said he was too scared. Mama and the other ducklings told him they knew he could do it. Little Quack looked at the water. He sniffed it. He touched it with his foot. Then he closed his eyes. He plunged in. “I did it!” he cried. Mama said she always knew he could. At last, all five ducklings paddled in the pond, proud as can be.

Froggy woke up and saw snow outside. He wanted to play, but his mother said frogs should sleep all winter and wake when the snow melted. Froggy got dressed and went outside, but he had forgotten his pants. He flopped back inside, took off his clothes, put on his pants, and went out again. Then his mother reminded him that he had forgotten his shirt and coat. Froggy went inside once more, put them on, and returned to the snow. His mother checked him again. Froggy had his mittens, scarf, coat, shirt, pants, boots, socks, and hat, but he had forgotten his underwear. Froggy felt embarrassed and went inside. He removed his clothes, put on his long johns, and began dressing again. He put on one sock, one boot, and one mitten, but he was too tired to finish. Froggy went back to sleep and said, “Good night, Froggy.”

Misha loved making pictures from numbers and sounds, but she found making friends difficult. She did not know what to do or say, so she wondered if she would ever have friends. One evening, she used paints, pencils, and other tools to cut, stick, glue, and sew a group of friends. She felt comfortable with them, even though they could not play tennis, soccer, or catch. At a noisy party, Misha could not join the other children, so she found a quiet corner and made more friends. Josh saw her work and asked her to show him how. Misha worried he might do it wrong or ruin everything, but she taught him. He made things without ruining them, and creating together was even better. Sue, Misha, and Josh built a whole town for their friends. Josh encouraged Misha to show the others. She joined them, and the friends she made helped her make real friends.

On a winter night, snow drifts down from the sky, falling through sycamore branches and onto a husky’s bushy tail. Fish huddle beneath a frozen pond, while snowy dust blows across a cold glasshouse. Trees look like slender ghosts through its glass panels, and the last logs are covered with snow. Along the winterbrook, rocks and sticks freeze in the ice, and footprints disappear under falling snow. Trees shudder in a rising storm, while an empty nest holds its twigs together against the wind. By morning, orange hills glow in the early light. In sunlight, slush and snow soak into the cold ground; in shadow, they stay still and icy. Then winter thaws. New leaves, waking animals, bright sun, budding flowers, green grass, and robins appear. The pond shines blue, fish wake, streams run down hills, dew covers meadows, and birds return. Goodbye, winter. Hello, spring, you.

Nate the Great is a detective. One night, Oliver says someone tips over his garbage can. Nate eats a pancake, then asks Rosamond and Esmeralda questions. They did not take the garbage. Nate thinks an animal or bird did it. He reads about night animals at the library. That night, he hides and looks for the garbage snatcher. He finds a skunk near some garbage. Nate thinks the case is solved, and tells Oliver to use mothballs. But the garbage can tips over again. Nate makes a new plan. He hides inside the can and waits. Sludge, his dog, comes and knocks off the cover. Nate learns that Sludge is the garbage snatcher. Sludge was hungry and tired of pancakes, so he looked for his own snack. Nate gives Sludge a bone and dog food. Sludge may be a great detective when he learns to sniff more and snatch less. Nate is very tired, and his first night case is over.

Red Bird finds a red button and says red is his favorite, but the button does nothing. Bluebird presses it and is surprised, so surprise is not nothing. Red Bird presses it, but it does not surprise him, and he becomes sad. He tries again, and the button surprises him, making the birds happy. They press it many times, but then say it does nothing. The button seems to make Red Bird mad, then calm. He says it cannot make him calm, mad, happy, surprised, scared, icky, or anything else. Yellow Bird says the button makes him funny, so everyone chants, “Funny, funny, funny!” and “Button, button, button!” until there is a crash. They decide the button does everything. Red Bird asks what they should do, and the answer is “More nothing.” The button gives him a headache because it was on the wormhole. This book makes me want to press a button. A button is found: “Beep! Press.” “I am impressed.”

George, a good and curious little monkey, lived with his friend, the man with the yellow hat. On Valentine’s Day, they invited the neighborhood children to celebrate. First, George and his friends decorated the house. George loved balloons and wondered how big one could get. Next, they decorated cookies with three colors of icing and many sprinkles. George enjoyed icing his cookie and juggling. Then everyone made valentines. George made a special card for the man with the yellow hat. He noticed a big box and thought about what he could create. George put a bow and glitter on it and cut a hole in the top. He was making a fancy box for valentines from his friends. While everyone cleaned up, George became sleepy and climbed into the box. The man with the yellow hat and the children looked for him, but found only the box. When the man lifted the lid, George popped out. Everyone was happy, and the children cheered, “Happy Valentine’s Day, George!”

Oh no! Goofy's cat is lost. We look for the cat. First, we ask if the cat is on the dock. No, a cow is on the dock. Next, we ask if the cat is up in the tree. No, an elephant is up in the tree. Then we look at the beach, but a bird is at the beach. We ask if the cat is flying the kite, but a duck is flying the kite. We look for the cat playing in the snow, but a penguin is playing in the snow. We ask if the cat is swimming in the water. No, a fish is swimming in the water. We look for the cat riding around and around, but a pig is riding around and around. At last, we ask, “Do you see Goofy's cat?” Yes! Goofy's cat is in the basket. We found Goofy's cat. Thanks for helping.

On Christmas Eve, the house was quiet, and the children slept in their beds while Mama and the narrator rested. The narrator heard a loud clatter outside and ran to the window. In the moonlit snow, a tiny sleigh came with eight reindeer and St. Nicholas. St. Nicholas called, “Now Dasher, now Dancer, now Prancer and Vixen, on Comet, on Cupid, on Donner and Blitzen!” The reindeer flew to the roof with a sleigh full of toys. St. Nicholas came down the chimney. He wore fur and carried a bundle of toys. He had a round belly, rosy cheeks, a white beard, and a happy smile. The narrator laughed because St. Nicholas looked kind. St. Nicholas filled all the stockings. Then he went back up the chimney, whistled to his reindeer, and flew away. Before leaving, he called, “Merry Christmas to all, and to all a good night!”

Mommy says I will do things on my own one day because I have grown. I stack rocks and blocks, and I love to sing with Dad. Dad makes me laugh because he cannot sing and dances badly. Mommy says we can dance when we listen for the beat, and if we fall, we should get back on our feet. I like to sing, dance, and make things grow. Mommy tells me to be patient because growing is slow. She says to dig a hole and plant one seed. On a bright, warm day, I plant many seeds. After time passes, many cucumbers grow. Mommy says we have enough to share, and sharing shows that we care. Mommy shares with me, so I know she cares a lot. She says I must rest and sleep to grow up strong. I go to bed quietly and listen to Mommy, because I have lots to learn.

Our cow is eating Moo when she notices the farmer. The farmer puts a sign on his car that says, “Car for sale.” After that, her Cal goes in a police car. Our cow tries to explain this to the officer, but the officer does not believe her explanation and “doesn't buy it.” Because the officer refuses to accept what she says, Our cow has to walk home. The story ends with Our cow walking home after the farmer’s car has the “Car for sale” sign, her Cal has gone in a police car, and the officer has rejected her explanation.

Our cow is eating Moo. Then she notices the farmer. The farmer puts a sign on his car. The sign says, “Car for sale.” And her Cal says goes a police car. So she tries to explain to the officer. The officer does not buy it, so she has to walk home. The story begins with the cow eating Moo and noticing the farmer. It continues when the farmer places the sale sign on his car, and when the cow tries to explain to the officer. It ends with the officer not believing her and the cow walking home.

Abuela, the narrator’s grandmother, takes the child on a bus to El parque El Lindo. Abuela speaks mostly Spanish. She and the child imagine flying with a flock of birds. They would soar over the city, parks, streets, factories, trains, and the sea. They would greet people with “Buenos dias.” They would visit ships carrying mangoes, bananas, and papayas. Then they would circle the Statue of Liberty, which reminds Abuela of arriving in this country. Next, they would fly to the airport, Tio Pablo and Tia Elisa’s store, and Las nubes, where clouds look like animals and a chair. After resting, they would fly above Nuestra Casa and downtown, waving to Papa at his workplace. Then they return to the park and walk beside the lake. Abuela wants another adventure, so she takes the child’s hand and says, “Vamos.” The child loves Abuela because she likes adventures.

Three little bears enter a spooky old tree. One carries a light, one carries a stick, and one carries a rope. They dare to go inside. They climb a twisty old stair. Then one bear has a light, one has a stick, and one has the shivers. They find a giant key and a moving wall. The bears go through the wall and into a spooky old hall because they dare. There they see a great sleeping bear. One bear still has the light, but two bears have the shivers. The bears go over the great sleeping bear. Now all three bears have the shivers, and they have no light, stick, or rope. They need to get out. They go up a ladder, through the floor, down a slide, and out a door. The three little bears run fast and get home, safe at last.

Little Sock lives in a drawer and gets worn and dirty. For him, every day is the same. The other socks seem happy, but Little Sock dreams of something different. He hears about Sock City, a magical place where every day brings a new adventure. The only way there is through a secret tunnel in the back of the dryer. Late one night, Little Sock climbs out of the drawer and enters the tunnel. It is dark and scary, but Little Sock stays brave. Finally, he sees a light and reaches Sock City. He finds big socks, new socks, old socks, sporty socks, straight socks, polka dot socks, and even smelly socks. All around him, different socks do different things. Little Sock has the best time and cannot wait to return. He may bring his friends, because every day in Sock City is a new adventure.

A new family of punctuation marks moved to Alphabet City and went to a new school. Exclamation Point led the way, excited to begin, while Question Mark worried and Period promised to tell them when to stop. Comma kept pausing and asked them to wait.

At school, the letters were confused because the newcomers were not letters. The punctuation family joined the class and helped make words: Exclamation Point added excitement, Question Mark asked questions, and Period ended sentences. Comma tried to fit in, but he felt useless because he only separated letters. He secretly left.

Without Comma, the letters made words faster and faster until the words filled the room. Period tried to stop them, but the letters crashed into one another and spilled into the hall. The punctuation marks found Comma and explained that every mark had a job. They brought him back. Comma stood among the letters and helped keep everything in order. The family told the letters, “Words need punctuation, and punctuation needs words.”

At five o’clock, the shop closes, and the donuts seem to sleep. Soon, donuts fill the shop, covered with golden sprinkles, frosting, jelly, maple, or powdered sugar. Sprinkles runs away, and the donuts travel in donut cars, trucks, trains, and a pirate ship. They play sports, dance in sprinkle rain, visit a doctor, and feel empty inside. At a donut farm, a robber runs away with money, but his police car stalls. A dog meets the robber, who is caught, and the dog returns. The donuts celebrate and sing because donuts can do anything. Wanting a long lifespan, they make a donut plan, with help from the cop, the crook, Pan, and Captain Hook. They test it, saying it must work better than the airplane. When the sun rises and the shop opens, the trays and bowls are empty. The donuts have a knack for holes. After loud knocking, someone suggests playing, but the final suggestion is to nap.

Judy Hopes and Nick Wild chase a thief in a stolen catering van through Zootopia, causing a lot of damage. Chef Bogo sends the partners to a class for partners in crisis, but Judy thinks they already work well together. At Zootopia’s 100th anniversary gala, Judy spots the stolen vans and meets Linkxley. Then Gary D. Snake appears, grabs Milton and the Lynxley journal, and says it will prove snakes are not bad. Judy and Nick help Gary escape, so the police think they are criminals. With help from Fufu and the clever beaver Nibbles Maple Stick, they follow Gary to Copenhofen. Gary and Pawbert rescue Judy, and Gary’s snake vision reveals a map. It leads to Angus’s lost home in Reptile Raven. Pawbert poisons Judy and tries to destroy the truth, but Gary saves her. Nick escapes, and the friends reach Reptile Raven. They find proof that Angus D. Snake created Zootopia, closing the case and proving Judy and Nick are great partners.

Miranda’s mother receives a postcard announcing that she will compete on The Twenty Thousand Dollar Pyramid on April 27. Miranda remembers a note from someone who is gone, asking her to write what happened during the fall and winter. Her mother prepares by marking a calendar, practicing speed rounds with Miranda and Richard, and hiding a spare key in the fire hose. The game uses seven words in thirty seconds, and winning the speed round leads to the winner’s circle and big money. Miranda explains her name, her life as a latchkey child, and her close friendship with Sal. After Sal and Miranda begin seeing the Laughing Man on their corner, he chants “Book bag, pocket shoe” and kicks at traffic. One fall day, a boy in a green army coat punches Sal and hits his face. Miranda tries to get him home, but Sal shuts his apartment door, ending their friendship.

Mom gets a postcard saying she will be a contestant on The Twenty Thousand Dollar Pyramid on April 27, after three years of trying. She has 21 days to practice, so Miranda writes seven-word cards, and Mom practices speed rounds with Richard. Richard is Mom’s boyfriend, and he teaches Miranda to tie knots. Miranda is a latchkey child who waits alone after school, so Mom hides a spare key in the fire hose. Miranda also keeps notes from someone who asked her to write the story of what happened that fall and winter. She thinks the true story began when Sal got punched. Miranda and Sal used to walk home together past the Laughing Man and the boys near a garage. One October day, a kid in a green army coat blocks them and punches Sal in the stomach and face. Sal cries, bleeds, and runs home after the Laughing Man speaks to them. Sal shuts his door on Miranda, and Miranda says this was the end of their friendship.

Three bears lived together in a house in the woods. They were a great huge bear, a middlesized bear, and a little small wee bear. One morning, they made porridge and went outside while it cooled. Goldilocks came to the house, entered, and tasted the porridge. The great huge bear’s was too hot, the middlesized bear’s was too cold, and the little small wee bear’s was just right, so she ate it all. She tried their chairs too; the little small wee bear’s was just right, but it broke beneath her. Upstairs, she tried their beds and fell asleep in the little small wee bear’s bed because it was just right. The bears came home and saw that someone had used their porridge, chairs, and beds. The little small wee bear found Goldilocks sleeping and cried, “Somebody has been lying in my bed. And here she is.” Goldilocks woke, jumped from the window, and ran away. The bears never saw her again.

The speaker gives a long list of playful commands. First, the listener claps hands, stomps feet, shakes arms, sits down, rubs a tummy, and pats a head. The listener finds something yellow and something red, reaches for the sky, wiggles toes, and touches a nose with a tongue. The listener roars like a lion, growls like a bear, gives a kiss, wiggles fingers, and slaps a knee. The speaker says, “I’ll tickle you if you tickle me,” then asks the listener to find something big and something small, spin without falling, close their eyes, count to four, and do a somersault. Next, the listener spreads feet, looks upside down, makes a silly face, acts like a clown, hops like a bunny, and flaps like a bird. The listener stays quiet as a mouse and does not say a word, then tells a name, age, and secret. The listener purrs like a kitten, barks like a dog, crawls like a baby, jumps like a frog, counts fingers and toes, and wiggles eyebrows and nose. Finally, the listener shows a smile and frown, stands on one foot, jumps up and down, flies like an airplane high in the sky, and waves bye-bye.

Pig was a pug who lived in a house with a wiener dog named Trevor. Pig was greedy and selfish, and he was almost never nice to Trevor. Trevor said Pig had great toys. He suggested that sharing might make playing more fun. Pig refused. He grumbled, “They’re mine. Go away,” and told Trevor to keep his paws off. Pig said he would never share and gathered his toys into a big pile. With a satisfied smile, he howled from the top and shouted, “Mine, mine, mine, mine!” Trevor saw that the pile was wobbling and cried, “Oh dear me! Watch out up there!” But pugs cannot fly. Later, things were different. Pig shared his toys, and Trevor became his friend. They played together while Pig was “on the mend.” Pig had changed from keeping all his toys for himself to sharing them with Trevor.

Cinderella, a kind girl, lives with her cruel stepmother and selfish stepsisters, Anastasia and Drizella. When the King announces a royal ball for the Prince, Cinderella may go only if she finishes her work and finds a dress. Her mouse and bird friends make her a lovely gown, but the stepsisters tear it apart. Cinderella weeps until her Fairy Godmother appears. Magic turns a pumpkin into a coach, mice into white horses, and Cinderella’s rags into a shimmering gown with glass slippers. The Fairy Godmother warns that the spell will end at midnight. At the ball, Prince Charming dances with Cinderella, but she runs away when the clock chimes twelve and loses a slipper. The next day, the Prince searches for the girl whose foot fits it. Cinderella’s friends free her from the attic, and she tries on the slipper. It fits perfectly, so she marries the Prince. Cinderella says, “If you keep on believing, your dreams will come true,” and they live happily ever after.

This is Max, a sweet-looking kitten who is sometimes dressed in bows. Max dislikes the bows because he is fearless and brave. He wants to chase a mouse, but first he must learn what Mouse looks like. He searches in a can, but Mouse is not there. Fly says a mouse scurried by, Fish says one dashed outside, Birds say Mouse scooted away, and Elephant says Mouse passed by. Then Monster says Mouse is asleep and Max may catch him quickly. Max thinks the huge creature is Mouse. He wakes it by bouncing on its head and says he is Max the Brave, who chases mice and might eat it. Max notices the creature has very big teeth, and then comes “Gulp, gulp. Yuck!” Max decides that chasing mice is not all it is cracked up to be. He does not need to be Max the Brave all the time, unless he is out chasing monsters.

Penelope was the only T-Rex in her school, so classmates often saw only a dinosaur. She loved playing, reading, drawing, and especially making music. When Mrs. Noodleman announced the talent show, Penelope signed up to perform “Rock and roll,” even though she felt nervous. At rehearsal, Penelope froze and could not sing or play guitar. She worried that dinosaurs could not rock and roll, crossed her name off the list, and told Daddy Rex she was “just a dinosaur.” Daddy Rex showed her a family photo album and explained that being a T-Rex was only part of who she was; she was also kind and caring, creative and adventurous, and could be anything she wanted. Penelope returned to the signup sheet. Her classmates asked to join her band, the Mustard Seeds, giving her courage. At the show, Penelope sang and played guitar. She and the Mustard Seeds came in second place, just behind Mabel Hastings and her dancing pony. That was okay with Penelope because she loved ponies.

Rey Montague was born in Little Rock, Arkansas, in 1935. At seven, she toured a submarine, and learning that engineers had built it inspired her dream of engineering. Her mother warned that racism, sexism, and segregated schools might block her, but Rey studied hard, taught herself mathematics, and graduated with honors. When college refused to let a Black student study engineering, she earned a business degree instead. In Washington, D.C., Rey became a Navy clerk typist, learned ship-design work and computers, and was promoted after completing her own and the engineers’ work during an illness. Although her boss treated her poorly because of her race, she kept working. When the president ordered a ship quickly, Rey created a computer system that completed its blueprints in 18 hours and 26 minutes. The ship was built, but she was excluded from its launch. She later became the Navy’s first woman to lead ship design and earned honors as a professional engineer. Her story says to study hard, stay focused, and never quit.

Rey Montague was born in Little Rock, Arkansas. At seven, her granddad took her to see a submarine. Rey asked who made it. “Engineers,” he said, and Rey decided to become an engineer. Rey was smart and worked hard, but schools were segregated, and some people said Black girls could not be engineers. Her mother told her to stay strong. Rey studied math and taught herself. College would not let her study engineering, so she studied business and graduated with honors. In Washington, D.C., Rey worked for the Navy as a clerk typist. She learned ship design and computers. When engineers were sick, Rey did their work and was promoted. She made a computer program that designed a ship in 18 hours. The ship was built, but she was not invited to its launch. Rey kept working. She became the Navy’s first woman to lead ship design and became an engineer. Her story says: work hard, stay focused, and do not give up.

On a farm, many baby animals have special names. A baby sheep is a lamb and runs in meadow grass. Kittens are baby cats; they play on the farm and sleep together in the Big Red Barn after the farmer gives them cow’s milk at night. A rabbit and guinea pigs live in tiny hutches. The rabbit sniffs noses with kittens and puppies because they are friends. A tired baby donkey sits down while someone tries to lead him with carrots tied to a stick. He says, “I know that trick.” Ducklings swim in the pond, but chicks cannot swim, so they stay out of the water and look for worms. Piglets sleep on clean straw and call for their mother if chased. Puppies stay close to the stable and bark at a shoe they pretend is a big cat. Baby goats, called kids, bump heads, while their father has horns and a pointed beard. Cygnets will grow white feathers and long necks, and a gosling will become a big Gray Goose. A foal can walk at birth and gallops after a week. A Shetland pony carries a kitten and puppy. A calf says, “Moo. It is time for lunch.”

Kindness includes saying hello and being patient. It includes helping and cheering. It includes trading treats and giving a boost. It includes taking turns and sharing. It includes offering comfort and visiting. It includes reaching out. The story names many kinds of kindness: saying hello, being patient, helping, cheering, trading treats, giving a boost, taking turns, sharing, offering comfort, visiting, and reaching out. These acts show kindness in many ways. Kindness is what makes us strong. The story ends with this repeated idea: kindness is what makes us strong.

On a beautiful summer afternoon in Bear Country, Brother, Sister, and Honeybear decorated their bikes with red, white, and blue ribbons for the Fourth of July parade. Papa sewed parade decorations and put on his old army uniform, while Mama explained that the holiday celebrated the birthday of their country. She and Papa told the cubs how settlers created a new country after refusing to be ruled by a faraway king. They signed a famous paper on July 4, and a war followed before they won. On July 4, the family joined the parade. The cubs rode with other children, and Papa marched with army bears. Bands played “The Stars and Bears Forever,” while fire engines, antique cars, tractors, wagons, floats, scouts, and cheerleaders passed by. Fertie Facel won first prize for his patriotic bike, and the cubs won second prize. That evening, fireworks filled the sky. Papa said, “God bless our country,” and everyone answered, “Amen.”

At first, narrator and other beans were one big pot of beans. They spent time together. Then narrator’s friends became famous cool beans because they could play guitar, draw superheroes, or jump high. Narrator tried sunglasses, slicked-back hair, and swaggering, but was still picked last and felt like an uncool bean with no special skills. The friends stopped spending time together, and narrator kept to himself. One day, narrator dropped lunch on his loafers, and a cool bean helped clean it up. After narrator scraped his knee, another cool bean dusted him off. Later, classmates laughed when narrator did not answer the teacher, but a cool bean whispered, “Hey, the teacher asked you to read from page 32,” and winked. Her kindness gave narrator confidence. He began spending time with the cool beans again. He realized that coolness means helping someone, giving a wink or nod, and pointing someone in the right direction. When asked, “You need a hand?” he answered, “Yes, please.”

A grape says he is sour because he remembers hurts and holds grudges. A banana bumped him, an orange did not call, and a lime kept his scarf. Long ago, he lived with his family in a big bunch. His grandparents taught him to be kind, forgiving, considerate, grateful, and sweet. On his birthday, he planned a big party, but nobody came. He felt hurt and became a grumpy grape. One day, the grape was late to meet Lenny. Lenny was angry and held a grudge. The grape saw that Lenny acted like him. He noticed the pretty evening and felt calm. At home, he found his birthday invitation. He had written May 31 instead of May 21. The empty party was his mistake. After that, he talked, listened, and worked things out. He let go of his grudges and became less sour. He and Lenny became friends again. The grape says kindness, forgiveness, consideration, and gratitude can make life sweet.

A boy named Buzz had a pet fly named Fly Guy. Fly Guy could say, “Buzz.” One day, Dad asked, “Who wants to go for a ride?” Buzz and Fly Guy went with him. With the windows down, wind blew Fly Guy out of the car and into a truck. Buzz cried, “Follow that truck!” The truck driver spit Fly Guy into a motorboat. Buzz followed the boat, but Fly Guy jumped away when he saw a bug on a hook. He landed on a circus train. A sleepy elephant blew him onto an airplane. The pilot turned on the wipers, so Fly Guy flew away. Then a rocket roared up. Buzz and Dad followed it and landed the rocket. Buzz asked if Fly Guy was safe. Dad said the rocket did not take them to space. They rode home, and Fly Guy said, “More rides.”

Long ago, segregation kept black and white people apart. They could not always live in the same neighborhoods, eat in the same restaurants, or attend the same schools. The United States government said segregation was wrong. Ruby Bridges went to a black kindergarten, but William Franz Elementary School was closer to her home. In 1961, Ruby was in first grade. Her mother took her there, and Marshalls kept them safe. Some people yelled at Ruby and took their children away. Ruby stayed with her teacher, Mrs. Henry. She learned math and reading, but wished for friends. After many months, children returned, and Ruby was very happy. People wrote about her bravery. Eleanor Roosevelt sent her a letter, and Norman Rockwell painted her picture. Ruby grew up, married, and had children. She and Mrs. Henry met again on television and stayed in touch. Now black and white children can attend the same schools. Ruby visits schools, tells her story, and says people can be friends and should be kind to each other.

In Little Nook, Rabbit, Boore, Beaver, and Squirrel promise to help Monster’s baby monster sleep. Monster leaves and tells the baby to behave, but she jumps from bed and plays. She makes a den, throws food and books, rides Beaver, steals cake, and swings on Squirrel’s tail. At last, she curls up in a blanket nest, and the tired babysitters fall asleep too. The baby wakes, takes cake, and escapes while they sleep. Rabbit finds crumbs, so the friends follow her trail through the forest. They find berry footprints at Boore’s den, broken sticks at Beaver’s dam, acorn shells in Squirrel’s tree, and mud at Rabbit’s log, but the baby is gone each time. The friends worry because they were trusted to care for her. At the forest’s end, they find the baby asleep in her bed. Monster thanks them, and they slump down, relieved. Then they remember their homes are still a mess.

Sarah does not want to get out of bed for her first day at a new school. She says she hates the school because she does not know anyone and must start over. Mr. Hartwell tells Sarah she must go and says she may meet new friends. Sarah gets dressed, says her head hurts, and walks with Mr. Hartwell to the car. On the drive, her hands are cold and clammy, and she feels like she cannot breathe. When they arrive, Sarah says she feels sick. Mr. Hartwell says she will love the school once she starts. Mrs. Burton, the principal, comes to the car and takes Sarah inside. She leads Sarah through the crowded halls and says everyone feels nervous on the first day. In the classroom, the children sit quietly and look up. Mrs. Burton brings Sarah to the front and introduces her as their new teacher, Mrs. Sarah Jane Hartwell.

Piggy shows Walt a new book about watching grass grow. As they read, the words say, “We are growing,” and Piggy suddenly grows. Soon, everyone grows in different ways: tall, curly, silly, pointy, crunchy, or dandiest. A dandelion is called a weed, but it says it has been called worse. Walt cannot name what he is because he is not the tallest, curliest, silliest, pointiest, crunchiest, or dandiest. The others try to help him think, but their excitement makes a mess. They also lose the things they had grown into, so they agree they will grow again. Before that happens, they clean the place. Then Walt realizes that he is neat, and the others agree that he is the neatest. They call themselves the stumplingest. Piggy and the others say the book is the funniest and that they love to read. At the end, they say they are the radius d end.

The song begins with “Let’s laugh, play, and sing.” It asks, “What are the parts of a baby?” and promises to tell everything. It points to baby’s eyes, nose, fingers, and toes. Then it names the baby’s head and hair, and says a hat goes on the head. Next come the ears, lips, knees, and hips. The baby’s tummy is named too. If tickling is a problem, the baby can turn over to show the bottom. The song then names the elbows and shoulders. The shoulders are shown shrugging. It names the baby’s arms and says they are made for super hugging. The song names these many parts as things people can see. It repeats that these are so many parts of baby, but these are just the things we see. At the end, it says the biggest part of baby is the love you get from me.

Every day, babies are everywhere, and a mama cares for them through busy nights and days. She changes diapers, washes shirts, burps babies, feeds them with a bottle, breast, or baby-led food, and cleans up drool, spit-up, and puréed fruit. Babies crawl, climb, eat dirt, and cry during tummy time, while the mama feels tired, overwhelmed, and messy. She swaddles a baby, turns on white noise, sings one more song, and walks, rocks, or takes midnight drives to help the baby sleep. She watches for gas and teething and enjoys the baby’s smile. When the fridge is empty, she goes shopping in yoga pants and dry shampoo, even though the stroller will not fit and the baby woke at five. There are tears, advice from strangers, sleepless nights, and baby blues. But other mamas help her feel less alone. The hard baby days pass, and motherhood makes it all worthwhile in the end.

Riley is 11 and lives a happy life with a loving family and great friends. Inside her mind, Joy works at headquarters with Anger, Fear, Disgust, and Sadness. Joy wants Riley to be happy. Anger keeps life fair, Fear keeps Riley safe, Disgust keeps Riley away from gross things, and Sadness makes Riley sad. Riley's memories are stored in spheres, and happy memories are yellow. Her five personality islands are Family Island, Honesty Island, Hockey Island, Friendship Island, and Goofball Island. You take charge, tell them it is time for bed, and start brushing their teeth. They argue and promise to do it later, so you squeeze out toothpaste and help with back molars. Then you get them into pajamas and move them toward the bedroom while phones, magazines, television, the cat, and dog distract them. If they sit down, they are hard to move, and small things upset them when they face getting into bed. You remain calm, do not negotiate, and get them into bed. Parents want favorite bedtime stories, usually three, and unexpected problems appear, such as a missing pillow, checking the dog, snacks, or water. You handle each incident calmly, tuck them in, kiss them goodnight, and take their cell phones.
